title: Contralateral cane support
stem: A client prescribed a cane for painful left-knee arthritis walks farther when the knee is unloaded. Which technique should the nurse reinforce?
options: Hold the cane in the left hand
Use whichever hand feels easiest each step
Change to two-handed walker use without reassessment
Hold the cane in the right hand
why: Same-side use provides less effective unloading of the painful knee.
Inconsistent technique reduces predictable support during gait.
A device change requires assessment rather than substituting for cane teaching.
Contralateral support reduces loading of the painful left knee.
takeaway: Use a cane on the side opposite the weaker leg.
learningObjective: Use a cane on the side opposite the weaker leg.

title: Walker rising
stem: A client safely walks with a walker but it tips toward them when they rise from a chair. The chair has armrests. Which change should the nurse teach?
options: Have a helper stabilize the walker for every rise
Rock several times while holding the walker
Push from the chair armrests before grasping the walker
Place the walker farther ahead before rising
why: This may limit movement but does not teach the independent technique the client can use.
Momentum while pulling can still tip the walker toward the client.
The stable chair supports rising without pulling the walker backward.
Extra reaching reduces stability and does not remove the pulling force.
takeaway: Rise using the chair before grasping the walker.
learningObjective: Rise using the chair before grasping the walker.

title: Crutch pressure
stem: An adult using axillary crutches develops hand tingling after walking. The nurse observes body weight resting on the pads. Which correction addresses the observed problem?
options: Encourage a tighter hand grip only
Transfer weight through the handgrips
Add thicker padding beneath each armpit
Schedule shorter walks without changing technique
why: Grip strength alone does not change weight resting on the axillary pads.
This relieves the observed nerve-compressing axillary pressure.
Padding does not eliminate pressure from body weight on the axillae.
Rest may reduce symptoms temporarily but leaves the cause in place.
takeaway: Keep body weight off the axillary crutch pads.
learningObjective: Keep body weight off the axillary crutch pads.

title: Wheelchair footplates
stem: A client cleared for a stand-pivot transfer is seated in a wheelchair. The brakes are locked, but the feet remain on the footplates. What should happen next?
options: Move footplates aside and place the feet securely
Apply a transfer belt and start the stand
Move the chair closer while the client begins rising
Recline the backrest before the stand
why: Stable floor contact is needed before initiating the stand.
A belt does not remove the footplate obstruction.
Chair position should be set before the client starts moving.
Reclining does not correct foot placement for this transfer.
takeaway: Clear wheelchair footplates before a standing transfer.
learningObjective: Clear wheelchair footplates before a standing transfer.

title: Stroke shoulder support
stem: A client with a flaccid arm after stroke reports shoulder discomfort during repositioning. Which change best addresses the likely mechanical cause?
options: Reposition less often to avoid all discomfort
Give the next prescribed analgesic before every turn
Encourage the client to lift with the weak arm
Support the affected arm throughout movement
why: Reduced movement leaves pressure risks and the mechanical cause unresolved.
Analgesia may help but does not correct unsupported limb traction.
A flaccid arm cannot provide reliable weight-bearing support.
Support limits traction on the weak shoulder.
takeaway: Protect a weak shoulder from traction during movement.
learningObjective: Protect a weak shoulder from traction during movement.

title: Passive range
stem: During prescribed passive elbow movement, a client with limited mobility reports pulling discomfort at the same point each time. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase repetitions while keeping the same painful range
Repeat after the next analgesic without changing the endpoint
Stop at the comfortable limit and reassess
Move slightly beyond the limit to lengthen the muscle
why: More repetitions do not make the painful endpoint appropriate.
Pain relief alone does not make the previously painful range appropriate.
The painful limit guides safe movement and may require plan revision.
Pushing through pain may injure restricted tissues.
takeaway: Perform passive movement gently within the tolerated range.
learningObjective: Perform passive movement gently within the tolerated range.

title: Active movement choice
stem: After stroke, a client can move the right arm through its full range but needs assistance on the left. Which plan best uses the client's abilities?
options: Complete right-arm exercises only on therapy days
Use active right-arm exercise with individualized left-arm assistance
Use passive movement for both arms to maintain symmetry
Focus exercise only on the weak left arm
why: Unnecessary restriction reduces opportunities for safe practice.
The plan preserves voluntary activity while addressing weaker-side needs.
This removes useful voluntary activity on the stronger side.
The stronger arm also benefits from ongoing functional use.
takeaway: Use active movement when the client can participate.
learningObjective: Use active movement when the client can participate.

title: Logroll alignment
stem: A postoperative client has a prescribed logroll technique. Which actions follow that plan? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on the movement sequence before turning
Keep shoulders and hips aligned during the turn
Raise the shoulders first to make the turn easier
Use a one-person turn because the client is light
why: Coordinated timing supports a controlled movement as one unit.
Alignment limits twisting targeted by the logroll order.
Moving the shoulders separately introduces trunk rotation.
Required assistance depends on alignment needs and ability, not weight alone.
takeaway: Coordinate a logroll to avoid twisting the trunk.
learningObjective: Coordinate a logroll to avoid twisting the trunk.

title: Gait endurance
stem: A rehabilitation client aims to walk to the dining room. They walk 20 metres steadily but become exhausted at 30 metres without chest pain or desaturation. Which plan best supports progress?
options: Complete the full route once daily despite exhaustion
Use a wheelchair for every trip until endurance is normal
Increase gait speed to finish before fatigue occurs
Repeat manageable distances with planned rests
why: Repeated excessive fatigue may undermine safe participation.
Exclusive substitution removes an opportunity to build walking tolerance.
Faster walking may increase exertion rather than reduce it.
Graded practice builds tolerance without repeatedly exceeding it.
takeaway: Progress mobility using observed tolerance and planned rest.
learningObjective: Progress mobility using observed tolerance and planned rest.

title: Weight-bearing clarification
stem: After ankle surgery, an adult has a right non-weight-bearing order and has practised transfers. Which observed action requires correction?
options: Adjusting clothing while seated before transferring
Requesting a rest after a transfer
Briefly loading both feet while standing to adjust clothing
Using the taught transfer device with staff nearby
why: Seated preparation reduces standing demands.
Rest responds appropriately to exertion during restricted mobility.
Even brief right-foot loading violates the current restriction.
The trained method supports adherence to the restriction.
takeaway: Apply the prescribed weight-bearing restriction during every transfer.
learningObjective: Apply the prescribed weight-bearing restriction during every transfer.

title: Seated alignment
stem: A wheelchair user reports thigh discomfort after meals. Their pelvis has slid forward and both feet dangle. Which intervention should the nurse prioritize?
options: Encourage repeated scooting back during every meal
Request seating reassessment and support the feet
Add a softer cushion without reassessing seat height
Shorten meals so the client sits for less time
why: Repeated correction alone does not address an unsuitable fit.
Seat and footrest fit directly affect the observed alignment problem.
A cushion may further raise the client above the footrests.
This limits exposure but leaves the seating cause unresolved.
takeaway: Match wheelchair seating to body dimensions and support needs.
learningObjective: Match wheelchair seating to body dimensions and support needs.

title: Bed mobility cue
stem: A client with mild weakness can bridge safely and wants to regain bed mobility. Which assistance best supports that goal?
options: Give stepwise cues and allow the client to contribute
Complete the turn quickly with two staff
Wait for full independent strength before practising
Use a mechanical aid for every movement regardless of ability
why: Supported practice uses the ability needed for the stated goal.
Staff movement alone does not practise the client's retained skill.
Safe graded participation can begin before complete independence.
Automatic equipment use may bypass feasible active participation.
takeaway: Invite safe participation in bed mobility.
learningObjective: Invite safe participation in bed mobility.

title: Contracture prevention
stem: An immobile client's ankles remain pointed downward on the mattress. Which measures belong in an individualized prevention plan? Select all that apply.
options: Include regular prescribed ankle movement
Place a pillow only beneath the knees
Rely on the mattress to position the feet
Support the ankles in the prescribed neutral alignment
why: Movement helps preserve available joint range.
This does not address the downward ankle position.
The observed resting posture shows the mattress is insufficient.
Neutral positioning limits prolonged shortening in plantar flexion.
takeaway: Combine alignment and movement to reduce contracture risk.
learningObjective: Combine alignment and movement to reduce contracture risk.

title: Hip precautions
stem: A client returning home after hip surgery must follow a specified hip-flexion limit. Which home detail should prompt equipment review?
options: The client has practised using a long-handled aid
The dining chair has firm armrests
The preferred chair is low and deeply cushioned
The toilet has the prescribed raised seat
why: Adaptive equipment can reduce bending during dressing.
Armrests assist a controlled rise without requiring a low seat.
Low seating can require flexion beyond the prescribed limit.
The raised seat supports the ordered movement limit.
takeaway: Match furniture and self-care aids to prescribed movement precautions.
learningObjective: Match furniture and self-care aids to prescribed movement precautions.

title: Transfer belt placement
stem: A client can partly bear weight but a standard transfer belt would cross a painful fresh abdominal incision. The transfer is not urgent. What is the best plan?
options: Use a single-person pivot without any support
Reassess for a suitable alternative transfer method
Place additional gauze under the same tight belt
Give analgesia and use the belt unchanged
why: Removing equipment without reassessment may create a fall risk.
The assistance should avoid injuring the surgical site.
Padding does not reliably remove incisional compression.
Pain relief does not eliminate mechanical stress on the incision.
takeaway: Adapt transfer equipment to wounds and other attachments.
learningObjective: Adapt transfer equipment to wounds and other attachments.

title: Fatigue during grooming
stem: A client with stable chronic lung disease wants to continue grooming independently but becomes breathless while standing. Which plan best meets that goal?
options: Arrange seated grooming with supplies within reach
Have staff complete all grooming
Move grooming to after a full bath
Encourage faster movements to shorten the task
why: Sitting and reduced reaching conserve energy for independent care.
This removes independence the client may retain with adaptation.
Fatigue after bathing may make the task harder.
Rushing can increase breathlessness and reduce control.
takeaway: Conserve energy by pacing and simplifying valued daily activities.
learningObjective: Conserve energy by pacing and simplifying valued daily activities.

title: One-handed dressing
stem: A client with right-arm weakness becomes frustrated trying to insert that arm after dressing the stronger arm. Which change should the nurse suggest?
options: Start with the stronger arm and pull the shirt over the weak elbow
Ask staff to dress both arms routinely
Place the shirt over the head before inserting either arm
Dress the weaker arm first
why: Starting on the strong side restricts fabric available around the weaker arm.
This bypasses an achievable adaptive technique.
This sequence limits access and garment movement around the weaker limb.
The loose garment allows easier placement of the less mobile limb.
takeaway: Dress the weaker limb first using adaptable clothing.
learningObjective: Dress the weaker limb first using adaptable clothing.

title: Clothing removal
stem: A client with left-arm weakness struggles to remove a shirt because the stronger arm remains inside it. Which technique should the nurse teach?
options: Ask staff to remove every garment
Pull the shirt over the head before freeing either arm
Remove the stronger arm first
Begin with the weaker arm every time
why: Automatic substitution does not build the available skill.
Freeing the stronger arm first provides assistance around the weak limb.
The freed arm can assist gentle removal from the weak side.
This keeps the useful arm enclosed during the harder part.
takeaway: Undress the stronger limb first to assist the weaker limb.
learningObjective: Undress the stronger limb first to assist the weaker limb.

title: Reacher use
stem: A client under temporary bending restrictions wants to retrieve a dropped sock independently. Which response best supports rehabilitation?
options: Encourage a seated forward reach to the floor
Offer the prescribed reacher and supervise practice
Pick it up immediately each time
Ask the client to wait for movement restrictions to end
why: Seated bending may still breach the prescribed limit.
The aid permits the task without prohibited bending.
Routine substitution prevents practice of a suitable adaptive skill.
The task is possible now with approved equipment.
takeaway: Use adaptive equipment to preserve function within restrictions.
learningObjective: Use adaptive equipment to preserve function within restrictions.

title: Walking aid reassessment
stem: A client who uses a walker safely on vinyl repeatedly catches its legs on the bedroom carpet. What should the nurse do first?
options: Assess the route and the suitability of the walker
Switch to a cane immediately
Advise the client to take larger steps
Have a helper lift the walker legs at the carpet edge
why: The surface-specific difficulty may need environmental or equipment changes.
Less support may be unsuitable without gait assessment.
Larger steps may reduce control without resolving equipment catch.
Ad hoc assistance does not establish route or device suitability.
takeaway: Reassess equipment and environment when gait performance changes.
learningObjective: Reassess equipment and environment when gait performance changes.

title: Resting hand position
stem: An immobile client has an individually fitted hand splint. Which care actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Follow the individual wearing schedule
Extend wearing time after a missed session without advice
Add thick padding to relieve tightness without reassessment
Inspect the skin at scheduled splint removal
why: The schedule balances alignment with tissue tolerance.
Extra wear may exceed skin tolerance.
Padding can further tighten a fitted device.
The device may cause hidden pressure or friction.
takeaway: Monitor skin and comfort with prescribed splints.
learningObjective: Monitor skin and comfort with prescribed splints.

title: Turning with tubes
stem: An adult with a urinary catheter and wound drain needs to turn in bed. Which preparation most directly prevents movement-related injury?
options: Ask the client to monitor the insertion sites while moving
Delay the turn until the next drain measurement
Arrange enough tubing slack and clear the turn path
Empty both containers regardless of their current fill
why: The client may not see or control all attachments.
Measurement timing does not remove the need for repositioning.
This reduces traction and avoids tubing becoming trapped.
Emptying alone does not prevent traction during the turn.
takeaway: Arrange tubes before movement to prevent traction and obstruction.
learningObjective: Arrange tubes before movement to prevent traction and obstruction.

title: Supported side lying
stem: A client without positioning restrictions reports knees rubbing together and hip discomfort in side lying. Which adjustment addresses both findings?
options: Ask the client to stay supine for every rest period
Support the upper leg with a pillow between the knees
Place another pillow beneath the head only
Raise the entire head of the bed
why: A comfortable preferred position may be possible with support.
Support separates bony surfaces and improves alignment.
Head support does not address hip or knee alignment.
Elevation does not separate the knees or support the upper leg.
takeaway: Support the limbs and separate bony surfaces in side lying.
learningObjective: Support the limbs and separate bony surfaces in side lying.

title: Bed exercise evaluation
stem: A client's mobility goal is transferring to the toilet with one helper. Which finding best indicates progress after a week of practice?
options: Transfers now require one helper rather than two
The exercise chart contains every planned session
Passive hip range remains unchanged
The client spends longer sitting in bed
why: Reduced assistance directly reflects the stated functional goal.
Completion records activity but not transfer ability.
Joint range alone does not show improved transfers.
Bed sitting does not demonstrate the transfer goal.
takeaway: Evaluate mobility plans against the client's functional goals.
learningObjective: Evaluate mobility plans against the client's functional goals.

title: Activity after bed rest
stem: A stable client becomes lightheaded during their first sitting attempt after prolonged bed rest. After safe reclining, what information is most useful for planning the next attempt?
options: Their preadmission daily walking distance
The distance from bed to the bathroom
Recent fluid balance and timing of antihypertensive doses
Symptoms and blood pressure response to position changes
why: Past endurance does not establish current postural tolerance.
Route length matters later but does not explain sitting symptoms.
These may explain intolerance, but current symptoms and blood pressure response most directly establish tolerance for the next attempt.
These findings assess the suspected intolerance of upright posture.
takeaway: Use the response to position changes to progress activity.
learningObjective: Use the response to position changes to progress activity.

title: Denture cleaning
stem: A client removes full dentures for cleaning. Which setup reduces breakage if they slip?
options: Run hot water over the dentures to make them easier to grip
Hold the dentures high above a towel-lined basin for better visibility
Line the basin with a towel
Use an empty hard basin
why: Hot water can damage denture materials and does not protect against impact.
A greater drop height adds avoidable risk; work close over a protected basin.
Padding cushions fragile dentures if dropped.
A hard surface can fracture dropped dentures.
takeaway: Protect dentures from impact and excessive heat.
learningObjective: Protect dentures from impact and excessive heat.

title: Denture-related soreness
stem: A client leaves dentures out because chewing hurts. What should the nurse do first?
options: Delay assessment until the next scheduled dental appointment
Inspect the mouth and assess fit
Request a softer menu before examining the mouth
Apply extra adhesive immediately
why: Current eating pain merits assessment and earlier dental review when indicated.
Sores or poor fit may explain painful chewing.
Texture changes may help intake but do not identify the painful oral cause.
Adhesive does not correct pressure sores or poor fit.
takeaway: Assess oral discomfort before changing the diet.
learningObjective: Assess oral discomfort before changing the diet.

title: Natural teeth care
stem: A dependent adult can tolerate assisted toothbrushing. Which care is appropriate?
options: Brush teeth gently with a soft brush
Use mouthwash as the only cleaning
Use moistened swabs instead of brushing intact teeth
Brush only on days when the client eats solid food
why: Mechanical cleaning removes plaque from natural teeth.
Rinsing alone does not adequately remove adherent plaque.
Swabs can moisten tissues but do not remove dental plaque as effectively as a brush.
Plaque forms even when the client receives a liquid diet or no oral food.
takeaway: Clean natural teeth mechanically when tolerated.
learningObjective: Clean natural teeth mechanically when tolerated.

title: Oral bleeding risk
stem: A client has fragile gums and reports bleeding after brushing with a firm toothbrush. There is no active bleeding now. Which change should the nurse recommend while reviewing the individualized oral-care plan?
options: Keep the firm brush and reduce brushing to once daily
Introduce flossing before each brushing session
Replace toothbrushing with an alcohol mouth rinse
Use a soft toothbrush with gentle pressure
why: Less frequent cleaning does not address trauma from firm bristles.
New flossing may add trauma; it should be considered within the individualized plan.
Rinsing alone does not adequately remove plaque, and alcohol may irritate the tissues.
Gentler mechanical cleaning addresses the observed source of trauma while preserving oral hygiene.
takeaway: Adapt oral care to tissue condition and bleeding risk.
learningObjective: Adapt oral care to tissue condition and bleeding risk.

title: Oral appliance storage
stem: A client removes a partial denture overnight. Which action best prevents loss?
options: Place it on the meal tray
Place it in an unlabelled medication cup
Use a labelled denture container
Wrap it in a tissue
why: Trays are removed and may carry dentures away.
An unlabelled small cup increases the chance of disposal or misidentification.
A dedicated identified container reduces accidental disposal.
Tissue can be mistaken for waste.
takeaway: Store oral appliances in clearly identified containers.
learningObjective: Store oral appliances in clearly identified containers.

title: Dry lips
stem: A client without oxygen therapy has cracked lips and intact oral swallowing. What should the nurse offer?
options: A plain water rinse as the only intervention
A compatible lip moisturizer
Frequent alcohol-based mouth rinses
Lemon swabs repeatedly
why: Rinsing the mouth does not provide sustained protection for cracked lip surfaces.
Moisturizer protects dry lip surfaces and improves comfort.
Alcohol can irritate and dry fragile tissues.
Acidity may irritate damaged lips and oral tissue.
takeaway: Choose gentle moisture support for cracked lips.
learningObjective: Choose gentle moisture support for cracked lips.

title: Bathing preferences
stem: A client who usually bathes in the evening declines a morning bath. What is the best plan?
options: Arrange an acceptable bathing time
Document refusal of all hygiene
Offer a morning bath before breakfast instead
Ask the family to persuade the client to accept mornings
why: Respecting routine can improve comfort and participation.
The client declined timing rather than every hygiene activity.
Changing the morning hour does not address the evening preference.
Persuasion is unnecessary when a feasible preferred time can be arranged.
takeaway: Adapt routine hygiene to the client's preferences when feasible.
learningObjective: Adapt routine hygiene to the client's preferences when feasible.

title: Bath temperature
stem: A client with reduced foot sensation prepares for a foot wash. Which instruction is appropriate?
options: Judge temperature with the numb foot
Rely on the usual tap setting without testing
Ask the client to keep the numb foot in the water briefly to test comfort
Check water with an intact-sensation area or thermometer
why: The affected foot may not detect a burn risk.
Tap settings do not reliably establish the final water temperature.
Reduced sensation makes foot discomfort an unreliable protection against burns.
Impaired sensation can prevent recognition of excessive heat.
takeaway: Verify water temperature independently when sensation is impaired.
learningObjective: Verify water temperature independently when sensation is impaired.

title: Perineal skin care
stem: An adult has frequent urinary leakage and fragile perineal skin. Which actions support comfort? Select all that apply.
options: Use repeated soap washes after every small leak
Apply barrier cream without cleansing visible urine first
Clean gently after leakage
Use the prescribed skin barrier
why: Frequent detergent exposure may irritate already fragile skin.
Barrier alone does not remove existing irritants from the skin.
Removing irritants limits prolonged skin exposure.
A barrier reduces contact with moisture and irritants.
takeaway: Use gentle cleansing and moisture protection after incontinence.
learningObjective: Use gentle cleansing and moisture protection after incontinence.

title: Foreskin replacement
stem: After hygiene for an uncircumcised adult, what should the nurse ensure?
options: Check urine colour and postpone examining the foreskin until the next care round
Return the foreskin to its usual position
Leave the foreskin retracted because the glans is still moist
Apply more cleansing solution to avoid touching the foreskin again
why: Urine appearance does not establish that the foreskin was safely returned after care.
A retracted foreskin can constrict the glans.
Return it promptly after gentle hygiene; prolonged retraction risks constriction.
Additional cleanser does not replace restoring the normal foreskin position.
takeaway: Replace the foreskin after retraction for hygiene.
learningObjective: Replace the foreskin after retraction for hygiene.

title: Eye crust removal
stem: A client has dried secretions on the eyelids. Which technique is appropriate?
options: Use gentle wipes with a clean surface each pass
Use one damp pad until both eyes appear clean
Apply firm pressure over the closed lids to lift the crusts quickly
Start wiping before moistening adherent crusts
why: Fresh wiping surfaces limit transfer of debris.
Reusing contaminated material can transfer secretions between surfaces.
Pressure and vigorous rubbing can injure delicate tissues; soften and wipe gently.
Moistening helps release crusts with less traction on delicate tissue.
takeaway: Soften eye debris and clean gently without rubbing the cornea.
learningObjective: Soften eye debris and clean gently without rubbing the cornea.

title: Hearing aid care
stem: A client asks the nurse to help clean a hearing aid. What should guide care?
options: Submerging the whole aid in water
Using alcohol on every component
Applying the cleaning method used for another model
The manufacturer's cleaning instructions
why: Moisture can damage electronic components.
A solvent may damage parts unless the device instructions permit it.
Different models may require different handling and cleaning methods.
Device materials and cleaning methods differ.
takeaway: Follow device instructions when cleaning hearing aids.
learningObjective: Follow device instructions when cleaning hearing aids.

title: Glasses before meals
stem: A client repeatedly misses food on the plate and asks where it is. Their glasses are on the bedside table. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask dietary services for a larger plate before checking vision
Begin a cognitive screen before offering the glasses
Offer cleaned glasses before further assessment
Begin feeding the client immediately
why: A larger plate does not first address the missing visual aid.
Correcting an obvious sensory barrier improves the validity of further assessment.
Correcting an obvious sensory barrier may improve feeding.
This bypasses a potentially correctable independence barrier.
takeaway: Address sensory aids before assuming loss of self-care ability.
learningObjective: Address sensory aids before assuming loss of self-care ability.

title: Shaving with fragile skin
stem: A client taking warfarin has fragile facial skin and wants help shaving. There is no active bleeding or skin lesion. Which method best reduces the risk of cuts?
options: Apply extra shaving cream and use a blade razor
Use an electric razor with gentle pressure
Use a new blade razor against the direction of growth
Use a blade razor with short repeated strokes
why: Cream may reduce friction but does not remove blade-cut risk in fragile skin.
An electric razor can reduce cuts compared with a blade razor; gentle pressure protects fragile skin.
A new blade does not remove cutting risk, and shaving against growth may add irritation.
Repeated blade strokes may increase skin trauma.
takeaway: Use gentle shaving methods matched to skin condition.
learningObjective: Use gentle shaving methods matched to skin condition.

title: Nail care limits
stem: A client with diabetes has a thick, curved toenail and reduced sensation. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Assessment by a qualified foot-care provider
Trim the curved nail with routine ward clippers
File the nail until the pressure discomfort disappears
Recommend prolonged soaking before ordinary clipping
why: Complex nails and sensory loss increase injury risk.
A thick curved nail with sensory loss exceeds routine low-risk nail care.
Reduced sensation makes discomfort an unreliable limit for extensive filing.
Soaking may macerate skin and does not remove the need for skilled assessment.
takeaway: Refer complex high-risk nail care to qualified support.
learningObjective: Refer complex high-risk nail care to qualified support.

title: Pruritic skin
stem: A client with dry itchy skin asks for help after bathing. Which measure is suitable?
options: Use hot water for a longer bath
Increase daily soap washing of itchy areas
Use a scented lotion the client has never tried
Apply an unscented emollient
why: Heat and prolonged washing can increase dryness.
Repeated washing can remove oils and worsen dryness.
Fragrance may irritate already sensitive skin.
Moisture retention can relieve dryness-related itching.
takeaway: Treat dry skin with gentle cleansing and moisturization.
learningObjective: Treat dry skin with gentle cleansing and moisturization.

title: Skin-fold moisture
stem: An adult's abdominal fold stays damp after bathing. Which action promotes comfort?
options: Apply a thick perfumed paste without assessment
Apply adhesive film across the fold without a skin assessment
Dry the fold gently and assess the skin
Place a folded towel in the fold for the full day
why: An unassessed product may trap moisture or irritate.
Occlusion may retain moisture and hides the underlying skin.
Moisture trapped in folds promotes irritation and breakdown.
A retained damp towel can trap moisture unless frequently assessed and managed.
takeaway: Assess and manage moisture in skin folds.
learningObjective: Assess and manage moisture in skin folds.

title: Perineal dignity
stem: A dependent client appears embarrassed during perineal care. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Continue the usual care sequence without asking whether the client wants to clean an accessible area
Explain each step before touch
Expose only the area being cleaned
Leave the perineum exposed while gathering supplies so cleaning can begin quickly
why: Offering feasible participation can preserve control and dignity.
Predictability supports comfort and participation.
Limited exposure protects warmth and dignity.
Gather supplies first and limit exposure to what is needed during care.
takeaway: Protect privacy and explain intimate care.
learningObjective: Protect privacy and explain intimate care.

title: Hair care in bed
stem: A bedbound client wants their hair washed and can tolerate it. What should the nurse plan?
options: Support alignment and protect bedding
Use the ordinary basin even if neck support is poor
Position the head at the bed edge before checking tolerance
Substitute dry shampoo without discussing the preference
why: Positioning and a suitable basin allow comfortable care.
Unsuitable equipment can strain the neck during washing.
Position should be assessed and supported before beginning the task.
An alternative should be agreed upon when the requested wash is feasible.
takeaway: Adapt hair washing to mobility and positioning tolerance.
learningObjective: Adapt hair washing to mobility and positioning tolerance.

title: Contact lens discomfort
stem: A client reports gritty eyes while wearing contact lenses overnight in hospital. What should the nurse do?
options: Instil lubricating drops without removing the lenses or assessing
Wait for routine morning care before addressing the discomfort
Cover the eyes to reduce visual effort while keeping lenses in
Help remove lenses using the appropriate method
why: Lubrication alone may leave an irritating lens in place and delay assessment.
Ongoing lens discomfort requires timely removal and assessment.
Resting the eyes does not remove the source of irritation.
Removal limits ongoing irritation and permits assessment.
takeaway: Remove irritating contact lenses and assess the eyes.
learningObjective: Remove irritating contact lenses and assess the eyes.

title: Morning mouth assessment
stem: Which findings during assisted oral care warrant follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Moist pink mucosa without pain
Intact mucosa beneath a well-fitting denture with no reported pain
New white patches with mouth soreness
A new ulcer limiting eating
why: This is a reassuring oral finding.
This is a reassuring finding, unlike new painful lesions.
These may indicate a treatable oral condition.
Painful tissue injury can reduce nutritional intake.
takeaway: Follow up oral lesions that affect comfort or intake.
learningObjective: Follow up oral lesions that affect comfort or intake.

title: Bathing fatigue
stem: Halfway through a bed bath, a stable client reports exhaustion. What is the best response?
options: Ask another staff member to finish immediately while the client rests in bed
Pause and agree on priority areas
Complete every area before allowing rest
Abandon all remaining hygiene without a revised plan
why: Changing caregivers does not reduce the client's immediate fatigue from continued care.
Rest and partial care respect current tolerance.
This ignores the client's stated exhaustion.
Care can be prioritized and rescheduled rather than left unplanned.
takeaway: Adjust hygiene duration to the client's energy level.
learningObjective: Adjust hygiene duration to the client's energy level.

title: Earwax self-care
stem: A client says they use cotton swabs deep inside the ear canal. Which teaching is appropriate?
options: Clean the outer ear and seek advice for blockage
Use a smaller swab to reach farther into the canal
Try wax-softening drops without checking ear symptoms or history
Start home irrigation whenever hearing seems reduced
why: Deep insertion can push wax inward or injure tissue.
A smaller object can still push wax inward or injure the canal.
Pain, drainage, or prior ear procedures may change whether drops are appropriate.
Hearing changes require assessment before assuming wax and irrigating.
takeaway: Avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.
learningObjective: Avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.

title: Skin tear dressing removal
stem: A client's fragile skin pulls when adhesive is removed. Which technique reduces trauma?
options: Remove the tape in one brisk upward motion
Keep the skin taut by pulling it away from the adhesive
Use repeated dry gauze rubbing to remove remaining adhesive
Support the skin while releasing adhesive slowly
why: Upward force can lift fragile epidermis with the adhesive.
This adds tissue tension instead of supporting skin at the release point.
Friction may injure the fragile surface; an appropriate removal method is needed.
Counter-support limits skin stretching and stripping.
takeaway: Support fragile skin during adhesive removal.
learningObjective: Support fragile skin during adhesive removal.

title: Client-led hygiene
stem: A client with arthritis can brush teeth with a built-up handle. Which outcome best indicates effective assistance?
options: The client can grip the adapted handle but still needs the nurse to do the brushing
The client finishes despite increased hand pain
The client completes brushing comfortably
The nurse finishes faster alone
why: Grip alone does not establish the intended comfortable self-care performance.
Completion with increased pain suggests the adaptation needs adjustment.
Adaptive support achieved the self-care goal.
Speed alone does not measure client independence.
takeaway: Evaluate adaptive hygiene by comfortable participation.
learningObjective: Evaluate adaptive hygiene by comfortable participation.

title: Mealtime alertness
stem: A client with an established dysphagia plan is unusually drowsy when lunch arrives. What should the nurse do before feeding?
options: Ask family to feed slowly
Assess alertness and swallowing readiness
Offer the usual thickened drink
Begin with the smallest portion
why: Changing feeders does not resolve the clinical change.
Today's reduced alertness may make the established plan insufficient.
Prescribed consistency does not overcome reduced airway protection.
Small portions still require adequate alertness and swallowing.
takeaway: Reassess readiness when alertness changes before oral intake.
learningObjective: Reassess readiness when alertness changes before oral intake.

title: Texture consistency
stem: A client prescribed minced food receives soup containing firm vegetable chunks. Which response best follows the swallowing plan?
options: Replace it with the prescribed texture
Add thickener without altering the chunks
Encourage extra chewing between sips
Serve only the broth without checking consistency
why: Mixed textures may exceed the assessed swallowing ability.
Thickening liquid does not change solid particle size.
Chewing advice does not replace the prescribed texture.
The broth may also fail the prescribed liquid consistency.
takeaway: Verify both food texture and liquid consistency.
learningObjective: Verify both food texture and liquid consistency.

title: Meal supervision
stem: A client has a prescribed slow-paced assisted feeding plan. Which observations indicate appropriate implementation? Select all that apply.
options: The client remains upright as prescribed
The feeder alternates spoonfuls rapidly
Conversation continues while food is swallowed
Each mouthful is swallowed before another
why: Position supports the assessed swallowing strategy.
Rapid alternating can overwhelm the planned swallowing pace.
Divided attention can interfere with this assisted feeding plan.
This prevents accumulating food faster than swallowing allows.
takeaway: Match feeding pace to observed swallowing.
learningObjective: Match feeding pace to observed swallowing.

title: Thickened fluid acceptance
stem: A client dislikes prescribed thickened fluids and drinks very little. What should the nurse do?
options: Thicken drinks further to improve safety
Record intake and wait several days
Discuss acceptable options with the swallowing team
Offer unrestricted thin water immediately
why: Extra thickness may reduce acceptance without addressing the prescription.
Persistent poor intake needs timely reassessment.
Intake and preference need a safe individualized adjustment.
A separate assessed water protocol would be required.
takeaway: Address poor acceptance without independently changing swallowing prescriptions.
learningObjective: Address poor acceptance without independently changing swallowing prescriptions.

title: Food pocketing
stem: A client recovering from stroke finishes lunch with food remaining in one cheek. What is the best next action?
options: Lay the client down for rest
Assist prescribed oral clearance and inspect
Offer another spoonful to stimulate swallowing
Give a large drink to wash it down
why: Residual food remains an aspiration and hygiene concern.
Retained food requires removal using the established safe method.
More food increases the retained bolus.
An unplanned liquid bolus may increase aspiration risk.
takeaway: Check oral clearance after meals when pocketing occurs.
learningObjective: Check oral clearance after meals when pocketing occurs.

title: Neglect at meals
stem: A client with left-sided neglect eats only food on the right. What supports rehabilitation during a supervised meal?
options: Cue scanning toward the overlooked side
Mix every food together centrally
Feed every mouthful from the right
Document poor appetite alone
why: Practice addresses neglect while supporting access to food.
This may improve access but does not practise scanning.
Exclusive right-side feeding reinforces inattention to the left.
Uneaten food reflects an observed perceptual barrier.
takeaway: Use specific cues to address perceptual barriers to eating.
learningObjective: Use specific cues to address perceptual barriers to eating.

title: Tremor and utensils
stem: A client with tremor spills food but can bring a spoon to the mouth. Which intervention best preserves independence?
options: Have staff provide complete feeding
Limit meals to finger foods exclusively
Increase spoonful size to reduce the number of movements
Trial assessed adaptive utensils
why: Full substitution bypasses the client's retained movement.
Some adaptation may help, but unnecessary restriction limits choice.
Larger spoonfuls can increase spillage and do not improve motor control.
Adaptation may improve control while preserving participation.
takeaway: Match eating aids to the observed functional barrier.
learningObjective: Match eating aids to the observed functional barrier.

title: Meal pain barrier
stem: A client leaves most food because mouth ulcers hurt. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Begin calorie counting as the only intervention
Explain the importance of completing meals
Assess oral pain and coordinate comfort care
Increase portion size at the next meal
why: Measurement identifies deficit but does not relieve the cause.
Education alone does not overcome painful lesions.
The stated intake barrier requires treatment and suitable food.
More food does not address pain with eating.
takeaway: Treat the specific barrier contributing to poor intake.
learningObjective: Treat the specific barrier contributing to poor intake.

title: Early satiety
stem: A client with cancer feels full after several bites but swallows safely. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Prioritize low-energy bulky foods
Offer small nutrient-dense portions more often
Add large drinks before each meal
Serve one large main meal daily
why: Bulk may fill the stomach without meeting nutritional needs.
This uses limited appetite to improve energy intake.
Premeal volume may worsen early satiety.
A large portion conflicts with the reported tolerance.
takeaway: Use nutrient density when meal volume is limited.
learningObjective: Use nutrient density when meal volume is limited.

title: Protected mealtime
stem: A dependent client misses meals because routine care repeatedly interrupts feeding. Which changes are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Reschedule nonurgent tasks around meals
Arrange reliable feeding assistance
Leave covered trays until the next shift
Record refusal when assistance is unavailable
why: Reducing interruptions protects the opportunity to eat.
Dependence requires planned help when food arrives.
Delay can reduce food quality and intake.
Lack of help is not a client refusal.
takeaway: Plan assistance and timing to make meals accessible.
learningObjective: Plan assistance and timing to make meals accessible.

title: Food preference assessment
stem: A client eats little hospital food but requests familiar foods compatible with the ordered diet. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that standard menus meet all needs
Require finishing the tray before alternatives
Ask relatives to bring anything without checking restrictions
Coordinate acceptable familiar choices
why: Nutritional adequacy on paper does not ensure consumption.
This may discourage intake without a clinical benefit.
Compatibility with the clinical diet still matters.
Preference-sensitive meals may improve actual intake.
takeaway: Use preferences within the prescribed nutrition plan.
learningObjective: Use preferences within the prescribed nutrition plan.

title: Fluid allowance distribution
stem: A client prescribed a daily fluid limit is thirsty by evening after drinking most of it at breakfast. Which plan helps?
options: Exclude soup from the intake total
Increase the limit whenever thirst occurs
Distribute the allowance across the day
Keep breakfast unchanged and reserve only medication sips for evening
why: Liquid foods contribute to the prescribed allowance.
Changing the restriction requires clinical review.
Planning preserves access to fluid during later hours.
Medication sips may not address avoidable early overuse; the whole-day allocation needs review.
takeaway: Plan fluid timing and count liquid foods consistently.
learningObjective: Plan fluid timing and count liquid foods consistently.

title: Restricted-fluid mouth comfort
stem: A client on a fluid restriction has dry mouth despite receiving the allotted drinks. Which measures fit the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Use alcohol-containing mouth rinse whenever dryness returns
Provide frequent oral hygiene
Count offered ice within the allowance
Provide unlimited ice chips
why: Alcohol-containing rinses may worsen dryness rather than relieve it.
Cleaning and moistening can improve comfort with limited intake.
Melted ice contributes to total fluid consumption.
Ice becomes fluid and can exceed the restriction.
takeaway: Relieve thirst while accounting for all fluid sources.
learningObjective: Relieve thirst while accounting for all fluid sources.

title: Meal intake documentation
stem: A client eats all yogurt but none of the vegetables or meat. Which record best supports nutritional review?
options: Record foods and approximate amounts eaten
Record half the tray eaten only
Record adequate appetite because yogurt was finished
Record refusal of the prescribed diet
why: Specific intake shows which nutrients may be missing.
A single fraction obscures the actual food pattern.
One accepted food does not establish adequate intake.
Selective intake needs description rather than interpretation.
takeaway: Describe actual intake when assessing nutritional adequacy.
learningObjective: Describe actual intake when assessing nutritional adequacy.

title: Vegetarian protein
stem: A client avoiding animal products needs added protein and has no relevant dietary restrictions. Which offered meal best addresses this need?
options: Clear vegetable broth with tea
Fruit salad with juice
White toast with jam
Lentil stew with whole-grain bread
why: This supplies little protein despite being plant based.
Fruit contributes nutrients but little protein.
This does not substantially address the protein goal.
Legumes provide a practical plant protein source.
takeaway: Identify acceptable protein sources within dietary preferences.
learningObjective: Identify acceptable protein sources within dietary preferences.

title: Low-sodium choices
stem: A client prescribed a sodium-restricted diet compares similar packaged soups. Which teaching is useful?
options: Choose the lowest calorie option
Compare sodium per serving without checking servings per container
Compare sodium for the amount actually eaten
Choose the product labelled natural
why: Calories do not reliably predict sodium content.
The amount actually eaten may contain several labelled servings.
Serving sizes affect the sodium consumed.
Natural labelling does not establish low sodium.
takeaway: Use serving size and sodium content together.
learningObjective: Use serving size and sodium content together.

title: Celiac meal review
stem: A client with celiac disease receives grilled meat, rice, and gravy of unknown ingredients. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer ordinary bread instead of the gravy
Verify the gravy ingredients before serving
Remove the rice because it is a grain
Serve gravy separately and let the client decide
why: Standard wheat bread would introduce gluten.
Wheat-containing thickeners may make gravy unsuitable.
Plain rice is naturally gluten free.
Unknown ingredients still prevent an informed food choice.
takeaway: Check hidden ingredients when implementing gluten avoidance.
learningObjective: Check hidden ingredients when implementing gluten avoidance.

title: Lactose intolerance planning
stem: A client reports cramps after milk but tolerates lactose-free milk. Which change best maintains nutrition?
options: Offer the tolerated lactose-free equivalent
Remove all dairy before considering lactose-free milk
Offer cream because the portion is smaller
Use an unfortified plant beverage without reviewing its nutrients
why: This preserves nutritional intake while addressing the trigger.
A tolerated nutritionally similar option avoids unnecessary food restriction.
Tolerance cannot be assumed from portion size alone.
Alternatives vary in protein and calcium; nutritional equivalence needs review.
takeaway: Use tolerated substitutes before broad food elimination.
learningObjective: Use tolerated substitutes before broad food elimination.

title: Nutrition referral evidence
stem: Which observations support dietitian review for a client recovering from a major illness? Select all that apply.
options: Repeated intake below usual portions
Preference for an alternative meal time
One skipped dessert after a full meal
Unintentional weight loss over several weeks
why: Persistent reduced intake can impair recovery.
Timing preference alone does not establish malnutrition.
An isolated omitted dessert is weak evidence of deficit.
A sustained loss suggests nutritional risk.
takeaway: Use intake and weight trends to identify nutrition risk.
learningObjective: Use intake and weight trends to identify nutrition risk.

title: Feeding tube oral care
stem: A client receiving all nutrition through a tube asks whether mouth care is still needed. Which response is best?
options: Only denture cleaning is needed
Use moistened swabs alone instead of brushing natural teeth
Oral tissues still need regular cleaning
Mouth care can stop until eating resumes
why: Gums and other oral surfaces still need care.
Swabs can moisten tissues but do not adequately replace plaque removal by brushing.
Tube feeding does not prevent oral plaque or dryness.
Lack of oral food does not eliminate oral-care needs.
takeaway: Continue oral hygiene during enteral feeding.
learningObjective: Continue oral hygiene during enteral feeding.

title: Feeding schedule tolerance
stem: A client feels nauseated during a prescribed tube-feeding increase. Vital signs are stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Record nausea only at the end of the shift
Assess tolerance and review the prescribed progression
Give the prescribed antiemetic and continue rate increases without reassessment
Dilute formula independently
why: Delayed review prolongs a potentially correctable problem.
Symptoms may require individualized adjustment with the team.
Symptom treatment does not replace tolerance assessment before further progression.
Unordered dilution changes nutrient delivery and contamination risk.
takeaway: Use symptoms to reassess enteral feeding progression.
learningObjective: Use symptoms to reassess enteral feeding progression.

title: Constipation baseline
stem: A client reports bowel movements every other day with soft stools and no discomfort. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: This may be the client's normal pattern
Daily laxatives are automatically indicated
The client should have a daily stool regardless of comfort
A stimulant laxative is needed whenever a day passes without stool
why: Comfort and stool consistency matter alongside frequency.
A comfortable established pattern does not require routine treatment.
A fixed daily target is unnecessary for a comfortable established pattern.
Soft comfortable alternate-day stools do not establish a need for stimulant treatment.
takeaway: Assess bowel function against the person's usual pattern.
learningObjective: Assess bowel function against the person's usual pattern.

title: Toileting after breakfast
stem: A client with chronic constipation often feels an urge after breakfast but postpones toileting. Which plan is useful?
options: Schedule toileting only before breakfast
Discourage responding to urges between rounds
Ask the client to strain at bedtime
Protect unhurried toilet time after breakfast
why: This ignores the client's observed urge pattern.
Repeated postponement may worsen constipation.
Forced straining does not use the natural urge.
The established urge offers a practical bowel routine.
takeaway: Build bowel routines around usual urges and meal responses.
learningObjective: Build bowel routines around usual urges and meal responses.

title: Fibre adjustment
stem: A client abruptly doubles fibre intake and develops bloating without alarm symptoms. What teaching is best?
options: Switch immediately to concentrated fibre at the same increased total
Maintain the abrupt increase without reviewing symptoms
Increase fibre gradually with appropriate fluids
Increase fibre further before reviewing fluid intake
why: Changing product does not reduce the abrupt increase that triggered bloating.
Persistent intolerance should guide adjustment rather than automatic continuation.
Gradual adjustment can reduce gas and improve tolerance.
Additional fibre without reviewing tolerance and fluids may worsen symptoms.
takeaway: Introduce fibre gradually and individualize fluid intake.
learningObjective: Introduce fibre gradually and individualize fluid intake.

title: Toileting posture
stem: A client strains while sitting on a high toilet with feet dangling. Which change should the nurse trial?
options: Coach stronger straining while the feet remain unsupported
Provide secure foot support
Ask the client to lean forward while keeping both feet off the floor
Add another raised seat without reviewing foot contact
why: Compensatory straining does not correct the unstable toileting posture.
Stable feet support a more effective toileting posture.
Leaning alone does not provide the needed stable foot support.
Further elevation may help some transfers but worsens this foot-support problem.
takeaway: Support the feet during seated toileting.
learningObjective: Support the feet during seated toileting.

title: Apparent diarrhoea
stem: An immobile client with several days of hard stools now leaks small amounts of liquid stool. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Possible retained stool with overflow
Whether the usual fibre goal was reached
Whether a larger continence product fits
Which antidiarrhoeal was previously effective
why: Liquid leakage can pass around an impacted mass.
Diet history matters but does not resolve possible impaction.
Containment does not identify the cause of leakage.
Suppressing stool before assessing retention may worsen the problem.
takeaway: Assess overflow when liquid leakage follows constipation.
learningObjective: Assess overflow when liquid leakage follows constipation.

title: Bowel diary
stem: A client has intermittent faecal urgency and wants to identify patterns. Which entries are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Food intake and associated symptoms
Only episodes requiring a linen change
Only foods the client considers unhealthy
Stool consistency and timing
why: These may reveal triggers needing further assessment.
This misses less severe but informative episodes.
Selective recording can obscure relevant associations.
Both help characterize the elimination pattern.
takeaway: Record bowel patterns systematically before attributing triggers.
learningObjective: Record bowel patterns systematically before attributing triggers.

title: Privacy and retention
stem: A postoperative client voids small amounts while repeatedly watching the open curtain. Bladder assessment shows no urgent retention. What should the nurse try?
options: Keep the curtain partly open to monitor progress continuously
Limit fluids until the client voids normally
Provide privacy and the usual safe position
Request catheterization as the first comfort measure
why: Necessary safety observation should still address the identified privacy barrier.
Restriction does not address inhibited voiding.
Environmental discomfort may interfere with normal voiding.
An invasive device is not the first response here.
takeaway: Address privacy and positioning barriers to elimination.
learningObjective: Address privacy and positioning barriers to elimination.

title: Functional incontinence
stem: A client feels urinary urgency but cannot undo small buttons before reaching the toilet. Which change targets the main barrier?
options: Offer the toilet before each staff break
Use easy-release clothing
Begin a bladder diary as the only measure
Offer a continence pad instead of toilet assistance
why: Staffing times alone do not address the fastening barrier or the individual urgency pattern.
Removing the fastening delay supports timely toileting.
Recording does not immediately address the observed access problem.
Containment does not remove the functional barrier.
takeaway: Identify and reduce functional barriers to continence.
learningObjective: Identify and reduce functional barriers to continence.

title: Prompted voiding
stem: A cognitively impaired client remains dry when reminded and assisted every few hours. Which care plan is appropriate?
options: Use an individualized prompted-voiding routine
Wait for the client to initiate every request
Provide pads without scheduled toilet offers
Reduce daytime drinks routinely
why: The observed response supports regular cueing and assistance.
The client has demonstrated a need for prompts.
Pads contain leakage but omit an effective intervention.
Restriction risks dehydration without treating the cueing deficit.
takeaway: Build continence care on responses to individualized assistance.
learningObjective: Build continence care on responses to individualized assistance.

title: Stress leakage
stem: A client leaks small amounts of urine when coughing but empties the bladder normally. Which teaching fits a prescribed pelvic-floor programme?
options: Bear down strongly during each contraction
Practise only by interrupting every void
Stop drinking before physical activity
Practise the taught contractions consistently
why: Bearing down increases pressure rather than lifting the pelvic floor.
Repeated interrupted voiding is not the routine exercise method.
Routine dehydration does not address pelvic-floor support.
Regular targeted exercise supports pelvic-floor function.
takeaway: Teach correct pelvic-floor technique within the individualized plan.
learningObjective: Teach correct pelvic-floor technique within the individualized plan.

title: Bladder diary interpretation
stem: A client's diary shows large evening drinks followed by several nocturnal toilet trips. There is no fluid restriction. Which discussion is most useful?
options: Use a larger night-time pad only
Schedule daytime toilet visits but leave evening drinks unchanged
Shift some intake earlier in the day
Eliminate fluids from lunch onward
why: Containment does not address the observed timing pattern.
Daytime toileting does not address the documented nocturnal volume pattern.
Timing may reduce nocturnal volume while preserving hydration.
Broad restriction is unnecessary and may impair hydration.
takeaway: Adjust fluid timing based on the observed voiding pattern.
learningObjective: Adjust fluid timing based on the observed voiding pattern.

title: Commode access
stem: A client can transfer safely with one helper but cannot walk to the bathroom before leakage occurs. Which plan best supports continence?
options: Provide a bedpan for every episode despite preference
Provide a bedside commode with timely assistance
Use an indwelling catheter for convenience
Tell the client to request help only after urgency peaks
why: The client can use a more functional seated option.
Shorter access matches the client's transfer ability.
Invasive drainage is not justified by this access problem.
Late requests increase the chance of leakage.
takeaway: Match toileting access to mobility and urgency.
learningObjective: Match toileting access to mobility and urgency.

title: Urinal positioning
stem: A male client with weak grip spills urine because he cannot hold the urinal steady. Which adaptation is most useful?
options: Assist positioning and support the urinal
Offer fewer drinks before toileting
Document total incontinence
Offer the urinal every two hours without help holding it
why: Targeted help addresses the grip deficit while permitting voiding.
Reducing hydration does not improve handling ability.
Spillage from handling is not proof of loss of bladder control.
Scheduled access does not resolve weak grip and unstable positioning.
takeaway: Distinguish device-handling difficulty from incontinence.
learningObjective: Distinguish device-handling difficulty from incontinence.

title: Comfortable bedpan use
stem: A client permitted head elevation reports difficulty using a bedpan while flat. Which change should the nurse make?
options: Leave the client flat but extend time
Choose a deeper pan solely to increase volume
Delay until the next scheduled round
Raise the head as tolerated and support alignment
why: Duration does not address the positional barrier.
Capacity does not correct the difficulty voiding flat.
Postponement may worsen discomfort and urgency.
A more upright position can facilitate elimination.
takeaway: Use the most natural safe elimination position available.
learningObjective: Use the most natural safe elimination position available.

title: Catheter discomfort
stem: A catheterized client reports pulling discomfort after moving into a chair. The tubing is taut. What should the nurse do first?
options: Increase fluid intake immediately
Begin a urine culture solely for discomfort
Reposition tubing and securement to remove traction
Request a larger catheter
why: Hydration does not remove the pulling force.
Assessing mechanical causes comes before assuming infection.
The observed tension provides a correctable mechanical cause.
A larger device does not relieve external traction.
takeaway: Relieve catheter traction before pursuing unrelated causes.
learningObjective: Relieve catheter traction before pursuing unrelated causes.

title: Drainage bag emptying
stem: A mobile client manages a catheter bag at home. Which observed practices indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: Waits until the bag is tightly distended
Avoids touching the outlet to the container
Secures the closed outlet after emptying
Rests the outlet inside collected urine
why: Overfilling can impair drainage and increase traction.
This limits contamination of the drainage outlet.
Closure prevents leakage and maintains device function.
Contact contaminates the drainage outlet.
takeaway: Empty the bag without contaminating or overstretching the system.
learningObjective: Empty the bag without contaminating or overstretching the system.

title: Catheter hygiene
stem: An adult with a long-term catheter asks how to clean around it. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Routine gentle hygiene according to the care plan
Use an antiseptic wash for every routine clean without an indication
Apply antibiotic ointment around the meatus routinely
Disconnecting the tubing during every bath
why: Ordinary cleaning removes secretions without unnecessary irritation.
Unnecessary antiseptic exposure can irritate tissue without replacing gentle routine hygiene.
Routine antibiotic application without indication is not required for ordinary catheter hygiene.
Repeated disconnection disrupts the closed drainage system.
takeaway: Use gentle external catheter hygiene while preserving the closed system.
learningObjective: Use gentle external catheter hygiene while preserving the closed system.

title: Continence product fit
stem: A client develops groin marks after a new absorbent product is introduced. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
options: Add a second product inside the first
Change products less often to reduce handling
Apply barrier cream without reviewing fit
Reassess size and skin condition
why: Layering may worsen tightness and heat.
Prolonged exposure may worsen skin irritation.
Barrier protection does not remove mechanical pressure.
Tight fit may cause friction and pressure.
takeaway: Check product fit when new pressure or friction marks appear.
learningObjective: Check product fit when new pressure or friction marks appear.

title: Ostomy pouch timing
stem: A client says the pouch pulls painfully when nearly full. Which teaching addresses this problem?
options: Change the whole appliance after every small output
Tighten the support belt firmly
Empty it before it becomes heavy
Add another layer of adhesive tape
why: Frequent removal can injure peristomal skin.
Extra compression does not solve pouch overfilling.
Earlier emptying reduces weight on the skin barrier.
Tape does not remove weight or correct overfilling.
takeaway: Avoid letting pouch weight strain the skin barrier.
learningObjective: Avoid letting pouch weight strain the skin barrier.

title: Peristomal leakage
stem: A client reports burning beneath a leaking ostomy barrier. What is the best response?
options: Wait until after the next meal for the routine appliance change
Remove the leaking appliance and assess the seal
Tape over the leak until the next routine change
Apply lotion beneath the new adhesive
why: Active leakage and burning need prompt assessment and skin protection.
Effluent contact can rapidly irritate peristomal skin.
Trapped effluent continues contacting the skin.
Some lotions prevent an effective barrier seal.
takeaway: Address leakage promptly to protect peristomal skin.
learningObjective: Address leakage promptly to protect peristomal skin.

title: Changing stoma size
stem: A new ostomy is less swollen than last week and the barrier opening now exposes surrounding skin. What should the nurse do?
options: Remeasure and refit the opening
Keep the original template until discharge
Cut the opening larger for ventilation
Fill the enlarged gap with extra paste without remeasuring
why: Postoperative size changes require reassessment of fit.
An outdated opening leaves skin exposed to effluent.
Further exposure increases the area at risk.
Accessories should not replace correction of an opening that no longer fits.
takeaway: Recheck stoma size as postoperative swelling resolves.
learningObjective: Recheck stoma size as postoperative swelling resolves.

title: Ostomy participation
stem: A client with a new colostomy is willing to watch but not yet touch the pouch. What best supports learning?
options: Require a complete change immediately
Have family perform all future care
Postpone all teaching until discharge morning
Agree on one manageable participation step
why: The demand exceeds the client's stated readiness.
This may prevent development of the client's own skills.
Delayed practice limits opportunities to gain confidence.
Graded practice builds confidence from current readiness.
takeaway: Build ostomy self-care through achievable agreed steps.
learningObjective: Build ostomy self-care through achievable agreed steps.

title: Ostomy teaching evaluation
stem: Which client actions demonstrate practical pouch-management learning? Select all that apply.
options: Adds tape over a leak and postpones barrier inspection
Relies only on the printed instruction sheet
Checks the seal when itching occurs
Shows how to empty and close the pouch
why: Leakage requires assessment of the seal and skin rather than concealment.
Possessing instructions does not demonstrate performance.
New itching may signal leakage requiring attention.
Return demonstration tests the actual self-care skill.
takeaway: Use observed self-care skills to evaluate ostomy teaching.
learningObjective: Use observed self-care skills to evaluate ostomy teaching.

title: Flatus and embarrassment
stem: A client with a colostomy avoids meals because of embarrassment about gas. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend skipping meals before every outing
Discuss individual food patterns and pouch options
Recommend avoiding all vegetables
Promise there will be no gas after healing
why: Routine meal omission can compromise intake and participation.
Practical strategies can improve confidence without sacrificing nutrition.
Broad restriction may reduce nutrition unnecessarily.
Gas can remain a normal part of bowel function.
takeaway: Address ostomy concerns with individualized practical strategies.
learningObjective: Address ostomy concerns with individualized practical strategies.

title: Bowel regimen evaluation
stem: An older adult is following an individualized bowel-care plan. Which finding most supports continuing the current plan?
options: The client's comfort and usual pattern are restored
Bowel movements are daily but still require straining
Bloating persists despite frequent small stools
Stool frequency increases but stools become watery
why: The goal is comfortable function rather than a fixed frequency.
Increased frequency without comfortable passage does not meet the bowel-care goal.
Persistent bloating suggests incomplete relief and warrants review.
Watery stools can cause harm and do not represent comfortable normalized function.
takeaway: Evaluate bowel care using comfort, consistency, and individual pattern.
learningObjective: Evaluate bowel care using comfort, consistency, and individual pattern.

title: Diarrhoea skin comfort
stem: An adult with frequent loose stools reports perianal burning. Which measures belong in the comfort plan? Select all that apply.
options: Apply the recommended moisture barrier
Use vigorous repeated soap scrubbing
Delay cleansing until several episodes accumulate
Clean gently and dry without rubbing
why: Protection reduces contact with subsequent stool.
Frequent friction and detergent can worsen irritation.
Longer contact increases exposure to stool irritants.
Gentle removal of irritants limits additional skin trauma.
takeaway: Protect perianal skin during frequent stool passage.
learningObjective: Protect perianal skin during frequent stool passage.

title: Toilet communication
stem: A client with expressive aphasia cannot reliably request toileting. Which intervention is most useful?
options: Interpret restlessness as refusal of care
Ask spoken questions only after restlessness develops
Provide an accessible agreed toileting signal
Provide a call bell without agreeing on a toileting signal
why: Restlessness may communicate an unmet elimination need.
A reactive series of questions is less reliable than an agreed accessible request.
A consistent signal addresses the communication barrier.
Bell access is helpful but does not establish how the specific need will be communicated.
takeaway: Adapt toileting communication to expressive ability.
learningObjective: Adapt toileting communication to expressive ability.

title: Night-time toileting balance
stem: A resident is awakened by fixed toileting rounds despite remaining dry most nights. What should guide revision?
options: Add fluids at every awakening
Review the diary and individual sleep pattern
Continue the schedule because it fits staffing
Remove night-time assistance entirely
why: Extra nocturnal intake may increase toilet need.
The plan should balance continence needs with restorative sleep.
Staff convenience alone does not justify repeated waking.
The resident may still need help when awake or urgent.
takeaway: Individualize night-time toileting using actual need and sleep effects.
learningObjective: Individualize night-time toileting using actual need and sleep effects.

title: Elimination goal setting
stem: A client wants fewer accidents during afternoon activities. Which goal best measures the success of the continence plan?
options: No more than one afternoon leakage episode over the next seven days
Demonstrate easier clothing fastenings by Friday
Record daily fluid intake for seven days
Describe two continence strategies at the next visit
why: A defined leakage outcome directly measures the goal of fewer afternoon accidents.
This measures a useful skill rather than the requested continence outcome.
This measures monitoring behaviour rather than the frequency of accidents.
This measures knowledge rather than success in preventing afternoon leakage.
takeaway: Measure continence outcomes against the client's chosen activity goals.
learningObjective: Select a time-defined continence outcome matching the client's goal.

title: Pain without speech
stem: A client with advanced dementia grimaces and guards a hip during turning. Which assessment approach is most useful?
options: Use the client’s previous numerical score as the current score during turning
Use heart rate as the sole pain measure
Use the family’s description of usual comfort without observing the client during care
Use an appropriate behavioural tool and collateral history
why: The new behaviour needs current assessment rather than copying a previous score.
Physiological changes are nonspecific and may be absent.
Collateral history helps but should be combined with current structured observation.
Observed behaviours and known baseline can indicate pain when speech is limited.
takeaway: Use structured behavioural assessment when reliable self-report is unavailable.
learningObjective: Use structured behavioural assessment when reliable self-report is unavailable.

title: Pain communication aid
stem: An alert intubated client can point accurately but cannot speak. What should the nurse try first for pain assessment?
options: Ask family to estimate the current pain
Wait until extubation to establish a score
Offer an accessible visual pain scale
Use only a behavioural pain score
why: A capable client can report through another communication route.
Communication adaptation allows assessment now.
The client can provide self-report through pointing.
Behavioural observation is secondary when reliable self-report remains possible.
takeaway: Adapt communication before abandoning pain self-report.
learningObjective: Adapt communication before abandoning pain self-report.

title: Different pain quality
stem: A client with stable chronic knee aching now describes burning feet at night. What is the best next step?
options: Record the highest number without location
Assess the new pain separately
Increase knee exercises as the main response
Use the old knee assessment unchanged
why: A score alone obscures the new symptom pattern.
A different site and quality may indicate another mechanism.
The new foot symptoms may have a different cause.
The previous assessment does not characterize burning feet.
takeaway: Assess new pain characteristics separately from an existing pain problem.
learningObjective: Assess new pain characteristics separately from an existing pain problem.

title: Functional comfort goal
stem: A client with persistent back pain wants to sit through dinner with family. Which goal best guides evaluation?
options: Tolerates the chosen sitting period with acceptable symptoms
Reports zero pain at every assessment
Takes every offered analgesic dose
Rests in bed throughout the evening
why: The outcome directly measures the client's meaningful activity.
Complete absence may be unrealistic and misses the functional goal.
Medication use is a process rather than functional outcome.
Avoidance does not meet the client's stated participation goal.
takeaway: Include meaningful function in comfort goals.
learningObjective: Include meaningful function in comfort goals.

title: Fear of movement
stem: A rehabilitation client avoids approved exercise because they expect pain. What should the nurse do?
options: Describe the usual benefits of exercise without asking what pain the client anticipates
Ask the client to complete the full planned session before deciding whether the fear was justified
Cancel all exercise until pain completely disappears
Explore the fear and plan a paced trial
why: General reassurance does not assess this client’s specific barrier.
An agreed paced trial is safer and more acceptable than using full-session completion as a prerequisite for discussion.
Avoidance may worsen deconditioning without resolving fear.
Collaboration addresses anticipation while respecting movement limits.
takeaway: Address fear and use graded activity within the plan.
learningObjective: Address fear and use graded activity within the plan.

title: Pain diary usefulness
stem: A client has intermittent headaches under assessment. Which diary entries are most useful? Select all that apply.
options: Only the worst episode each month
Only the pain score without duration
Timing, triggers, and associated symptoms
Treatments tried and the observed response
why: Selective recording misses frequency and variation.
Intensity alone omits clinically useful temporal information.
Patterns can guide assessment of the headache episodes.
Response helps judge effectiveness and possible overuse.
takeaway: Record pain context and response as well as intensity.
learningObjective: Record pain context and response as well as intensity.

title: Cold application tolerance
stem: A client prescribed a cold pack for an ankle sprain reports burning beneath it. What should the nurse do first?
options: Encourage distraction from the sensation
Remove the pack and inspect the skin
Add another layer while leaving the pack in place
Wait until the prescribed interval ends
why: Distraction should not conceal a possible tissue injury.
Burning may indicate cold-related tissue injury or intolerance.
Inspection is needed before continuing after a warning symptom.
A scheduled duration does not override skin intolerance.
