learningObjective: Stop thermal therapy when abnormal sensations suggest injury.

title: Heat precautions
stem: A client with numb feet requests a heating pad for comfort. Which action is best?
options: Assess sensation and choose a safer comfort plan
Use the lowest setting for the usual prescribed interval without checking sensation
Ask the client to remove it when too hot
Place a towel over the heating pad and rely on the client to report discomfort
why: Reduced sensation can prevent recognition of heat injury.
A low setting does not remove burn risk when protective sensation is impaired.
The client may not reliably feel excessive heat.
A barrier does not make impaired sensation a reliable way to regulate exposure.
takeaway: Avoid relying on impaired sensation to regulate heat exposure.
learningObjective: Avoid relying on impaired sensation to regulate heat exposure.

title: Relaxation preference
stem: A client with recurrent tension discomfort dislikes guided imagery but enjoys quiet music. What is the best plan?
options: Continue imagery because it is commonly recommended
Schedule the music only after the client has attempted guided imagery
Choose a standard relaxation recording without asking which music the client finds comfortable
Offer preferred music as an adjunct
why: A disliked intervention may increase frustration rather than comfort.
Requiring a disliked strategy first ignores a feasible preferred adjunct.
The client’s preference should guide an acceptable intervention.
A chosen acceptable strategy is more likely to support relaxation.
takeaway: Match nonpharmacological comfort strategies to client preference.
learningObjective: Match nonpharmacological comfort strategies to client preference.

title: Breakthrough pattern
stem: A client reports pain reliably worsening during evening wound care despite acceptable comfort at rest. What should the nurse report?
options: Only the total daily analgesic amount
That the client is generally comfortable
The predictable procedure-related timing
Only the lowest daytime pain score
why: Amount alone does not show when coverage is inadequate.
A global label hides pain during necessary care.
The team can plan anticipatory relief for that specific event.
That omits the recurrent distressing episode.
takeaway: Identify predictable painful activities when planning comfort care.
learningObjective: Identify predictable painful activities when planning comfort care.

title: Touch consent
stem: A client with chronic pain stiffens when a nurse starts a back rub. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask a family member to perform the same massage
Stop and ask about touch preferences
Continue with lighter pressure without asking
Explain that massage usually reduces pain
why: Changing the person does not resolve the client's preference.
The response suggests the intervention may be unwelcome.
Consent and preference still need clarification.
Average benefit does not establish this client's comfort.
takeaway: Confirm consent and preference for hands-on comfort measures.
learningObjective: Confirm consent and preference for hands-on comfort measures.

title: Nausea environmental trigger
stem: A client receiving treatment reports nausea when strong food odours enter the room. Which plan best targets this trigger?
options: Offer tolerated low-odour foods in a ventilated setting
Provide larger hot meals less often
Serve the usual hot meal covered, then uncover it fully at the bedside
Use a strongly scented room freshener before delivering meals
why: This reduces the identified stimulus while supporting intake.
Hot food odours and large portions may worsen symptoms.
Uncovering a hot meal may still expose the client to the identified odour trigger.
Another strong odour may worsen nausea instead of reducing the trigger.
takeaway: Modify identified environmental nausea triggers.
learningObjective: Modify identified environmental nausea triggers.

title: Vomiting positioning
stem: An alert weak client in bed begins vomiting and cannot turn independently. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Measure the emesis before repositioning
Offer water to rinse immediately during vomiting
Finish obtaining a detailed nausea history
Assist a safe side or upright position

Oral fluid during active emesis may increase aspiration risk.
Immediate positioning precedes extended history taking.
Positioning helps protect the airway during active vomiting.
takeaway: Protect the airway during vomiting before detailed assessment.
learningObjective: Protect the airway during vomiting before detailed assessment.

title: Restless discomfort
stem: A nonverbal client repeatedly pulls at clothing and shifts in a chair during afternoon care. Which assessments most directly help identify a current physical source of discomfort? Select all that apply.
options: The usual duration of afternoon naps
The timing of the most recent family visit
Toileting need and abdominal fullness
Skin pressure and positioning

Social context may matter but does not directly assess a physical cause of this restlessness.
Elimination discomfort can produce restless movement and needs current assessment.
Pressure or an uncomfortable position can drive repeated shifting.
takeaway: Assess unmet physical needs before interpreting restlessness behaviourally.
learningObjective: Assess unmet physical needs before interpreting restlessness behaviourally.

title: Sleep pattern assessment
stem: A hospitalized client reports poor sleep but naps for several hours each afternoon. What should the nurse explore first?
options: Preferred room temperature and bedding
Usual routine and daytime sleep pattern
The time the evening medication round occurs
The amount of light entering the room overnight
why: Environment may contribute but the long afternoon naps are the most specific cue in this case.
The several-hour naps may reduce night-time sleep drive; compare with the usual sleep-wake routine.
Medication timing may matter, but the reported daytime sleep pattern should be explored first.
Light can disturb sleep, but no light-related cue is supplied; start with the documented pattern.
takeaway: Assess the full sleep-wake pattern before selecting interventions.
learningObjective: Assess the full sleep-wake pattern before selecting interventions.

title: Nocturnal symptom cause
stem: A client repeatedly awakens with shortness of breath and needs extra pillows. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess the respiratory change and escalate
Offer a sleep aid as the first response
Add more pillows and document improved comfort without assessing the change
Record the awakenings as insomnia and discuss sleep hygiene at the next routine visit

Sedation does not address the possible physiological cause.

Breathing-related awakenings need physiological assessment, not an insomnia label alone.
takeaway: Investigate physiological symptoms causing repeated awakening.
learningObjective: Investigate physiological symptoms causing repeated awakening.

title: Sleep environment choice
stem: A stable client sleeps lightly and is disturbed mainly by hallway conversation. Which agreed intervention targets that cause?
options: Move the bedtime two hours earlier
Offer earplugs without discussing whether the client can hear needed alarms or communication
Cluster all care but leave avoidable hallway conversation unchanged
Reduce nearby noise and offer acceptable sound protection
why: Earlier sleep does not remove hallway noise.

takeaway: Select sleep interventions that match the identified disturbance.
learningObjective: Select sleep interventions that match the identified disturbance.

title: Night-time care scheduling
stem: Which actions can support sleep for a stable client without compromising necessary monitoring? Select all that apply.
options: Omit ordered observations without review
Complete every nonurgent task whenever staff are free
Coordinate compatible nonurgent care tasks
Review whether routine tasks can occur before bedtime

Uncoordinated timing creates unnecessary interruptions.

Individual scheduling protects the sleep period.

learningObjective: Coordinate routine care around sleep while preserving required monitoring.

title: Caffeine and sleep
stem: A client has difficulty falling asleep after several late-evening coffees. Which trial is most reasonable?
options: Take an additional nap before bedtime
Move caffeine earlier and monitor sleep
Replace coffee with caffeinated cola
Stay in bed longer each morning immediately

Timing targets a plausible stimulant-related contributor.

learningObjective: Assess stimulant timing when planning sleep improvement.

title: CPAP comfort

options: Assess fit and arrange appropriate adjustment
Tighten straps to stop all mask movement
Accept stopping therapy without discussing alternatives
Place thick unapproved padding under the seal

learningObjective: Address interface discomfort to support prescribed sleep therapy.

title: Palliative positioning choice
stem: A dying client becomes distressed with large turns but tolerates small shifts. Which plan best balances comfort and skin care?
options: Continue large turns on a rigid schedule
Use a pressure-redistributing mattress and omit assessment of the discomfort during positioning
Repeat the same large turn after an analgesic without asking whether the client prefers smaller shifts
Agree on tolerated small changes and reassess

A mattress does not replace attention to comfort and skin response.

Comfort goals and tissue tolerance should guide individual positioning.
takeaway: Individualize repositioning to comfort and goals at end of life.
learningObjective: Individualize repositioning to comfort and goals at end of life.

title: Family food concerns
stem: A dying client has little desire to eat, and family worry they are causing suffering. What should the nurse explain?
options: Present artificial feeding as the expected next step before discussing the client’s wishes
Set a calorie target for the family to meet before exploring the client’s comfort
Offer desired intake as tolerated and discuss comfort goals
Describe reduced intake only as a nutritional deficit that must be corrected
why: The benefits, burdens and goals need individual discussion; escalation is not automatic.
An imposed target may increase distress and ignores the dying person’s preferences.
Reduced intake may accompany dying; comfort guides support.
Reduced intake during dying should be discussed in the context of comfort, wishes and the whole clinical situation.
takeaway: Discuss intake in relation to the dying client's comfort and wishes.
learningObjective: Discuss intake in relation to the dying client's comfort and wishes.

title: Breathlessness positioning
stem: A client with stable chronic breathlessness prefers sitting forward with arms supported. What should the nurse do?
options: Focus only on the saturation number
Support the position and reassess comfort
Change to the unit’s standard upright posture despite the client preferring the supported forward position
Document relief but remove the arm support when the client rests

An individually helpful supported posture can reduce effort.
Standard posture should not override a safe individually relieving position without clinical reason.
The arm support is part of the helpful position and should not be removed without reassessing effect.
takeaway: Support positions that relieve breathlessness and evaluate the response.
learningObjective: Support positions that relieve breathlessness and evaluate the response.

title: Comfort measure evaluation
stem: A client trialling music for procedural anxiety says pain is unchanged but they feel less tense. What is the best interpretation?
options: The strategy helped anxiety but did not relieve the pain
The strategy was ineffective because the pain score did not fall
The lower tension shows that less analgesia is now required
The unchanged pain score makes the tension report unreliable
why: The intervention targeted anxiety; less tension is a meaningful benefit while persistent pain still needs its own management.
A strategy can help one targeted symptom without changing another.
Reduced tension alone does not demonstrate adequate pain relief or justify changing analgesia.
Anxiety and pain may change differently; neither report invalidates the other.
takeaway: Evaluate each symptom targeted by a comfort intervention.
learningObjective: Evaluate each symptom targeted by a comfort intervention.

title: Fatigue priorities
stem: A client with chronic illness has energy for one morning activity and values attending a family video call. What should guide planning?
options: Complete the full morning hygiene routine before the call because hygiene is normally scheduled first
Ask the family to reschedule the call without first discussing the client’s priorities
Combine bathing and the call so both are completed during the same energy period
Prioritize the meaningful activity with rest around it
why: A fixed task sequence may exhaust capacity for the client’s chosen activity.
Planning should begin with the client’s valued activity and available energy.
Simultaneous demands may undermine participation and comfort; individualized pacing is preferable.
Energy conservation should support the client's own priorities.
takeaway: Allocate limited energy around the client's meaningful priorities.
learningObjective: Allocate limited energy around the client's meaningful priorities.

title: Heel unloading
stem: A bedbound client's heels remain against the mattress despite a pillow under the knees. Which adjustment best addresses heel pressure?
options: Place the pillow higher under the thighs
Massage the heels during each round
Support the lower legs so the heels are free
Add a softer sheet over the heels
why: Thigh support may leave the heels resting on the mattress.
Massage does not provide sustained unloading and may damage vulnerable tissue.
The support must remove direct heel contact.
A sheet does not reliably unload the pressure.
takeaway: Verify that heel-offloading actually removes heel contact.
learningObjective: Verify that heel-offloading actually removes heel contact.

title: Support surface review
stem: A client develops new pressure discomfort despite a specialty mattress. What should the nurse conclude?
options: The turning interval can be lengthened if the mattress is functioning
The whole prevention plan needs reassessment
The discomfort should settle once the client adapts to the surface
Adding folded blankets is the best way to improve the mattress effect
why: Equipment function does not establish individual tissue tolerance.
A support surface does not remove the need for individualized positioning.
New discomfort requires assessment rather than assumed adaptation.
Extra layers can interfere with intended pressure redistribution; review the whole plan.
takeaway: Reassess positioning and skin response despite a pressure-redistributing surface.
learningObjective: Reassess positioning and skin response despite a pressure-redistributing surface.

title: Sliding in bed
stem: A client repeatedly slides down when the head of the bed is raised. What change reduces shear while meeting clinical elevation needs?

Pull the client upward by dragging the sheet beneath them
Keep the head fully raised at all times
Add more bedding beneath the sacrum
why: Reducing sliding limits opposing forces on skin and deeper tissue.
Dragging can add friction and shear.
Extra elevation may increase sliding when not clinically necessary.
More layers do not reliably prevent shear.
takeaway: Reduce sliding and use suitable assistance to limit shear.
learningObjective: Reduce sliding and use suitable assistance to limit shear.

title: Chair pressure relief
stem: A wheelchair user can perform prescribed weight shifts but forgets during long activities. Which plan is most useful?

Ask the client to shift when discomfort first develops
Replace the cushion before evaluating how reminders work
Agree on reminders within the activity routine
why: The skill is present; the immediate barrier is remembering during activities.
Waiting for symptoms may not provide timely pressure relief, particularly with reduced sensation.
Equipment review may be appropriate, but a new cushion does not address forgetting an effective prescribed skill.
Cues support sustained use of an effective existing skill.
takeaway: Integrate pressure relief into the client's actual activities.
learningObjective: Integrate pressure relief into the client's actual activities.

title: Moisture versus pressure
stem: A client has diffuse superficial perineal irritation after repeated loose stools, without a focal bony-prominence lesion. Which assessment matters most?

Time spent supine since the last assisted turn
Distribution and exposure to stool

takeaway: Use location, appearance, and exposure to assess skin damage.
learningObjective: Use location, appearance, and exposure to assess skin damage.

title: Darker skin assessment
stem: An immobile client with darkly pigmented skin reports sacral tenderness without obvious redness. Which current local findings best help assess possible pressure-related tissue change? Select all that apply.

Local warmth or coolness compared with surrounding skin
Changes in firmness or skin colour from baseline
The colour documented at admission without re-examining the area
why: The score informs prevention but does not directly examine the painful sacral tissue.

Texture and baseline comparison support assessment across skin tones.

takeaway: Include temperature, texture, and symptoms in skin assessment.
learningObjective: Include temperature, texture, and symptoms in skin assessment.

title: Small position changes

Leave the painful position unchanged all shift
Continue the full turn without pausing
Replace repositioning with a thicker dressing alone

A dressing does not necessarily unload deeper pressure.
takeaway: Adapt pressure relief to tolerance while addressing pain.
learningObjective: Adapt pressure relief to tolerance while addressing pain.

title: Device-related inspection

Apply bulky padding inside without checking fit
Inspect only the visible chin
Inspect contact areas using the approved method

Padding can alter support and pressure distribution.

title: Cushion selection

Place a waterproof sheet tightly across the cushion
Seek an individualized seating and cushion review
Add a second ring cushion

takeaway: Select cushions by individual pressure distribution and function.

title: Repositioning outcome
stem: Which observations most directly show whether an individualized turning plan is protecting the client while remaining tolerable? Select all that apply.

Skin condition at vulnerable sites
Comfort and tolerance between turns
The percentage of scheduled turns documented as completed
why: The count does not establish actual offloading or tissue response.
Tissue response shows whether protection is effective.

Adherence is useful process information but does not itself demonstrate comfort or tissue protection.

learningObjective: Evaluate pressure prevention by tissue response and client tolerance.

title: Linen wrinkles

options: Remove the ridge and reassess the skin
Add another pad over the folded one
Provide analgesia before examining the bedding
Wait until the next full linen change
why: The localized pressure source needs correction and inspection.

learningObjective: Investigate and remove localized pressure from bedding or equipment.

title: Skin tear comfort

Avoid the usual upper-body activities until the next dressing change
Review dressing securement and clothing contact
why: Extra contact pressure and friction may worsen trauma; assess dressing and clothing fit.

A correctable snagging problem may be solved without unnecessary functional restriction.

learningObjective: Prevent avoidable friction and traction around fragile wounds.

title: Dependent oedema positioning

Legs are supported without pressure behind the knees

why: Narrow support can create pressure and poor alignment.
New numbness warrants reassessment of position and circulation.
Support can assist venous return without focal compression.
Focal pressure may impede circulation.
takeaway: Elevate limbs with distributed support and monitor tolerance.
learningObjective: Elevate limbs with distributed support and monitor tolerance.

title: Compression hosiery fit
stem: A client prescribed compression hosiery develops a deep crease where the top was rolled down. What should the nurse do?
options: Replace it with the next larger size without remeasuring the limb
Remove the constricting roll and reassess fit
Add tape to hold the roll
Leave it because tighter pressure is more effective

learningObjective: Apply prescribed hosiery smoothly without constricting rolls.

title: Moist wound edge
stem: A wound's surrounding skin becomes white and soggy beneath a repeatedly saturated dressing. What should the nurse report?

Expected moisture from a healthy granulating wound
Likely infection because the dressing remains wet
Dry skin requiring a thicker layer of moisturizer

learningObjective: Distinguish balanced wound moisture from periwound maceration.

title: Adhesive sensitivity
stem: A client develops an itchy outline matching the dressing adhesive while the wound itself improves. What should the nurse do?

Increase adhesive coverage to protect the rash
Stop all wound protection without another plan
Assess possible adhesive irritation and review securement
why: The localized adhesive outline suggests another possibility.
More exposure may worsen a contact reaction.
The wound still needs appropriate protection.
The distribution suggests a product-related skin reaction.
takeaway: Use the distribution of skin changes to guide product assessment.
learningObjective: Use the distribution of skin changes to guide product assessment.

title: Gentle cleansing choice
stem: A client with recurrent skin tears finds ordinary tape removal painful. Which prevention discussion is useful?
options: Place the same tape on a new fragile area each day
Clean adhesive residue with vigorous rubbing
Review skin-friendly fixation and removal methods
Use stronger tape so changes are less frequent
why: Rotating trauma does not solve the underlying issue.

learningObjective: Reduce repeated adhesive trauma in fragile skin.

title: Skin inspection teaching

Use a mirror or agreed assistance
Rely on pain to identify a problem

learningObjective: Adapt foot inspection to visual reach and sensation.

title: Sock seam pressure

Add another thick sock for cushioning
Wait for the client to report pain
Apply cream but continue the same sock

title: Sweating and bedding

title: Repositioning preference

Reserve the preferred position until after the standard turn sequence is complete
Incorporate it with appropriate support and skin assessment
Use the preferred position whenever requested without checking the skin
why: A helpful position still needs review of pressure exposure and individual tolerance.
An inflexible sequence may unnecessarily postpone a safe relieving position.
Preference can be honoured while maintaining pressure management.

takeaway: Combine preferred comfort positions with individualized skin protection.

title: Support removal assessment
stem: A client says a heel boot feels tight after swelling increases. What should the nurse do?

Assess skin and circulation and review device fit

title: New seating endurance

Maintain the same total sitting time and reassess at the weekly review
