title: Pressure plan teach-back
stem: A family caregiver will help a dependent client at home. Which demonstration best shows understanding of the positioning plan?
options: Promises to turn only when redness appears
Uses a fixed method despite new pain
Shows the taught turn and checks the exposed skin
Describes the purpose of the support mattress
why: Waiting for visible injury misses preventive relief.
Pain should trigger reassessment and adaptation.
Performance links safe movement with tissue assessment.
Understanding equipment is useful but does not demonstrate the required positioning technique.
takeaway: Evaluate caregivers by demonstrating the individualized prevention plan.
learningObjective: Evaluate caregivers by demonstrating the individualized prevention plan.

title: Toddler autonomy at meals
stem: A hospitalized toddler eats little when spoon-fed but reaches for safe finger foods. Swallowing is normal. Which plan best supports intake?
options: Offer milk before the meal to improve intake before trying food
Offer suitable finger foods with supervision
Offer the same spoon-fed meal more frequently
Ask a second adult to assist spoon-feeding
why: A filling drink may displace food and does not address the demonstrated interest in self-feeding.
Self-feeding uses the child's emerging independence.
Frequency does not address the observed wish for control.
Another feeder may reproduce the same barrier.
takeaway: Use developmentally appropriate participation to support eating.
learningObjective: Use developmentally appropriate participation to support eating.

title: Preschool pain scale
stem: A four-year-old understands simple pictures but struggles with numerical rankings. Which pain assessment approach is best?
options: Use an age-appropriate faces tool as instructed
Practise the numerical ranking several more times before offering another scale
Use the parent's estimate instead of trying self-report
Infer severity from whether the child plays briefly
why: The tool matches the child's demonstrated communication ability.
The demonstrated difficulty suggests adapting the tool rather than insisting on an unsuitable abstract scale.
The child may report reliably with an appropriate tool.
Play does not exclude pain or replace assessment.
takeaway: Match pain tools to demonstrated developmental understanding.
learningObjective: Match pain tools to demonstrated developmental understanding.

title: Comfort during a blood draw
stem: A four-year-old needs venipuncture and wants a parent nearby. Which actions support coping? Select all that apply.
options: Use an agreed safe comfort position
Promise the needle will not hurt
Use detailed anatomical terminology to explain the procedure
Offer an age-appropriate distraction choice
why: Supportive positioning can improve security during the procedure.
An inaccurate promise may undermine trust.
A four-year-old needs simple concrete preparation matched to understanding, rather than technical anatomical detail.
A chosen suitable distraction can reduce procedural distress.
takeaway: Prepare honestly and use developmentally appropriate comfort support.
learningObjective: Prepare honestly and use developmentally appropriate comfort support.

title: School-age privacy
stem: A school-age child receiving hygiene assistance becomes embarrassed when visitors enter. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain the child's care needs in front of visitors
Ask the parent to choose without involving the child
Restore privacy and ask about participation preferences
Finish the exposed part of care before asking the visitors to leave
why: That may increase unwanted disclosure and embarrassment.
The child's developmental ability supports meaningful participation.
School-age children benefit from control over exposure and self-care.
Restore privacy promptly rather than prolonging the child’s discomfort.
takeaway: Include children in choices about privacy and personal care.
learningObjective: Include children in choices about privacy and personal care.

title: Child routine and sleep
stem: A stable hospitalized child has difficulty settling without the usual bedtime story. What is the most useful plan?
options: Explain the entire hospital schedule at bedtime
Incorporate the familiar routine when feasible
Move bedtime later until the child is exhausted
Use the ward’s standard bedtime activity instead of the usual story
why: Detailed information may stimulate rather than settle the child.
Predictable cues can support sleep in an unfamiliar setting.
Exhaustion can increase distress and does not restore routine.
A standard substitute may not provide the familiar settling cue the child is missing.
takeaway: Preserve familiar sleep cues during hospitalization.
learningObjective: Preserve familiar sleep cues during hospitalization.

title: Infant feeding cues
stem: During a bottle feed, an infant turns away, relaxes the hands, and stops sucking. Breathing is comfortable. What should the nurse do?
options: Pause and assess whether feeding is complete
Encourage finishing because a fixed volume remains
Increase nipple flow to shorten the feed
Repeatedly reposition the nipple to trigger sucking
why: Satiety and disengagement cues guide responsive feeding.
A remaining volume alone does not override feeding cues.
Faster flow may overwhelm the infant's coordination.
Repeated prompting may disregard satiety or fatigue.
takeaway: Respond to infant feeding cues rather than volume alone.
learningObjective: Respond to infant feeding cues rather than volume alone.

title: Bottle-flow assessment
stem: An infant coughs and gulps with a new faster-flow nipple but previously fed comfortably. What should the nurse do first?
options: Continue until the infant learns the new flow
Increase the bottle angle to speed completion
Add thickener without an assessed prescription
Pause feeding and reassess flow and coordination
why: Repeated coughing signals a current safety problem.
Faster delivery may worsen the mismatch.
Consistency changes require an appropriate feeding plan.
The timing suggests flow may exceed the infant's capacity.
takeaway: Assess nipple flow when feeding coordination changes.
learningObjective: Assess nipple flow when feeding coordination changes.

title: Breastfeeding position comfort
stem: A breastfeeding parent reports back strain from leaning toward the infant. Which adjustment best addresses the observed posture?
options: Suggest shorter feeds before assessing positioning
Place support only beneath the parent's feet
Bring the supported infant toward the breast
Raise the feeding chair while leaving the infant at the same unsupported height
why: Reducing feeding time does not correct the posture.
Foot support may help but does not directly bring the infant closer.
Adequate support reduces prolonged forward bending.
Changing the chair alone may preserve the need to lean; support the infant near the breast.
takeaway: Support the infant and parent to reduce feeding-related strain.
learningObjective: Support the infant and parent to reduce feeding-related strain.

title: Feeding access after surgery
stem: A parent recovering from abdominal surgery wants to feed their infant without pressure on the incision. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Keep the usual position and shorten each feed when the incision hurts
Assist a supported position avoiding incision pressure
Use the usual cross-body position with a pillow pressing against the incision
Arrange for staff to give every feed while the parent remains in bed
why: Shortening feeds does not correct the mechanical pressure and may interfere with feeding.
Position adaptation can preserve the parent's chosen feeding role.
A pillow is not helpful if it maintains pressure on the painful area; individualize support.
Temporary help may be useful, but full substitution is unnecessary if a comfortable supported position is feasible.
takeaway: Adapt infant-holding positions to postoperative comfort and ability.
learningObjective: Adapt infant-holding positions to postoperative comfort and ability.

title: Small frequent fluids
stem: A child with mild gastroenteritis is alert and has an oral-rehydration plan. Large drinks provoke vomiting. What should the nurse try?
options: Offer the prescribed solution in small frequent amounts
Give the full planned amount rapidly again
Substitute undiluted juice without reviewing the plan
Withhold the planned solution until the next scheduled meal
why: Smaller volumes may be better tolerated.
Repeated large volumes reproduce the trigger.
High-sugar drinks may worsen gastrointestinal symptoms.
Prolonged interruption may worsen dehydration; use smaller tolerated amounts according to the plan.
takeaway: Use small frequent volumes within the oral-rehydration plan.
learningObjective: Use small frequent volumes within the oral-rehydration plan.

title: Nappy-area irritation
stem: An infant has superficial irritation after frequent stools. Which care measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use gentle cleansing and the recommended barrier
Use perfumed wipes repeatedly until the area feels dry
Apply a thicker barrier layer and extend the interval between changes
Change soiled nappies promptly
why: This protects fragile skin without excessive friction.
Fragrance and repeated rubbing may worsen irritation.
Barrier products do not replace reducing contact with stool and moisture.
Reduced stool contact limits further irritation.
takeaway: Limit irritant contact and friction in nappy-area care.
learningObjective: Limit irritant contact and friction in nappy-area care.

title: Toilet-training regression
stem: A toilet-trained preschooler has accidents during hospitalization and appears distressed. What should the nurse do?
options: Restart a demanding training schedule immediately
Wait for the child to manage without reminders
Assess illness-related barriers and offer supportive routines
Use the pre-admission toileting schedule unchanged because the child was trained
why: Acute illness may reduce readiness for intensive training.
Temporary support may be needed in the unfamiliar environment.
Unfamiliar surroundings and illness can disrupt toileting skills.
Illness and an unfamiliar environment may change timing, access or readiness; assess current barriers.
takeaway: Support toileting during illness without blaming developmental regression.
learningObjective: Support toileting during illness without blaming developmental regression.

title: Adolescent self-care
stem: An adolescent with a temporary arm cast wants to manage bathing privately. What is the best plan?
options: Use a sponge bath chosen by staff without asking which tasks the adolescent can manage
Agree on safe adaptations and available help
Have the parent perform the whole bath
Assume complete independence because of age
why: A safe plan should incorporate retained ability and privacy preferences.
Planning balances privacy with temporary functional limits.
The adolescent may retain substantial independent ability.
A cast creates specific needs regardless of maturity.
takeaway: Balance adolescent privacy with assessed physical assistance needs.
learningObjective: Balance adolescent privacy with assessed physical assistance needs.

title: Perineal postpartum comfort
stem: A postpartum client reports perineal stinging when urine contacts a repaired tear. Vital signs and wound findings are reassuring. What should the nurse discuss?
options: Review gentle rinsing during voiding and the prescribed comfort plan
Reducing fluids to avoid urinating
Use a strong antiseptic wash after every void
Use fragranced wipes after voiding to reduce the sensation of irritation
why: Gentle appropriate perineal care may reduce urine-contact irritation while continued assessment identifies new concerns.
Restriction may concentrate urine and worsen discomfort.
Unprescribed harsh products can irritate healing tissue; use the recommended gentle method.
Fragrance may irritate healing tissue rather than address urine-contact stinging.
takeaway: Target local postpartum discomfort without compromising hydration or hygiene.
learningObjective: Target local postpartum discomfort without compromising hydration or hygiene.

title: Pregnancy rest positioning
stem: A pregnant client in the third trimester becomes lightheaded while lying flat for care. What should the nurse do first?
options: Finish the care quickly before repositioning
Raise only the feet while remaining flat
Raise the head slightly while leaving the client mostly supine
Assist a side-lying position and reassess
why: Continuing flat may prolong symptoms.
This may not relieve the source of vessel compression.
A small head lift may not relieve uterine vessel compression; side-lying more directly addresses the positional cue.
Uterine pressure while supine can impair venous return.
takeaway: Respond to late-pregnancy supine symptoms with repositioning and reassessment.
learningObjective: Respond to late-pregnancy supine symptoms with repositioning and reassessment.

title: Infant oral comfort
stem: A caregiver reports an infant becoming fussy during feeds with persistent white oral patches. What should the nurse do?
options: Change to a faster nipple to complete feeding before the infant becomes fussy
Assume milk residue without checking persistence and tissue
Assess the mouth and arrange appropriate clinical review
Wipe repeatedly with gauze and continue until all white areas are removed
why: A flow change does not address possible painful lesions and can create feeding difficulty.
A description alone cannot reliably distinguish residue from lesions.
Painful persistent patches may affect feeding and need treatment.
Persistent adherent patches should be assessed rather than repeatedly rubbed, which may damage tissue.
takeaway: Assess persistent oral changes that interfere with infant feeding.
learningObjective: Assess persistent oral changes that interfere with infant feeding.

title: Sensory-sensitive child
stem: A child becomes distressed by bright lights and several staff talking during routine care. Which plan best supports comfort?
options: Complete the care with fewer explanations so the encounter ends sooner
Reduce simultaneous stimuli and use a predictable approach
Explain the procedure with several staff at once
Complete all care rapidly without warning
why: Reducing information without agreed predictable cues may increase uncertainty and distress.
The observed triggers suggest benefit from a calmer setting.
Multiple voices may intensify the identified overload.
Unpredictable touch may increase distress.
takeaway: Adapt stimulation and predictability to the child's observed needs.
learningObjective: Adapt stimulation and predictability to the child's observed needs.

title: Juvenile arthritis self-care
stem: A child with morning hand stiffness struggles with buttons but improves later. Which plan best supports school preparation?
options: Allow extra time and use easier fastenings
Practise the usual buttons repeatedly before leaving to build speed
Have an adult dress the child for every task
Schedule all dressing practice at peak stiffness
why: Timing and adaptation address stiffness without removing participation.
Practice at peak stiffness may increase pain and delay preparation; adapt timing and fastenings.
The child may manage much of dressing with adaptation.
Practice should account for pain and functional tolerance.
takeaway: Adapt daily routines to predictable variation in joint function.
learningObjective: Adapt daily routines to predictable variation in joint function.

title: Older adult thirst access
stem: An older adult drinks little because the jug is too heavy but readily accepts a light cup. Which change best addresses the problem?
options: Provide a larger jug less often
Focus only on explaining dehydration risks
Document refusal whenever the jug remains full
Offer accessible lightweight drink containers
why: A heavier container may worsen access.
Knowledge does not solve the grip and lifting problem.
Unused inaccessible fluid is not necessarily refusal.
The observed barrier is handling rather than dislike of fluids.
takeaway: Distinguish inability to access fluids from unwillingness to drink.
learningObjective: Distinguish inability to access fluids from unwillingness to drink.

title: Arthritis meal preparation
stem: A client with painful hands can eat independently but struggles to open meal packages. Which assistance is best?
options: Replace every meal with liquids
Encourage repeated forceful package twisting
Open difficult packaging and preserve self-feeding
Feed the entire meal to avoid hand use
why: Liquid substitution may restrict nutrition and choice unnecessarily.
This may increase pain without improving access.
Targeted setup addresses the barrier without replacing retained skills.
Complete feeding is unnecessary based on current ability.
takeaway: Provide setup assistance when the eating skill itself is intact.
learningObjective: Provide setup assistance when the eating skill itself is intact.

title: Visual impairment orientation
stem: A client with longstanding blindness receives a meal in an unfamiliar setting. Which assistance is useful?
options: Name foods without describing their positions
Describe food locations consistently and ask preferences
Move dishes repeatedly to make more room
Begin feeding without discussing ability
why: Food identity alone may not provide adequate access.
Clear spatial information supports independent eating.
Changing locations can disrupt the orientation provided.
Blindness alone does not imply feeding dependence.
takeaway: Orient food placement using an agreed consistent method.
learningObjective: Orient food placement using an agreed consistent method.

title: Hearing support in care
stem: A client answers hygiene questions incorrectly when staff wear masks and speak from the doorway. What should the nurse try first?
options: Face the client and use accessible communication
Increase voice volume from the same doorway position
Assume the client has new cognitive decline
Ask a relative to answer every preference question
why: Distance and lost visual cues may explain the misunderstanding.
Volume alone may not restore visual cues or speech clarity; establish accessible communication.
Communication barriers should be addressed before that inference.
The client may communicate directly with suitable support.
takeaway: Correct communication barriers before inferring impaired understanding.
learningObjective: Correct communication barriers before inferring impaired understanding.

title: Caregiver respite for routines
stem: A home caregiver is exhausted and begins missing a dependent client's evening care. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Provide a longer checklist without discussing workload
Assume the caregiver no longer wants involvement
Move the evening tasks to a longer morning routine without reviewing workload
Assess essential needs and arrange sustainable support
why: More instructions do not create additional capacity.
Exhaustion does not establish unwillingness.
Rescheduling may shift rather than solve overload; assess needs and practical support.
Reliable assistance protects care while addressing caregiver capacity.
takeaway: Match home-care routines to realistic caregiver capacity.
learningObjective: Match home-care routines to realistic caregiver capacity.

title: Personal ritual at meals
stem: A client wishes to say a short prayer before assisted feeding. Food remains safely warm. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the client to postpone the prayer until after feeding so the meal round stays on schedule
Ask family to perform the ritual elsewhere
Allow the ritual before beginning
Begin feeding while the client prays
why: A brief safe preference can be accommodated without overriding the client’s preparation ritual.
The client asked to participate personally before eating.
The request can be accommodated without compromising intake.
This interrupts the requested preparation and attention to eating.
takeaway: Accommodate meaningful mealtime practices when clinically feasible.
learningObjective: Accommodate meaningful mealtime practices when clinically feasible.

title: Adaptive equipment outcome
stem: A client tries a plate guard for one-handed eating. Which observation most directly shows benefit?
options: The nurse completes feeding more quickly
More food reaches the mouth without assistance
The client can explain how the guard attaches
The guard stays attached on an unused plate
why: Staff speed does not measure the client's independence.
This measures the functional task the device targets.
Knowledge does not establish successful eating performance.
Equipment stability alone does not demonstrate feeding benefit.
takeaway: Evaluate feeding aids through actual task performance.
learningObjective: Evaluate feeding aids through actual task performance.

title: Parkinson freezing episode
stem: A client with Parkinson disease freezes at a doorway but remains balanced with assistance. Their therapy plan includes external movement cues. What should the nurse try?
options: Use the rehearsed stepping cue
Pull the client forward to start the step
Ask for faster steps immediately
Give several different instructions at once
why: A familiar cue can help initiate movement during freezing.
External pulling can destabilize the client without restoring controlled movement.
Rushing may worsen initiation and balance.
Competing instructions can increase motor-planning demands.
takeaway: Use the individual's rehearsed cue during gait freezing.
learningObjective: Use the individual's rehearsed cue during gait freezing.

title: Predictable mobility periods
stem: A client with Parkinson disease transfers more easily during a predictable period of better movement. What should guide nonurgent bathing?
options: Keep a fixed unit time despite repeated difficulty
Complete bathing before the client is fully awake
Increase transfer repetitions during the difficult period
Schedule it during the observed better-function period
why: A rigid schedule ignores a useful functional pattern.
Reduced alertness may increase assistance needs.
Extra attempts do not use the more effective time window.
Timing can reduce effort and improve participation.
takeaway: Schedule demanding care when the client's function is best.
learningObjective: Schedule demanding care when the client's function is best.

title: Residual-limb sock wrinkle
stem: A prosthesis user reports localized stump discomfort, and a wrinkle is found in the prescribed sock. What should the nurse do?
options: Shorten walking distance but leave the fit unchanged
Use analgesia before inspecting the limb
Remove the prosthesis and assess the pressure area
Add another sock over the wrinkle
why: Reduced exposure does not correct the pressure source.
Pain control should not delay assessment of a mechanical injury.
A focal wrinkle can create tissue injury beneath the socket.
Additional bulk may increase pressure without removing the cause.
takeaway: Investigate focal discomfort beneath a prosthesis before further use.
learningObjective: Investigate focal discomfort beneath a prosthesis before further use.

title: Phantom limb pain
stem: After amputation, a client describes painful toes on the absent foot. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Use relaxation first and assess the absent-foot pain only if it persists
Assess the pain and discuss the prescribed management plan
Reassure that absent tissue cannot generate pain
Record only discomfort in the surgical incision
why: An adjunct does not replace initial assessment of a real reported pain experience.
Phantom pain is a real experience requiring assessment.
This dismisses a recognized pain phenomenon.
That omits the distinct pain the client describes.
takeaway: Recognize phantom pain as distinct from residual-limb wound pain.
learningObjective: Recognize phantom pain as distinct from residual-limb wound pain.

title: Amputation positioning plan
stem: A client after above-knee amputation has a prescribed positioning programme to maintain hip extension. Which practice needs review?
options: Resting with the hip flexed over pillows for long periods
Following the therapist's tolerated extension positions
Reporting incision discomfort during an exercise
Changing position with trained assistance
why: Prolonged flexion opposes the extension goal.
Prescribed positioning supports the stated rehabilitation goal.
Symptoms help adapt the plan safely.
Assistance supports participation within current ability.
takeaway: Match resting positions to the prescribed contracture-prevention goal.
learningObjective: Match resting positions to the prescribed contracture-prevention goal.

title: Heat-sensitive fatigue
stem: A client with multiple sclerosis becomes exhausted after a hot shower but manages a cooler seated wash well. What is the best plan?
options: Repeat the hot shower to build tolerance
Move the hot shower later without changing temperature
Have staff complete the same hot shower faster
Use the tolerated cooler seated method
why: Repeated heat exposure may reproduce symptom worsening.
Timing alone does not address the observed trigger.
Reduced duration may not remove heat sensitivity.
The client's response identifies a practical energy-conserving adaptation.
takeaway: Use observed temperature and activity tolerance to adapt hygiene.
learningObjective: Use observed temperature and activity tolerance to adapt hygiene.

title: Communication during dependent care
stem: An adult with motor neuron disease understands care but cannot speak or move the hands. Eye-gaze communication is reliable. What should the nurse do?
options: Interpret silence as agreement
Use a standard written checklist for the client to mark independently
Use eye-gaze choices before positioning and care
Rely on family for every choice
why: Motor impairment does not establish consent or preference.
The client cannot move their hands; use the established accessible eye-gaze method.
A reliable communication route preserves preferences and participation.
The client can communicate directly through an established method.
takeaway: Use the established communication method during dependent physical care.
learningObjective: Use the established communication method during dependent physical care.

title: Reflux at bedtime
stem: A client with reflux reports symptoms after a large late supper and lying down immediately. Which plan best targets that pattern?
options: Use only a bedtime diary without changing the trigger
Trial an earlier smaller meal and remain upright afterward
Keep the late meal time but remove one suspected food without changing meal size or recumbency
Add a larger evening drink before lying down
why: Monitoring alone does not address the identified pattern.
Meal size and recumbency are relevant modifiable triggers.
Food triggers may matter, but this does not address the observed large late meal and immediate lying down.
Extra gastric volume may worsen symptoms.
takeaway: Match reflux self-care to meal timing and posture triggers.
learningObjective: Match reflux self-care to meal timing and posture triggers.

title: Bedding pressure and gout
stem: A client with acute gout says even the sheet touching the toe is painful. What comfort intervention is most appropriate?
options: Use an appropriate support to keep bedding off the toe
Tuck the sheet tightly to prevent movement
Use a thinner sheet but tuck it firmly against the foot
Massage the toe before replacing the sheet
why: This removes the specific contact stimulus.
Tension increases contact pressure on the painful toe.
Reduced weight does not remove the painful contact stimulus.
Touch and movement may intensify the acute joint pain.
takeaway: Remove avoidable contact pressure from a highly tender joint.
learningObjective: Remove avoidable contact pressure from a highly tender joint.

title: Taste changes during treatment
stem: A client reports a metallic taste during treatment and eats less, without dysphagia. Which approach is most useful?
options: Insist on the usual menu until taste normalizes
Choose a fixed low-protein menu before asking which foods are tolerated
Increase every portion before checking preferences
Trial tolerated foods and utensils while tracking intake
why: The current menu is not supporting adequate intake.
A broad preset restriction can reduce intake and does not identify individual tolerance.
More disliked food does not address altered taste.
Individual experiments can identify acceptable options and protect nutrition.
takeaway: Individualize food choices when taste changes reduce intake.
learningObjective: Individualize food choices when taste changes reduce intake.

title: Mucositis food choice
stem: A client with painful oral mucositis can swallow safely. Which offered food is most likely to be tolerated?
options: Hot tomato soup with crackers
Salted chips with a fizzy drink
Smooth cool custard without irritating additions
Crisp toast with citrus marmalade
why: Heat, acidity, and rough pieces may increase discomfort.
Sharp texture and carbonation can irritate sore tissue.
A soft nonacidic texture reduces mucosal irritation.
Rough texture and acidity may aggravate lesions.
takeaway: Choose soft nonirritating foods when oral mucosa is painful.
learningObjective: Choose soft nonirritating foods when oral mucosa is painful.

title: Meal pace with involuntary movement
stem: A client with involuntary movements spills food and tires during meals. Which assessments most directly determine safe individualized feeding assistance? Select all that apply.
options: The usual total duration of the unit meal service
Trunk support and utensil control
Swallowing safety and endurance
The number of staff assigned to the dining area
why: A service schedule does not assess the client’s motor, swallowing or endurance needs.
Postural and motor findings identify practical adaptations.
These determine safe pace and the level of support.
Staffing affects delivery but does not establish the individual level of feeding assistance.
takeaway: Assess posture, motor control, swallowing, and endurance when movement disrupts eating.
learningObjective: Assess posture, motor control, swallowing, and endurance when movement disrupts eating.

title: Low-vision contrast
stem: A client with low vision misses pale food on a white plate despite wearing the prescribed glasses. Which adaptation should the nurse trial?
options: Use a contrasting plate with adequate lighting
Use a larger white plate while keeping the same lighting
Move the plate repeatedly during eating
Provide verbal food names without adjusting visibility
why: Contrast improves visual distinction when acuity remains limited.
Size alone does not fix poor food-to-plate contrast.
Movement can make localization less predictable.
Naming helps but leaves the demonstrated contrast barrier unchanged.
takeaway: Use contrast and lighting to improve access for low vision.
learningObjective: Use contrast and lighting to improve access for low vision.

title: Ostomy body comfort
stem: A client with a secure colostomy pouch worries its bulk will interfere with a social outing. Which practical discussion is appropriate?
options: Skip the meal before the outing to keep the pouch empty
Advise a very tight belt over the stoma
Suggest changing the whole appliance after every small output
Plan pouch emptying and comfortable clothing before leaving
why: Skipping food does not reliably eliminate output and may unnecessarily restrict nutrition and participation.
Compression may cause discomfort and interfere with the appliance.
Unnecessary changes can irritate skin and increase burden.
Preparation can reduce bulk while supporting participation.
takeaway: Plan practical pouch care around valued social activities.
learningObjective: Plan practical pouch care around valued social activities.

title: Transfer-board preparation
stem: A client trained for a seated transfer-board technique cannot stand. Which setup issue should be corrected before starting?
options: The client follows the taught hand-placement sequence
The required assistant is present
A large height difference between the two surfaces
The wheelchair is positioned near the bed
why: Following the trained method supports controlled movement.
Trained assistance supports the prescribed transfer plan.
An unsuitable slope can make the lateral transfer unsafe.
Close positioning reduces the gap when set up appropriately.
takeaway: Check surface height and alignment for transfer-board movement.
learningObjective: Check surface height and alignment for transfer-board movement.

title: Standing tolerance evaluation
stem: A client practising standing for dressing can now stand two minutes with the prescribed aid and no dizziness. Which finding best supports progressing the task?
options: The client completed seated exercises yesterday
Maintained balance and tolerable symptoms during practice
The walking aid has been adjusted to the prescribed height
The planned discharge date is closer
why: Seated exercise does not directly establish current standing ability.
Observed safe performance supports a graded next step.
Correct equipment setup is necessary but does not alone show current balance or symptom tolerance.
A schedule cannot replace functional evidence.
takeaway: Progress standing tasks using observed balance and symptom tolerance.
learningObjective: Progress standing tasks using observed balance and symptom tolerance.

title: Arthritis joint protection
stem: A client with painful finger joints twists a small stiff tap repeatedly during hygiene. Which adaptation best reduces the specific strain?
options: Use a suitable lever attachment
Practise tighter gripping until the tap turns
Ask the client to wash less often
Replace the small tap with another round tap of the same diameter
why: A lever reduces the need for forceful small-joint gripping.
Greater force may aggravate painful joints.
Reducing hygiene does not solve the equipment barrier.
A similar round grip may retain the painful twisting demand; a suitable lever changes the task.
takeaway: Adapt controls to reduce painful small-joint loading.
learningObjective: Adapt controls to reduce painful small-joint loading.

title: Splint wearing tolerance
stem: A client develops sweating and itch beneath a prescribed removable wrist splint, without injury. What should the nurse review?
options: Keep the splint on longer to improve adaptation
Apply powder beneath it without checking compatibility
Shorten daily wear independently before discussing the prescribed schedule
Skin care and the prescribed removal schedule
why: More uninterrupted wear may worsen moisture irritation.
Products can affect skin or device fit and require appropriate guidance.
Changing therapeutic wear time should be coordinated while skin irritation and safe care are reviewed.
Moisture control and planned inspection can improve tolerance.
takeaway: Review skin care and wearing instructions when splint tolerance changes.
learningObjective: Review skin care and wearing instructions when splint tolerance changes.

title: Home bath access
stem: A client can wash independently but cannot step safely over the bath edge. Which referral goal is most useful?
options: Teach a longer washing sequence
Recommend more upper-body exercise before any equipment review
Assess bathing equipment and the entry method
Arrange complete bed baths indefinitely without assessment
why: Technique within the bath does not solve entry difficulty.
Exercise alone may not address the immediate access problem.
The main barrier is access rather than washing ability.
A suitable adaptation may preserve preferred independent bathing.
takeaway: Separate access barriers from ability to perform self-care once positioned.
learningObjective: Separate access barriers from ability to perform self-care once positioned.

title: Night-time leg comfort
stem: A client reports leg discomfort after prolonged dependent sitting; the established plan permits elevation. Which outcome should guide evaluation of the position?
options: The pillows remain exactly where staff placed them
Symptoms improve without numbness or skin pressure
The feet are as high as possible
The client remains in one position all night
why: Equipment placement does not itself demonstrate clinical benefit.
Comfort benefit must be accompanied by acceptable tissue tolerance.
Maximum height is not the goal and may reduce tolerance.
Prolonged unvaried positioning can create pressure.
takeaway: Evaluate limb positioning by relief and tissue tolerance.
learningObjective: Evaluate limb positioning by relief and tissue tolerance.

title: Recorded oral intake
stem: A client is served 150mL tea, 90mL milk and 60mL water. They leave 30mL of tea and finish the milk and water. What oral fluid intake should be recorded? Use mL.
options: 270mL
300mL
240mL
210mL
why: Actual intake is (150−30)+90+60=270mL.
300mL is the amount served, before subtracting the tea left.
240mL omits the water rather than subtracting the measured tea remainder.
210mL subtracts the milk rather than the measured remainder.
takeaway: Record the amount actually consumed, accounting for measured leftovers.
learningObjective: Calculate measured oral intake by subtracting leftovers from the amounts served.

title: Meal supplement contribution
stem: A prescribed supplement provides 200 kcal per 100 mL. A client drinks 150 mL. How much energy was consumed? Use whole kcal.
options: 200 kcal
150 kcal
400 kcal
300 kcal
why: This assumes only the labelled 100 mL portion was consumed.
This incorrectly equates millilitres with kilocalories.
This counts 200 mL rather than the measured 150 mL.
Two kcal per mL multiplied by 150 mL equals 300 kcal.
takeaway: Use the label concentration and actual amount consumed.
learningObjective: Use the label concentration and actual amount consumed.

title: Care-related embarrassment
stem: A client avoids asking for continence help because they fear being a burden. Which response best supports timely basic care?
options: Offer more absorbent products without discussing the concern
Ask family to remind staff at each visit instead of agreeing a direct request method
Agree on a discreet request method and expected support
Tell the client to wait until routine rounds
why: Containment alone does not address reluctance to request help.
Intermittent reminders do not provide a reliable immediate way for the client to obtain assistance.
A concrete plan addresses the barrier to seeking assistance.
Waiting may increase leakage and distress.
takeaway: Make assistance requests accessible and dignified.
learningObjective: Make assistance requests accessible and dignified.

title: Rest after exertion
stem: A stable client becomes tired after therapy and asks to postpone a nonurgent shower until afternoon. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete both activities consecutively to free the afternoon
Reassess tolerance and negotiate a later time
Keep the original time because supplies are ready
Shorten tomorrow’s therapy before reassessing today’s task sequence
why: Additional exertion may exceed the client's present endurance.
Planned rest can support participation in both activities.
Preparation does not establish current activity tolerance.
One tired interval should prompt current pacing review rather than unilateral reduction of rehabilitation.
takeaway: Coordinate rehabilitation and personal care around recovery periods.
learningObjective: Coordinate rehabilitation and personal care around recovery periods.

title: Home comfort plan review
stem: A client says the written comfort plan is too complex to use when symptoms worsen. What should the nurse do?
options: Simplify it around agreed actions and reassess teach-back
Add more background information to every step
Ask the client to highlight the current document and keep the full sequence
Give the same document to a relative without checking who is available during symptoms
why: Usable instructions improve the chance of effective self-care.
Extra detail may worsen the stated usability problem.
Highlighting may help some readers but does not necessarily resolve the reported complexity; agree usable actions and check understanding.
A support person can help, but availability and understanding must be assessed alongside a usable client plan.
takeaway: Make comfort instructions usable under the conditions in which they are needed.
learningObjective: Make comfort instructions usable under the conditions in which they are needed.

title: Unexpected cuff reading
stem: A comfortable client has a new high automated blood pressure. The cuff barely closes around a large upper arm. What should happen first?
options: Request extra antihypertensive medication immediately
Repeat on the same arm with the same cuff
Compare with a reading taken last month only
Repeat using the correct cuff size
why: Treatment should not rely on a visibly unsuitable measurement setup.
Repetition preserves the identified source of error.
Historical values cannot validate today's technique.
An undersized cuff can overestimate pressure.
takeaway: Correct an identified measurement problem before interpreting an isolated result.
learningObjective: Correct an identified measurement problem before interpreting an isolated result.

title: Irregular pulse count
stem: A client reports intermittent palpitations. The radial pulse is irregular during a short count. Which assessment is most useful next?
options: Repeat only after the next scheduled round
Use the automated blood-pressure machine’s displayed pulse rate as the complete rhythm assessment
Count the apical pulse for a full minute
Multiply a ten-second count by six
why: Symptoms and a new irregularity need timely assessment.
An automated displayed rate does not replace assessment of a symptomatic irregular rhythm.
A full assessment better characterizes an irregular rhythm.
A brief sample may misrepresent an irregular rate.
takeaway: Use a full-minute assessment for an irregular pulse.
learningObjective: Use a full-minute assessment for an irregular pulse.

title: Respiratory sampling
stem: A postoperative client has shallow irregular breaths after analgesia. Which observation is most useful for detecting deterioration?
options: Whether the client denies pain
Rate, depth, and alertness together
A fifteen-second count alone
Oxygen saturation without examining the client
why: Pain relief does not establish respiratory safety.
Ventilation adequacy involves more than respiratory frequency.
A short count may miss irregularity and reduced depth.
Supplemental oxygen may mask inadequate ventilation.
takeaway: Assess respiratory depth and consciousness alongside rate.
learningObjective: Assess respiratory depth and consciousness alongside rate.

title: Capillary glucose contamination
stem: A well client has an unexpectedly high finger-stick result after peeling an orange. What is the best first response?
options: Wash and dry the hands, then repeat
Administer correction insulin from the unconfirmed result
Wipe only with a dry tissue and repeat
Document the result as the new baseline
why: Sugar residue can falsely elevate a capillary reading.
Treatment could be inappropriate if the sample was contaminated.
A dry wipe may leave surface sugar residue.
A potentially contaminated result requires verification.
takeaway: Use clean dry hands for reliable capillary glucose testing.
learningObjective: Use clean dry hands for reliable capillary glucose testing.

title: Weight trend technique
stem: A client's weight appears to rise sharply, but today's measurement used a different scale and heavy clothing. Which action improves interpretation?
options: Average both measurements immediately
Assume fluid overload without assessment
Convert today’s weight by subtracting a standard clothing allowance without reweighing
Repeat under comparable measurement conditions
why: Averaging does not correct incompatible conditions.
Measurement differences may explain some of the apparent change.
An assumed clothing correction does not account for scale differences or actual clothing weight.
Standardization helps distinguish real change from measurement variation.
takeaway: Use consistent conditions when interpreting weight trends.
learningObjective: Use consistent conditions when interpreting weight trends.

title: Urine trend verification
stem: A stable postoperative client's chart shows no urine for six hours, but a family member reports two toilet visits. What should the nurse do?
options: Label the charted absence as oliguria and request treatment before checking the reported voids
Enter estimated volumes from memory
Clarify and assess the missing output
Report confirmed anuria from the chart
why: Assess and reconcile the conflicting information before presenting absent output as confirmed.
Unmeasured voids should not be documented as measured amounts.
Incomplete recording may mimic reduced renal output.
The chart conflicts with reported voiding and needs verification.
takeaway: Verify missing output without inventing volumes.
learningObjective: Verify missing output without inventing volumes.

title: Platelet result context
stem: A client awaiting an invasive procedure has platelets 48 × 10⁹/L; the laboratory range is 150–400. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Proceed because haemoglobin is normal
Notify the procedural team before proceeding
Record it for routine discharge teaching
Repeat routine vital signs as the sole response
why: Haemoglobin does not measure platelet-mediated clotting.
Marked thrombocytopenia increases procedural bleeding risk.
The result affects today's procedure safety.
Normal vital signs do not remove the bleeding risk.
takeaway: Escalate abnormal platelets before an invasive procedure.
learningObjective: Escalate abnormal platelets before an invasive procedure.

title: Anaemia trend
stem: A postoperative client's haemoglobin falls from 126 to 89 g/L with increasing dizziness on sitting. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess for bleeding and promptly escalate
Attribute the fall to IV-fluid dilution and continue routine observation without assessing symptoms
Repeat the blood sample before checking circulation because a laboratory error is possible
Hold the next anticoagulant dose and wait for the next routine review without contacting the team
why: The symptomatic decline needs evaluation for blood loss.
Dilution can affect the value, but new dizziness with this decline needs assessment for bleeding/perfusion.
Confirmation may be appropriate, but should not delay assessing a symptomatic client.
Medication decisions do not replace prompt evaluation of possible acute bleeding.
takeaway: Interpret haemoglobin changes together with symptoms and timing.
learningObjective: Interpret haemoglobin changes together with symptoms and timing.

title: Renal baseline
stem: A dehydrated adult’s creatinine rises from 70 to 145 µmol/L in two days. Which interpretations should guide the nurse’s report? Select all that apply.
options: Recent medicines and contrast exposure may help explain the change
A potassium result within range would exclude important renal impairment
A normal voiding frequency would show that the creatinine rise is insignificant
Urine volumes and fluid balance help characterize the current response
why: Potential renal stressors should be reported with the acute trend.
A potassium result alone cannot exclude renal impairment.
Frequency does not establish total output or negate the acute creatinine change.
Measured output and balance help describe renal and volume status alongside the laboratory trend.
takeaway: Communicate renal trends with output and relevant exposures.
learningObjective: Communicate renal trends with output and relevant exposures.

title: Sodium symptoms
stem: A client has sodium 122 mmol/L (reference 135–145) and new confusion. What is the best response?
options: Request a repeat sodium before checking neurological status because the first value may be erroneous
Repeat the orientation check after a rest period before reporting the sodium result
Promptly assess neurological status and escalate
Apply a fluid restriction without reporting the new confusion or clarifying the cause
why: Verification must not delay assessment of a symptomatic electrolyte abnormality.
A new neurological change with sodium 122 needs prompt evaluation, not normalization.
Neurological change with marked hyponatraemia needs urgent review.
Treatment depends on clinical cause and symptoms; a unilateral restriction does not replace urgent assessment/escalation.
takeaway: Pair electrolyte results with neurological findings when setting urgency.
learningObjective: Pair electrolyte results with neurological findings when setting urgency.

title: Sample haemolysis
stem: A stable adult has potassium 6.7 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) in a sample labelled significantly haemolysed. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Wait for the routine morning laboratory draw because haemolysis usually raises potassium
Assess and urgently arrange verification with the team
Use a normal pulse rate to decide that the elevated value is an artefact
Treat the value as definitive without noting haemolysis
why: Possible artefact does not exclude dangerous true hyperkalaemia.
Assess promptly and urgently verify with the team; specimen quality affects interpretation.
A normal pulse rate does not exclude clinically important hyperkalaemia.
The haemolysis warning is relevant to verification and treatment decisions.
takeaway: Investigate unreliable critical results promptly rather than dismissing them.
learningObjective: Investigate unreliable critical results promptly rather than dismissing them.

title: Inflammatory marker limits
stem: A client's white-cell count is mildly elevated after surgery, but they are afebrile and stable. What is the best interpretation?
options: Assess the trend and other clinical findings
Diagnose wound infection immediately
Conclude infection is impossible without fever
Request antibiotics solely from the count
why: A white-cell rise alone does not establish infection.
The isolated result lacks local or systemic infection evidence.
Afebrile clients can still develop infection.
Treatment requires clinical evaluation of a likely cause.
takeaway: Interpret laboratory abnormalities within the clinical picture.
learningObjective: Interpret laboratory abnormalities within the clinical picture.

title: Anticoagulation test relevance
stem: A client taking warfarin has a prescribed INR target documented in the plan. Which information is most useful when a new INR arrives?
options: Compare only with the laboratory's healthy-person range
Assume every elevated INR indicates active haemorrhage
Compare with the previous INR only, without checking the current prescribed target
Compare it with that target and bleeding findings
why: The intended therapeutic range differs from untreated values.
An elevated result indicates risk, not proof of bleeding.
A previous value may also be outside target; compare with the current therapeutic plan and clinical bleeding findings.
The individual target and symptoms guide escalation.
takeaway: Interpret anticoagulation monitoring against the prescribed therapeutic target.
learningObjective: Interpret anticoagulation monitoring against the prescribed therapeutic target.

title: Low potassium cues
stem: A client on prolonged gastric suction has potassium 2.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) and weakness. Which assessment deserves priority?
options: Test leg strength in detail before checking the pulse and rhythm
Assess oral intake and gastric losses before obtaining current cardiac findings
Cardiac rate and rhythm with escalation
Repeat assessment of bowel motility
why: Confirming the weakness does not take priority over the potential cardiac conduction complication.
Loss history matters, but cardiac assessment should not be postponed in this symptomatic low-potassium case.
Potassium depletion can disturb cardiac conduction.
Ileus can accompany depletion, but cardiac conduction effects take priority.
takeaway: Consider cardiac complications when potassium is low.
learningObjective: Consider cardiac complications when potassium is low.

title: Albumin interpretation
stem: A client with inflammation and oedema has low albumin. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Double dietary protein without team assessment
Use a broader nutrition assessment
Diagnose poor protein intake from albumin alone
Assume normal nutrition because oedema increases weight
why: Nutrition changes should reflect the whole clinical picture.
Albumin is affected by inflammation and fluid status.
The result has important non-nutritional influences.
Fluid weight can hide loss of body tissue.
takeaway: Do not use albumin alone to diagnose malnutrition.
learningObjective: Do not use albumin alone to diagnose malnutrition.

title: Urine culture contamination
stem: A client's urine culture reports mixed flora after collection from an unclean bedpan. The client is stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Discuss recollection using the ordered clean method
Assume several simultaneous infections
Use whichever organism has the highest colony count without reviewing collection quality
Discard symptoms because the sample is poor
why: Contamination limits interpretation of the original sample.
Mixed organisms can reflect collection contamination.
A mixed contaminated specimen may not support reliable organism-specific interpretation; clinical context and recollection matter.
Symptoms still require assessment despite an unreliable specimen.
takeaway: Link culture interpretation to specimen quality.
learningObjective: Link culture interpretation to specimen quality.

title: Twenty-four-hour collection
stem: A client misses one void during a timed 24-hour urine collection. What should the nurse do?
options: Collect the next void separately and add it after the planned 24-hour endpoint
Extend collection by an arbitrary hour
Send the collection without noting the omission
Notify the laboratory and follow restart instructions
why: An extra later void does not reliably replace analytes from a missed interval; obtain laboratory guidance.
An extra hour does not reliably replace the missed sample.
The laboratory needs the limitation to interpret validity.
An incomplete timed sample may invalidate the result.
takeaway: Report omissions in timed specimens rather than concealing them.
learningObjective: Report omissions in timed specimens rather than concealing them.

title: Midstream collection
stem: An adult can independently collect a prescribed midstream urine specimen. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Catch the first urine immediately to avoid losing organisms from the sample
Rest the open lid inner-surface down on the bedside table while collecting
Begin voiding before collecting the sample
Avoid touching the inside of the container
why: The requested midstream sample begins after initial voiding.
Contact with the surface can contaminate the lid and specimen container.
Midstream collection reduces contamination from initial urethral washout.
Contact can introduce organisms into the specimen.
takeaway: Preserve clean collection technique for a midstream specimen.
learningObjective: Preserve clean collection technique for a midstream specimen.

title: Sputum quality
stem: A client submits thin clear saliva for a sputum culture. What should the nurse do?
options: Collect immediately after mouthwash without checking instructions
Coach a deep cough and recollect as ordered
Send it as adequate because volume is sufficient
Pool several saliva samples until the requested volume is reached
why: Some collection preparations may affect specimen quality.
A lower-respiratory sample is needed for the requested test.
Volume does not establish respiratory specimen quality.
Increasing saliva volume does not turn it into a lower-respiratory specimen.
takeaway: Assess whether a sample represents the site being tested.
learningObjective: Assess whether a sample represents the site being tested.

title: Occult-blood instructions
stem: A client has a home stool test kit, but its instructions differ from a previous kit. What should the nurse advise?
options: Follow the current kit's specific instructions
Apply every restriction from the old kit
Collect during visible rectal bleeding without checking guidance
Transfer a specimen into a standard urine container because all stool tests use the same preservative
why: Collection and dietary requirements vary by test method.
Unneeded restrictions can confuse or impair completion.
Active bleeding may affect interpretation and requires appropriate advice.
Collection device and preservative depend on the specific stool test; follow its current instructions.
takeaway: Use instructions specific to the test being performed.
learningObjective: Use instructions specific to the test being performed.

title: Blood culture timing
stem: Blood cultures and antibiotics are newly ordered for a deteriorating client. Collection can occur promptly. What should the nurse coordinate?
options: Wait for the next fever peak
Start the antibiotic and collect cultures at the next routine phlebotomy visit
Delay antibiotics until preliminary culture results are available
Collect cultures before antibiotics without delaying urgent care
why: Waiting can delay needed antimicrobial treatment.
When collection is promptly possible without treatment delay, pretreatment sampling improves yield.
Cultures should not delay urgent antimicrobial treatment while results are awaited.
Pre-treatment sampling improves yield while preserving timely treatment.
takeaway: Coordinate cultures and treatment without unnecessary delay.
learningObjective: Coordinate cultures and treatment without unnecessary delay.

title: Unexpected laboratory identity
stem: A laboratory result lists the correct name but a different date of birth from the client. What should happen before using it?
options: Copy it into the chart and clarify later
Ask the sending unit to confirm the name alone before accepting the result
Resolve the identification discrepancy
Accept it because names match
why: Incorrect attribution can trigger unsafe decisions.
One matching identifier does not resolve the conflicting date of birth.
Treatment requires confirmation that the result belongs to this client.
Names alone do not reliably establish identity.
takeaway: Resolve mismatched identifiers before acting on a laboratory result.
learningObjective: Resolve mismatched identifiers before acting on a laboratory result.

title: Test result follow-through
stem: A client is discharged with an important test still pending. Which actions reduce follow-up risk? Select all that apply.
options: Document the pending test without assigning anyone to review the result
Confirm who will review and communicate it
Give the client a clear follow-up contact
Assume no telephone call means a normal result
why: Recording a pending result does not establish accountable follow-up.
Named responsibility prevents results being overlooked.
The client needs a route if no result arrives.
Silence does not establish that the result was reviewed.
takeaway: Assign responsibility and a clear contact for pending results.
learningObjective: Assign responsibility and a clear contact for pending results.

title: Specimen transport delay
stem: A freshly collected urine specimen remains unrefrigerated because transport is delayed. What should the nurse do?
options: Check laboratory time and storage requirements
Send it later without noting the delay
Freeze it without laboratory guidance
Refrigerate the sample now and omit documenting how long it remained at room temperature
why: Delay can alter results and may require recollection.
Unreported delay prevents assessment of specimen suitability.
Unapproved storage can damage specimen integrity.
Later cooling does not undo the delay; the laboratory needs the time/storage history.
takeaway: Follow test-specific storage requirements when transport is delayed.
learningObjective: Follow test-specific storage requirements when transport is delayed.

title: Laboratory trend communication
stem: When reporting a clinically important laboratory change, which details most directly help the receiving clinician judge its urgency? Select all that apply.
options: Current symptoms and relevant treatment
The date of the next routine outpatient appointment
The client’s usual diet before admission
Previous value and collection times
why: The client’s response and treatment context help establish urgency and possible causes.
A routine appointment date does not show how urgently the current change needs assessment.
Background diet may add context for some results, but current symptoms and the magnitude/rate of change more directly establish urgency.
Comparing values and times shows the magnitude and rate of change.
takeaway: Communicate the result, trend, and current clinical context.
learningObjective: Communicate the result, trend, and current clinical context.

title: Bowel preparation difficulty
stem: A client preparing for colonoscopy vomits repeatedly and cannot finish the prescribed preparation. What should the nurse advise?
options: Skip the remainder without informing the team
Use an over-the-counter substitute independently
Contact the procedural team for an individualized plan
Continue the same volume rapidly
why: The bowel may be inadequately prepared for visualization.
Different preparations have different risks and instructions.
Incomplete preparation and vomiting may require revised instructions.
Faster intake may worsen vomiting and intolerance.
takeaway: Report inability to complete bowel preparation before the procedure.
learningObjective: Report inability to complete bowel preparation before the procedure.

title: After colonoscopy
stem: Several hours after colonoscopy, a client develops worsening abdominal pain and fever. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Use the routine postprocedure advice for mild gas pain and reassess after rest
Arrange urgent clinical assessment
Encourage walking for presumed retained gas only
Give the prescribed analgesic and antipyretic before deciding whether further assessment is needed
why: Worsening pain with fever exceeds expected transient bloating and warrants urgent assessment.
These findings can indicate a significant procedural complication.
Fever with worsening pain is not routine gas discomfort.
Symptom relief must not postpone evaluation of possible perforation or other complication.
takeaway: Escalate fever and worsening pain after colonoscopy.
learningObjective: Escalate fever and worsening pain after colonoscopy.

title: Sedated discharge
stem: A client feels alert after procedural sedation and plans to drive home. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow discharge restrictions and confirm safe transport
Allow driving after a short hallway walk
Offer coffee to reverse sedation
Use the client's normal blood pressure as clearance
why: Subjective alertness does not establish restored driving ability.
Walking does not test all effects relevant to driving.
Caffeine does not reliably reverse psychomotor impairment.
Blood pressure does not establish safe reaction time.
takeaway: Apply post-sedation transport instructions despite perceived alertness.
learningObjective: Apply post-sedation transport instructions despite perceived alertness.

title: Upper endoscopy intake
stem: A client returns after throat anaesthetic for upper endoscopy and requests tea. What determines readiness for oral intake?
options: The client's report of thirst alone
Absence of abdominal pain
A fixed interval after the procedure without checking recovery of throat sensation or swallowing
Recovery criteria and swallowing safety per protocol
why: Thirst does not establish recovery of safe swallowing.
Abdominal comfort does not assess pharyngeal sensation.
Elapsed time alone is insufficient; follow protocol recovery criteria and assess swallowing safety.
Pharyngeal anaesthesia can temporarily impair airway protection.
takeaway: Confirm swallowing safety before intake after throat anaesthesia.
learningObjective: Confirm swallowing safety before intake after throat anaesthesia.

title: Endoscopy warning signs
stem: Which post-upper-endoscopy findings require prompt reporting? Select all that apply.
options: Mild temporary throat irritation without other symptoms
Brief bloating that steadily improves
New breathing difficulty
Severe persistent chest or abdominal pain
why: Minor irritation can occur after instrumentation.
Improving transient bloating is less concerning than severe symptoms.
This may indicate an airway or procedural complication.
Severe pain can signal a significant complication.
takeaway: Teach specific warning signs after endoscopy.
learningObjective: Teach specific warning signs after endoscopy.

title: Kidney biopsy bleeding
stem: After kidney biopsy, a client has increasing flank pain, tachycardia, and falling blood pressure. What is the priority?
options: Give the prescribed analgesic and repeat vital signs at the routine interval before notifying the team
Urgently assess and escalate possible bleeding
Treat the lightheadedness as residual sedation because the biopsy dressing is dry
Assess whether the client can stand before deciding if the blood-pressure drop is significant
why: Analgesia alone risks delaying response to worsening pain with circulatory deterioration.
The combined findings suggest clinically important haemorrhage.
A dry dressing does not exclude internal bleeding and the combined trend needs urgent assessment.
Mobilization is unsafe while possible circulatory compromise is being assessed.
takeaway: Recognize bleeding through combined post-biopsy trends.
learningObjective: Recognize bleeding through combined post-biopsy trends.

title: Biopsy preparation medicines
stem: Before an elective biopsy, a client mentions an anticoagulant omitted from the medication list. What should the nurse do?
options: Notify the procedural team before proceeding
Record the medicine and proceed because the most recent haemoglobin is normal
Tell the client to stop it for a week independently
Add the anticoagulant to the medication list without alerting the procedural team
why: Anticoagulant exposure changes bleeding-risk planning.
Normal haemoglobin does not establish that the anticoagulant-related procedure risk has been addressed.
Interruption requires a clinician-directed balance of bleeding and clotting risk.
Updating a list alone may not communicate the time-sensitive bleeding-risk change.
takeaway: Reconcile bleeding-risk medicines before invasive testing.
learningObjective: Reconcile bleeding-risk medicines before invasive testing.

title: Cystoscopy aftercare
stem: A client reports inability to urinate and increasing suprapubic discomfort after cystoscopy. What is appropriate?
options: Use the routine advice for mild burning and wait for symptoms to settle
Continue encouraging usual fluids without checking bladder distension or output
Arrange a routine urine culture and defer bladder assessment until the sample is obtained
Promptly assess and contact the procedural team
why: Painful inability to void differs from expected transient irritation.
The suspected retention/obstruction needs assessment rather than hydration advice alone.
Inability to void with pain requires timely assessment; inability to provide a sample is part of the concern.

takeaway: Differentiate mild expected irritation from postprocedure retention.
learningObjective: Differentiate mild expected irritation from postprocedure retention.

title: ERCP complication cue
stem: After ERCP, a client develops persistent severe upper abdominal pain with vomiting. Which response is best?
options: Give the prescribed antiemetic and assess only whether the vomiting stops
Discharge because the procedure report was normal
Escalate for assessment of a complication
Apply routine advice for transient post-endoscopy bloating without reviewing the pain pattern
why: The severe persistent abdominal pain also needs prompt complication assessment.
A normal procedural report does not exclude later complications.
Pancreatitis and other complications require prompt evaluation.
Severe persistent pain with vomiting is beyond expected mild transient bloating.
takeaway: Monitor for delayed complications after an apparently completed procedure.
learningObjective: Monitor for delayed complications after an apparently completed procedure.

title: Liver biopsy monitoring
stem: A client returning from liver biopsy looks pale and reports new lightheadedness. Which assessments most directly evaluate possible bleeding with impaired perfusion? Select all that apply.
options: The client’s usual response to venepuncture
Vital signs and their change from baseline
Abdominal discomfort and evidence of bleeding
The planned timing of the next oral analgesic
why: A usual fainting response may add history but does not establish the cause of this post-biopsy change.
Vital-sign trends help identify circulatory deterioration.
Abdominal findings and bleeding evidence help assess a procedural complication.
Medication timing does not directly evaluate circulation or bleeding.
takeaway: Assess for internal as well as visible bleeding after biopsy.
learningObjective: Assess for internal as well as visible bleeding after biopsy.

title: Contrast history
stem: Before contrast-enhanced CT, a client describes wheezing and facial swelling during a previous contrast injection. What should the nurse do?
options: Alert radiology before contrast is given
Record a seafood allergy instead
Proceed because the previous reaction resolved
Ask the client to take a home antihistamine without orders
why: A previous significant reaction changes preparation and risk assessment.
The relevant history is the actual prior contrast reaction.
Resolution does not remove recurrence risk.
Premedication requires an appropriate directed plan.
takeaway: Clarify actual contrast reactions before repeat exposure.
learningObjective: Clarify actual contrast reactions before repeat exposure.

title: Renal function before imaging
stem: A client scheduled for contrast imaging has a newly reported acute decline in kidney function. What is the best action?
options: Assume last month's creatinine remains sufficient
Use an old normal result because the contrast order has already been signed
Start extra hydration without reviewing the prescribed fluid restriction
Communicate the change to the imaging team
why: An acute change makes the older result less relevant.
The imaging team must know about a new renal change before weighing current risks and benefits.
Hydration decisions must be individualized to current kidney and cardiac/fluid status.
Current renal status may alter imaging and hydration decisions.
takeaway: Share new renal impairment before contrast decisions.
learningObjective: Share new renal impairment before contrast decisions.

title: MRI implant uncertainty
stem: A client scheduled for MRI says they have an implanted device but cannot identify it. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the client whether magnets usually bother them
Remove jewellery and proceed
Pause entry pending device verification by MRI staff
Assume all recent implants are compatible
why: Subjective experience cannot establish MRI safety.
External metal removal does not resolve implant uncertainty.
Device-specific compatibility must be confirmed before exposure.
Compatibility depends on the particular device and conditions.
takeaway: Verify an implant's MRI conditions before entering the scanner area.
learningObjective: Verify an implant's MRI conditions before entering the scanner area.

title: MRI claustrophobia
stem: A client with severe claustrophobia has an elective MRI tomorrow. Which plan best reduces an avoidable failed examination?
options: Promise the scan will be brief without checking
Notify the team early and plan support
Wait until the scan begins to discuss it
Arrange a sedative for the morning of the scan without checking radiology instructions, monitoring or transport
why: Inaccurate reassurance can undermine informed preparation.
Preparation allows individualized strategies or ordered medication planning.
Late disclosure limits preparation options.
Medication support needs coordinated authorization and a safe procedural/recovery plan.
takeaway: Identify procedure tolerance barriers early enough to plan.
learningObjective: Identify procedure tolerance barriers early enough to plan.

title: Pregnancy and imaging
stem: Before planned radiographic imaging, a client of childbearing potential says pregnancy is possible. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow screening policy and notify the imaging team
Use a previous negative pregnancy test as clearance without checking timing or current history
Automatically defer every radiographic examination until after delivery
Proceed without communicating because exposure is brief
why: Pregnancy status may affect imaging decisions and preparation.
A past result may not reflect current pregnancy possibility; apply the current screening policy.
Necessary imaging requires an individualized clinical risk-benefit decision, not universal deferral.
The team needs relevant pregnancy information regardless of duration.
takeaway: Communicate possible pregnancy before radiation-based procedures.
learningObjective: Communicate possible pregnancy before radiation-based procedures.

title: Procedural fasting ambiguity
stem: A client's elective procedure instructions conflict with a new order allowing breakfast. What should the nurse do?
options: Choose whichever instruction is newest without checking
Apply a universal midnight-fast rule
Ask a colleague to choose the fasting rule they usually use for that procedure
Clarify with the procedural team before intake
why: The new order may not account for the planned procedure.
Fasting requirements vary by procedure and anaesthetic plan.
Habit does not resolve the specific contradictory instructions; clarify with the responsible team.
Procedure-specific fasting requirements need a consistent plan.
takeaway: Resolve conflicting preparation instructions before acting.
learningObjective: Resolve conflicting preparation instructions before acting.

title: Procedure communication needs
stem: A client with hearing impairment will need to follow breathing instructions during a biopsy. Which preparation is most useful?
options: Give louder verbal instructions without checking whether the client can distinguish them
Explain the instructions only after sedation
Agree on accessible cues before starting
Remove a hearing aid needed for the procedure without agreeing on an alternative cue
why: Volume alone does not establish reliable communication for time-sensitive breath cues.
Sedation may reduce comprehension and recall.
Reliable communication supports cooperation during time-sensitive instructions.

takeaway: Plan accessible communication before a cooperative procedure.
learningObjective: Plan accessible communication before a cooperative procedure.

title: Postprocedure baseline
stem: A client with long-standing unequal pupils is scheduled for a procedure requiring sedation. What should the nurse document beforehand?
options: Wait until recovery to record pupil findings
Current neurological findings and established baseline
Only a generic statement that the client is normal
Assume asymmetry means the procedure must be cancelled
why: A recovery-only assessment cannot establish the preprocedure baseline.
Baseline documentation helps distinguish later changes from chronic findings.
That omits the relevant existing asymmetry.
A chronic stable finding needs context rather than automatic cancellation.
takeaway: Record relevant baseline abnormalities before procedures.
learningObjective: Record relevant baseline abnormalities before procedures.

title: Skin preparation reaction
stem: A client awaiting a procedure reports a prior blistering reaction to the planned antiseptic. What is the best action?
options: Clarify the reaction and alert the procedural team
Use less of the same product without discussion
Apply a barrier cream under the antiseptic independently
Proceed if there is no current rash
why: An alternative preparation may be needed to avoid injury.
Dose reduction does not establish tolerance.

A prior reaction remains relevant without an active rash.
takeaway: Address preparation-product reactions before exposure.
learningObjective: Address preparation-product reactions before exposure.

title: Sedation reassessment
stem: A client's discharge time has arrived, but they remain difficult to keep awake. What should the nurse do?
options: Discharge if a relative promises close observation
Allow additional sleep and reassess at the next routine recovery check
Use the elapsed recovery time because the procedure was uncomplicated
Assess responsiveness and breathing and obtain urgent recovery review
why: Home supervision does not replace adequate immediate recovery.
Difficulty arousing needs active immediate assessment, not a routine deferred check.
Elapsed time does not establish physiological readiness.
Assess airway protection, ventilation and responsiveness promptly while obtaining appropriate help.
takeaway: Use recovery criteria rather than elapsed time alone.
learningObjective: Use recovery criteria rather than elapsed time alone.

title: Bronchoscopy bleeding
stem: A client has a small blood streak after bronchoscopy, then develops repeated bright-red expectoration and dyspnoea. What changed the priority?
options: A single small blood streak immediately after airway instrumentation
A mild sore throat that improves while the client rests
Increasing bleeding with respiratory symptoms
The mere presence of any cough
why: A small isolated streak can occur, unlike progressive bleeding with dyspnoea.
Improving local irritation is less concerning than new progressive bleeding and respiratory symptoms.
The new pattern suggests a complication needing urgent assessment.
Some coughing can occur after airway instrumentation.
takeaway: Reassess when minor expected symptoms become progressive or systemic.
learningObjective: Reassess when minor expected symptoms become progressive or systemic.

title: Lumbar puncture headache
stem: After lumbar puncture, a client develops a headache that is much worse upright and improves lying down. What should the nurse do?
options: Treat the symptoms as dehydration without reporting their relation to posture and the procedure
Assess and report the positional pattern
Diagnose migraine without further assessment
Document only the pain score while the client is lying comfortably
why: A clear postural/procedural pattern needs assessment and communication rather than assumption.
The pattern helps identify a postprocedural headache and guide treatment.
The temporal and positional features require procedure-related evaluation.
The positional change is essential information and should not be omitted because resting pain improves.
takeaway: Describe positional features when assessing postprocedure headache.
learningObjective: Describe positional features when assessing postprocedure headache.

title: Thoracentesis surveillance
stem: Following thoracentesis, a client develops new pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, and reduced breath sounds on that side. What should the nurse do?
options: Activate urgent assessment for a respiratory complication
