Encourage repeated forceful coughing first
Attribute symptoms to anxiety without examination
Arrange a routine chest radiograph and wait for the result before escalating the new symptoms
why: The findings may indicate pneumothorax or another complication.
This delays assessment of new respiratory compromise.
Unilateral findings require clinical investigation.
Imaging may be required, but active respiratory deterioration needs urgent assessment/support while it is arranged.
takeaway: Treat new unilateral respiratory findings after thoracentesis as significant.
learningObjective: Treat new unilateral respiratory findings after thoracentesis as significant.

title: Procedure teaching recall
stem: A client cannot recall discharge warnings after receiving sedation. Which approach is most useful?
options: Repeat all verbal instructions once and discharge without checking what was understood
Rely on the signed discharge sheet
Ask the client to initial each warning on the sheet as the only understanding check
Review accessible written warnings with the client and designated support person, checking the action plan
why: Repetition alone does not address sedation-related recall impairment.
A signature does not demonstrate retained understanding.
Initials do not demonstrate retained understanding or an actionable follow-up plan.
Sedation may impair recall; agreed support and teach-back help reinforce essential actions while respecting consent.
takeaway: Reinforce post-sedation teaching using accessible written and support-person guidance.
learningObjective: Reinforce post-sedation teaching using accessible written and support-person guidance.

title: Procedure handover content
stem: When receiving a client after an invasive procedure, which handover details most directly guide immediate recovery monitoring? Select all that apply.
options: The originally planned date of discharge
The client’s usual exercise routine before admission
Procedure-specific restrictions and monitoring orders
Sedation given and the last observations
why: The original discharge plan does not establish present recovery needs.
Baseline activity can inform later planning but does not specify immediate postprocedure monitoring.
These guide current restrictions and required observations.
Sedative exposure and recent observations help anticipate and detect recovery complications.
takeaway: Receive an actionable recovery handover after invasive procedures.
learningObjective: Receive an actionable recovery handover after invasive procedures.

title: Drain output stops
stem: A closed wound drain stops collecting fluid while swelling develops near the incision. What should the nurse do first?
options: Record zero output as improvement
Assess the tubing and operative area promptly
Remove the drain because output has ceased
Increase compression without examining the site
why: The new swelling contradicts uncomplicated improvement.
Obstruction may prevent drainage and allow fluid accumulation.
Cessation with swelling does not establish readiness for removal.
External pressure does not identify the drainage problem.
takeaway: Interpret drain output together with the wound and tubing assessment.
learningObjective: Interpret drain output together with the wound and tubing assessment.

title: Drain suction seal
stem: A prescribed bulb-suction drain repeatedly expands immediately after compression. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Check closure and connections using the device instructions
Measure output only at the usual time
Apply wall suction without a new plan
Replace the dressing without checking the system
why: Loss of seal can prevent the intended suction.
Measurement alone does not correct lost suction.
The device may not be designed for that pressure.
An intact dressing does not ensure a functioning suction circuit.
takeaway: Investigate failure of a closed drain to maintain prescribed suction.
learningObjective: Investigate failure of a closed drain to maintain prescribed suction.

title: Separate drains
stem: A client has two surgical drains with different amounts and colours of output. How should the nurse document drainage?
options: Record the combined volume and describe the overall colour
Record each volume but use one colour description for both
Record each colour and estimate volumes from bulb fullness
Measure and describe each drain separately
why: Combining obscures which operative area produced the change.
Each drain has a distinct appearance that should remain attributable to that drain.
Measure each volume; bulb fullness is not a reliable substitute for measurement.
Site-specific trends can identify which area has changed.
takeaway: Track each drainage source separately.
learningObjective: Track each drainage source separately.

title: Wound-edge separation
stem: During removal of ordered sutures, a wound edge begins to separate. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply closure strips and continue removing the remaining sutures
Cover the gap with a dressing and reassess after the remaining sutures are removed
Stop and obtain wound assessment
Continue removing the remaining sutures
why: A new separation requires reassessment before further removal, even if temporary support is applied.
Completing removal may enlarge the separation; stop and obtain assessment.
New separation requires reassessment before further removal.
Further removal may worsen the opening.
takeaway: Stop suture removal if wound edges separate.
learningObjective: Stop suture removal if wound edges separate.

title: Hidden dressing loss
stem: A postoperative client lies on a damp blood-stained sheet despite a small stain on the visible dressing. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Use the small visible stain to estimate total loss
Assess the full wound area and circulation
Reinforce the visible stain alone
Change the linen before assessment
why: Visible dressing area may underestimate hidden drainage.
Dependent drainage may hide a larger blood loss.
This misses blood that has tracked beneath the client.
Comfort care should not delay evaluation of possible bleeding.
takeaway: Look for concealed bleeding when surface findings do not fit.
learningObjective: Look for concealed bleeding when surface findings do not fit.

title: Gastric suction replacement
stem: A client with gastric suction has increasing thirst, dry mucosa, and rising pulse. Which information is most useful to report?
options: Suction losses and prescribed fluid replacement received
Mouth-care frequency and the effect on reported thirst
Prescribed suction setting and the time the system was last checked
The usual daily oral intake before admission
why: Unreplaced losses may contribute to volume depletion.
These describe comfort, but not the fluid deficit suggested by rising pulse and dryness.
Equipment details matter, but measured loss and replacement more directly quantify the possible deficit.
The usual intake does not establish current losses or replacement received.
takeaway: Compare gastrointestinal losses with replacement and clinical response.
learningObjective: Compare gastrointestinal losses with replacement and clinical response.

title: Tube drainage change
stem: A gastric decompression tube has no output, and abdominal distension increases. What should the nurse do?
options: Clamp it because no output suggests recovery
Begin feeding through the same tube
Increase suction beyond the prescribed setting
Assess position indicators and tubing patency per policy
why: Increasing distension argues against assuming recovery.
The new symptoms require assessment before changing use.
More pressure may injure tissue and does not verify position.
A displaced or obstructed tube may stop effective decompression.
takeaway: Investigate loss of decompression when symptoms worsen.
learningObjective: Investigate loss of decompression when symptoms worsen.

title: Urinary catheter obstruction
stem: A catheterized client develops bladder discomfort and no urine drainage. Tubing is kinked under the thigh. What should the nurse do first?
options: Request increased analgesia as the sole response
Replace the catheter before correcting tubing
Relieve the kink and reassess drainage
Obtain a urine culture before checking drainage
why: Pain relief does not restore urine flow.
Replacement is unnecessary before addressing the visible kink.
A visible mechanical obstruction is immediately correctable.
Culture does not relieve the identified obstruction.
takeaway: Correct visible drainage obstruction and reassess its effect.
learningObjective: Correct visible drainage obstruction and reassess its effect.

title: Post-removal voiding
stem: After catheter removal, a client reports frequent small voids and lower abdominal fullness. Which assessment is most useful?
options: Compare oral intake with the total volume voided since removal
Post-void bladder assessment per protocol
Inspect the colour and clarity of the latest urine
Count voiding episodes during the previous shift
why: Balance helps contextualize output but cannot determine current residual urine.
Small voids can coexist with substantial retained urine.
Appearance does not establish whether the bladder emptied.
Frequency alone cannot distinguish small complete voids from retention.
takeaway: Assess emptying when small frequent voids accompany fullness.
learningObjective: Assess emptying when small frequent voids accompany fullness.

title: Bladder irrigation balance
stem: An ordered bladder irrigation infuses 1200 mL. The drainage bag contains 1650 mL. What urine output should be documented, assuming no other fluid inputs? Use mL.
options: 450 mL
why: Subtracting irrigant from total drainage gives 450 mL.
This includes the 1200 mL of irrigation fluid.
This is the irrigation input, not urine produced.
Adding input to drainage double-counts irrigation.
takeaway: Subtract irrigation input from total drainage to estimate urine output.
learningObjective: Subtract irrigation input from total drainage to estimate urine output.

title: Irrigation obstruction cue
stem: During prescribed bladder irrigation, drainage slows and the client reports suprapubic pressure. What is the priority?
options: Increase inflow before assessing outflow
Give the prescribed antispasmodic and then reassess drainage
Lower the irrigation bag to slow inflow until the next observation
Pause irrigation inflow, assess outflow, and follow the obstruction protocol
why: More inflow can worsen distension if drainage is blocked.
Symptoms may reflect obstructed outflow; symptom treatment must not delay checking drainage.
Reducing flow alone does not establish that outflow is safe.
Continuing inflow with impaired drainage can overdistend the bladder; act on patency and escalate per protocol.
takeaway: Check drainage promptly when bladder irrigation causes pressure.
learningObjective: Check drainage promptly when bladder irrigation causes pressure.

title: Chest drain positioning
stem: A client with a chest drain is transferred to a chair. Which observations require correction? Select all that apply.
options: The unit is secured upright
Connections remain secured as prescribed
The collection unit lies above chest level
Tubing is compressed beneath the chair leg
why: Upright positioning supports correct system operation.
Secure connections help preserve system integrity.
Elevation can interfere with the intended drainage system.
Compression can obstruct drainage from the pleural space.
takeaway: Maintain unobstructed dependent chest drainage during movement.
learningObjective: Maintain unobstructed dependent chest drainage during movement.

title: Chest drain bubbling
stem: A water-seal chamber develops continuous bubbling that was previously intermittent. The client is stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase suction beyond the order
Assess the client and check connections per protocol
Clamp the tube and leave it clamped
Add water to the suction-control chamber to reduce the new water-seal bubbling
why: Changing pressure does not identify the leak source.
A new continuous air leak pattern needs investigation.
Prolonged unplanned clamping can trap pleural air.
Suction-control adjustments do not identify a new air leak in the water-seal system.
takeaway: Investigate a changed chest-drain air-leak pattern.
learningObjective: Investigate a changed chest-drain air-leak pattern.

title: Chest drain sudden cessation
stem: A client with a chest drain becomes more breathless as previously active drainage suddenly stops. What should guide the response?
options: Urgent client and system assessment
Assume the lung has fully re-expanded
Empty the collection unit by disconnecting it
Wait for the daily radiograph
why: Symptoms make obstruction or another complication concerning.
Stopped drainage alone does not establish recovery during worsening symptoms.
Unplanned disconnection can compromise the system.
Acute respiratory change cannot await routine imaging.
takeaway: Interpret drainage cessation in the context of the client's condition.
learningObjective: Interpret drainage cessation in the context of the client's condition.

title: Compression device use
stem: A postoperative client has prescribed intermittent pneumatic compression while in bed. Which observations support effective implementation? Select all that apply.
options: The device cycles while prescribed therapy is needed
One larger sleeve size is used for every client to avoid tightness
The machine is off for every sleeping period
Sleeves fit according to device instructions
why: A disconnected machine does not provide prophylactic compression.
Sizing must match the client and device instructions; a universal oversize can impair intended compression.
Unordered long interruptions reduce prescribed prophylaxis.
Correct fit supports intended compression without excessive pressure.
takeaway: Check fit and actual operation of prescribed compression devices.
learningObjective: Check fit and actual operation of prescribed compression devices.

title: New calf finding
stem: A postoperative client reports unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. What is the best action?
options: Increase exercise intensity to reduce swelling
Apply a tighter compression stocking to the swollen leg
Assess and promptly notify the clinical team
Massage the calf before walking
why: New symptoms require assessment before progression.
New unilateral swelling and tenderness require assessment for thrombosis before independently changing compression.
New unilateral findings may indicate venous thrombosis.
Massage is inappropriate when thrombosis is suspected.
takeaway: Evaluate new unilateral leg symptoms before routine activity.
learningObjective: Evaluate new unilateral leg symptoms before routine activity.

title: Incision splinting
stem: A client avoids coughing after abdominal surgery because of incisional pulling. Which intervention best supports pulmonary hygiene?
options: Use incentive spirometry in place of the prescribed coughing exercises
Teach gentle incision support during prescribed coughing
Encourage only shallow breaths until healing
Replace all coughing with throat clearing
why: Inspiratory expansion does not replace needed secretion clearance through effective coughing.
Support can reduce discomfort and permit effective clearance.
Shallow breathing can promote retained secretions and atelectasis.
Throat clearing may not mobilize lower-airway secretions.
takeaway: Support the incision to enable prescribed coughing and deep breathing.
learningObjective: Support the incision to enable prescribed coughing and deep breathing.

title: Incentive device technique
stem: A client using an ordered incentive spirometer exhales forcefully into it. Which instruction is correct?
options: Inhale slowly through the mouthpiece as taught
Exhale faster to raise the marker
Keep taking short rapid breaths
Use it only when saturation falls
why: The device encourages sustained inspiratory expansion.
Forceful exhalation does not perform the intended exercise.
Rapid shallow breaths do not achieve sustained expansion.
Prescribed prevention should not depend solely on desaturation.
takeaway: Verify inspiratory technique when evaluating incentive spirometry use.
learningObjective: Verify inspiratory technique when evaluating incentive spirometry use.

title: Postoperative delirium prevention
stem: A high-risk older adult is alert after surgery but has misplaced hearing aids and glasses. Which actions reduce preventable disorientation? Select all that apply.
options: Provide orientation and preserve sleep where feasible
Remove the clock and calendar to reduce visual clutter
Keep the blinds closed throughout the daytime to maintain a sleep setting
Restore accessible sensory aids
why: Orientation and appropriate sleep support cognitive function.
Clock/calendar cues can support orientation rather than being routine clutter.
Maintaining darkness throughout daytime can disrupt day-night cues; preserve a suitable rhythm.
Accessible hearing and vision aids help interpret the environment.
takeaway: Support orientation, sensory access, and sleep in at-risk clients.
learningObjective: Support orientation, sensory access, and sleep in at-risk clients.

title: Pressure under oxygen tubing
stem: A client using continuous nasal oxygen has new tenderness behind one ear. What should the nurse do?
options: Tighten tubing to reduce movement
Apply tape over the painful spot without inspection
Inspect the skin and adjust pressure while continuing oxygen
Cover the tender area with a dressing and keep the same tubing tension
why: More tension may worsen local pressure.
Concealment can delay recognition of skin injury.
Maintain necessary therapy while assessing and offloading the local pressure source.
A covering alone may not remove the mechanical pressure; inspect and adjust the cause.
takeaway: Assess and offload device pressure without losing necessary treatment.
learningObjective: Assess and offload device pressure without losing necessary treatment.

title: Wound trajectory
stem: A wound has decreasing dimensions and healthy granulation, with unchanged mild serous drainage. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The wound has reached a plateau because drainage is unchanged
The trend is consistent with progress
Unchanged drainage proves treatment failure
Granulation means infection is present
why: The decreasing size and healthy tissue show progress despite stable mild serous drainage.
Size reduction and granulation support healing assessment.
Drainage alone does not override the improving wound dimensions.
Healthy granulation is part of tissue repair.
takeaway: Evaluate wound healing using multiple consistent measurements.
learningObjective: Evaluate wound healing using multiple consistent measurements.

title: Drain removal teaching
stem: A client is going home with two prescribed bulb-suction wound drains. Which demonstrations show effective home-care technique? Select all that apply.
options: Measures and records drain-specific output
Shows how to secure tubing during movement
Empties both drains into one container before measuring
Reconnects the bulb with it fully expanded after emptying
why: Home trends inform follow-up and removal decisions.
Securement reduces accidental traction at the site.
Combining loses the drain-specific trend.
The prescribed bulb suction requires compression before secure closure, following device instructions.
takeaway: Use return demonstration for home drainage care.
learningObjective: Use return demonstration for home drainage care.

title: Postoperative oral intake
stem: After abdominal surgery, a client prescribed diet advancement develops repeated vomiting and increasing distension. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue the next diet stage on schedule
Give the prescribed antiemetic and advance the diet if vomiting briefly stops
Record nausea without changing the plan
Pause advancement and assess with the team
why: A schedule does not override new intolerance.
Temporary symptom relief does not establish restored gastrointestinal tolerance when distension is increasing.
Repeated vomiting and distension require active review.
New intolerance may indicate impaired gastrointestinal function.
takeaway: Reassess diet progression when postoperative intolerance develops.
learningObjective: Reassess diet progression when postoperative intolerance develops.

title: Neuromuscular baseline
stem: Before applying a prescribed splint, which findings directly establish a distal neurovascular baseline for comparison after application? Select all that apply.
options: The size of a superficial bruise over the injured area
The pain score during movement of the injured joint
Distal movement and sensation
Distal colour, temperature, and circulation findings
why: Bruising matters, but it does not establish distal neurological or circulatory function.
Pain contributes to broader assessment, but does not directly establish the specified distal motor/sensory/perfusion baseline.
These establish neurological function before immobilization.
These establish perfusion for comparison after application.
takeaway: Record distal neurovascular findings before immobilization.
learningObjective: Record distal neurovascular findings before immobilization.

title: Cast education evaluation
stem: A client with a new cast says itching makes them want to insert a pen beneath it. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Blow warm air under the cast to dry the skin
Discuss safe itch relief and assess persistent irritation
Suggest a narrower object
Recommend lotion poured inside
why: Warm air can increase heat and irritation; use approved safe relief and assess persistent symptoms.
Objects can injure concealed skin beneath the cast.
Smaller objects can still damage skin and become trapped.
Moisture may damage the lining and macerate skin.
takeaway: Protect concealed skin while investigating persistent cast discomfort.
learningObjective: Protect concealed skin while investigating persistent cast discomfort.

title: Respiratory trend report
stem: A client with pneumonia now needs more oxygen than yesterday to remain in the prescribed target range. What should the nurse report?
options: The increased requirement despite a similar saturation
That saturation is unchanged, so status is unchanged
The current saturation and target range, omitting the flow-rate change
The admission room-air saturation and original oxygen prescription
why: Stable saturation achieved with more support can conceal worsening function.
The oxygen requirement is part of the clinical trend.
The increase in support is necessary to interpret the apparently stable saturation.
The original values provide context but omit the current deterioration in support needs.
takeaway: Interpret oxygen saturation alongside the support required to achieve it.
learningObjective: Interpret oxygen saturation alongside the support required to achieve it.

title: Oximetry and symptoms
stem: A client with darkly pigmented skin has worsening dyspnoea despite an apparently acceptable pulse-oximeter reading. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the displayed saturation and investigate anxiety as the main cause
Subtract a fixed percentage from every reading
Change the probe site and await the next routine observation before escalating
Assess the whole clinical picture and escalate the mismatch
why: An apparently acceptable reading does not exclude hypoxaemia or another serious cause of worsening dyspnoea.
No universal numerical correction is established for individuals.
Measurement verification is useful but must not delay assessment and escalation of worsening symptoms.
Device limitations can contribute to missed hypoxaemia.
takeaway: Act on concerning symptoms even when oximetry appears reassuring.
learningObjective: Act on concerning symptoms even when oximetry appears reassuring.

title: Respiratory reassessment content
stem: Which observations most directly evaluate respiratory improvement during treatment of a respiratory infection? Select all that apply.
options: The time at which the latest antibiotic dose was given
Completion of the prescribed sputum specimen collection
Work of breathing and activity tolerance
Oxygen requirement and respiratory-rate trend
why: Dose timing measures treatment delivery rather than respiratory response.
Specimen collection supports diagnosis but does not show whether respiratory function improved.
These reflect functional respiratory response.
Support needs and rate help identify improvement or worsening.
takeaway: Evaluate treatment through symptoms, function, and support needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate treatment through symptoms, function, and support needs.

title: Secretion clearance
stem: A weak postoperative client has audible secretions and an ineffective cough. Which finding most changes the urgency?
options: Respiratory rate remaining at the documented baseline
Increasing drowsiness with poorer airway clearance
Small amounts of sputum becoming easier to expectorate
Mild incisional discomfort unchanged from baseline
why: A stable rate is less concerning than new drowsiness with impaired airway clearance.
Reduced alertness threatens ongoing airway protection.
Improved clearance is less urgent than a decline in alertness and cough effectiveness.
Stable discomfort is less urgent than declining airway protection.
takeaway: Escalate when reduced alertness compounds ineffective airway clearance.
learningObjective: Escalate when reduced alertness compounds ineffective airway clearance.

title: Fluid deficit trend
stem: An adult with diarrhoea has less urine, postural dizziness, and increasing pulse. Which information should guide escalation?
options: Intake and estimated losses with current observations
Stool frequency and the last bowel movement time
Reported thirst and the amount of water offered
Usual weight and pre-illness drinking habits
why: The combined pattern suggests clinically important volume depletion.
This describes part of the loss but misses its amount and the current perfusion response.
Offered water is not necessarily consumed or sufficient; integrate actual intake, losses and observations.
Baseline habits give context but do not characterize the current deficit.
takeaway: Combine losses, output, and perfusion findings when assessing dehydration.
learningObjective: Combine losses, output, and perfusion findings when assessing dehydration.

title: Heart failure home monitoring
stem: A client follows an individualized heart-failure action plan. Which changes should prompt using its contact instructions? Select all that apply.
options: Increasing breathlessness during usual activities
Weight measured after meals rather than before
Unchanged mild ankle swelling already addressed in the plan
Rapid weight increase beyond the plan's limit
why: Functional deterioration can signal worsening congestion.
Technique variation needs correction before trend interpretation.
An unchanged baseline does not carry the same urgency as new worsening.
A defined change may reflect fluid accumulation.
takeaway: Use individualized thresholds and symptom changes in home monitoring.
learningObjective: Use individualized thresholds and symptom changes in home monitoring.

title: Renal output and obstruction
stem: A client with known prostate enlargement reports lower abdominal pressure and minimal urine despite normal intake. What should the nurse assess?
options: Reduced renal production from fluid depletion
Urine concentration after reduced overnight drinking
Possible bladder retention
Increased urine loss from an unrecorded diuretic dose
why: Dehydration is possible, but normal intake with pressure and prostate enlargement makes retention the more direct concern.
Concentration does not explain lower abdominal pressure and very limited emptying.
Obstruction can reduce voided output without stopping urine production.
Diuretic-related excess output does not fit the described pressure with minimal voiding.
takeaway: Distinguish reduced urine production from impaired bladder emptying.
learningObjective: Distinguish reduced urine production from impaired bladder emptying.

title: Potassium in salt substitutes
stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a potassium-restricted plan and has replaced table salt with a product labelled low sodium. Which teaching is most important before continued use?
options: Use the package’s serving size to decide whether it fits the plan
Review whether potassium chloride is an ingredient with the renal team
Continue using it while symptoms of high potassium are absent
Use the last normal potassium result as clearance for regular use
why: Serving size alone does not establish potassium content or fit with the prescribed restriction.
Some low-sodium substitutes contain potassium chloride and need review against the renal plan.
Important potassium elevation may occur without reliable warning symptoms.
A prior normal result does not establish safety of a new regular potassium source.
takeaway: Check potassium content before using low-sodium salt substitutes with kidney disease.
learningObjective: Identify potassium-containing salt substitutes that may conflict with a renal diet.

title: Neurological trend
stem: A client under neurological observation was oriented earlier but now repeatedly misidentifies place and is harder to wake. What should the nurse do?
options: Check responsiveness, airway and breathing while activating urgent review
Give the prescribed analgesic and repeat orientation after it takes effect
Wait for the next routine observation time
Assume tiredness because it is evening
why: Declining consciousness requires immediate patient assessment and urgent escalation with baseline comparison.
Analgesia does not address new impaired arousal and must not delay urgent assessment.
An acute change requires assessment sooner than routine timing.
Time of day does not safely explain a new decline.
takeaway: Communicate neurological change relative to the documented baseline.
learningObjective: Communicate neurological change relative to the documented baseline.

title: Headache red flags
stem: Which headache reports require urgent assessment rather than routine comfort measures alone? Select all that apply.
options: Headache with new weakness or altered consciousness
A familiar mild headache relieved by usual measures
A mild gradual headache after missed sleep without new signs
Sudden severe onset unlike prior headaches
why: Associated neurological change raises urgency.
An unchanged responsive pattern is less urgent.
The described pattern lacks the listed acute neurological warning signs.
An abrupt unusual headache can indicate serious pathology.
takeaway: Assess onset and associated neurological features when triaging headache.
learningObjective: Assess onset and associated neurological features when triaging headache.

title: Seizure recovery change
stem: A client with a known seizure disorder remains unusually unresponsive much longer than their documented recovery pattern. What should the nurse do?
options: Place the client in their usual sleep position and reassess at the next scheduled check
Wait for the next scheduled medication round
Assess airway, breathing and responsiveness and obtain urgent review
Assume all post-seizure sleep is expected
why: Atypical prolonged unresponsiveness requires immediate reassessment rather than assuming sleep.
Medication timing does not justify delaying evaluation.
A prolonged altered state differs from the known recovery pattern and may indicate an ongoing emergency.
The atypical duration needs reassessment.
takeaway: Compare post-event recovery with the person's established pattern.
learningObjective: Compare post-event recovery with the person's established pattern.

title: Diabetes foot surveillance
stem: A client with neuropathy notices a painless blister under a shoe. Which action is best?
options: Treat only the dry surrounding skin
Protect the area and arrange timely foot assessment
Continue the same shoe until pain develops
Open the blister to reduce pressure independently
why: The new lesion itself needs assessment.
Loss of pain does not mean the lesion is minor.
Neuropathy can hide worsening tissue injury.
Unplanned opening can introduce infection and damage tissue.
takeaway: Escalate new foot injury even when neuropathy masks pain.
learningObjective: Escalate new foot injury even when neuropathy masks pain.

title: Reduced intake with insulin
stem: A client prescribed mealtime insulin is vomiting and cannot tolerate lunch. What should the nurse do before the scheduled dose?
options: Assess glucose and clarify the sick-day or medication plan
Give the usual meal dose without review
Omit every insulin dose for the day independently
Wait to check glucose until dinner
why: Food intolerance changes the relationship between insulin and intake.
Usual dosing may be unsafe when expected carbohydrate is absent.
Some insulin remains necessary; the plan requires individualized review.
Current intolerance and insulin timing need timely assessment.
takeaway: Reassess glucose and the prescribed plan when expected intake changes.
learningObjective: Reassess glucose and the prescribed plan when expected intake changes.

title: New bruising assessment
stem: A client taking an anticoagulant develops multiple unexplained bruises. Which additional findings most directly assess the extent of bleeding or injury-related bleeding risk? Select all that apply.
options: Recent falls or other trauma
The colour changes in a single resolving bruise
Whether the anticoagulant was taken before or after breakfast
Bleeding from gums, urine, or stool
why: Injury history changes the assessment of occult bleeding risk.
A resolving local bruise does not assess the new pattern’s extent or injury exposure.
Meal timing does not directly assess the extent of bleeding or recent injury.
Other sites help assess the extent of bleeding.
takeaway: Assess bleeding across sites and ask about injury when bruising increases.
learningObjective: Assess bleeding across sites and ask about injury when bruising increases.

title: Infection without fever
stem: A frail older adult becomes acutely less functional with new cough and reduced intake but no fever. What should the nurse do?
options: Treat the reduced intake as the main cause and monitor after nutritional supplements
Use a routine cough suppressant and reassess at the next scheduled review
Assess for acute illness despite the normal temperature
Exclude infection because fever is absent
why: Poor intake may be a manifestation of acute illness; new cough and functional decline warrant assessment now.
Symptom suppression does not evaluate the associated acute functional deterioration.
Older adults may show infection through functional and cognitive changes.
No fever does not reliably rule out infection.
takeaway: Recognize atypical acute illness presentations in older adults.
learningObjective: Recognize atypical acute illness presentations in older adults.

title: Diabetic autonomic symptoms
stem: A client with diabetes becomes dizzy during standing and has a marked positional blood-pressure drop. After safe seating, what should the nurse report?
options: The diabetes history and most recent glucose result
Position-linked symptoms and measured pressure changes
The pressure after seated recovery and the duration of rest
Recent antihypertensive timing and the usual baseline pressure
why: Glucose is relevant, but this omits the measured positional pressure response associated with symptoms.
These document orthostatic intolerance needing plan review.
Recovery information alone omits the symptomatic standing response.
These may help identify causes but should accompany the direct position-linked observations.
takeaway: Report the relationship between position, symptoms, and blood pressure.
learningObjective: Report the relationship between position, symptoms, and blood pressure.

title: Liver disease observations
stem: A client with chronic liver disease has increasing abdominal girth and new confusion. Which findings indicate current deterioration that should be promptly communicated? Select all that apply.
options: The new change in mental status
The abdominal trend with weight and symptoms
Prominent abdominal veins unchanged from prior assessment
Usual mild ankle swelling without recent increase
why: This may reflect a serious complication requiring assessment.
Fluid accumulation and associated symptoms need evaluation.
This chronic stable observation is less urgent than the new neurological and fluid trends.
The unchanged baseline adds less urgency than new confusion and increasing abdominal girth.
takeaway: Escalate new cognitive changes in chronic liver disease.
learningObjective: Escalate new cognitive changes in chronic liver disease.

title: Ostomy high output
stem: A client with a new ileostomy reports markedly more watery output with dizziness and reduced urine. What is the best response?
options: Reduce oral fluids to slow the intestinal output
Increase plain water and defer contacting the team until the next day
Change to a larger pouch and review output at the next routine visit
Assess hydration and promptly contact the team
why: Reducing intake may worsen dehydration and requires individualized team advice.
Symptomatic high losses need prompt assessment; fluid and electrolyte replacement should follow an individualized plan.
A larger appliance manages containment but does not address dizziness and low urine output.
High losses with perfusion symptoms suggest dehydration risk.
takeaway: Link increased ileostomy losses to hydration and urine output.
learningObjective: Link increased ileostomy losses to hydration and urine output.

title: Constipation alarm pattern
stem: A client requesting a laxative reports severe new abdominal pain, vomiting, and no passage of gas. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase fibre as the immediate treatment
Give the prescribed antiemetic and reassess after the next bowel-care round
Assess and urgently seek clinical review
Administer the usual laxative before assessment
why: Fibre does not address a possible obstructed bowel.
Symptom relief must not delay urgent assessment of possible obstruction.
The pattern may indicate obstruction rather than routine constipation.
Stimulating the bowel may be inappropriate with suspected obstruction.
takeaway: Assess obstruction warning signs before routine constipation treatment.
learningObjective: Assess obstruction warning signs before routine constipation treatment.

title: Swallow screen limits
stem: A client passes an initial swallowing screen but later coughs during meals and loses weight. What is the best interpretation?
options: The meal symptoms can be managed under the existing plan because the earlier screen was normal
A reassessment is needed despite the earlier screen
The weight loss is nutritional, since a swallowing problem would have been found on the screen
The coughing is unlikely to affect intake if it occurs only during some meals
why: A previous screen does not address later cough and weight loss.
A screen is time-specific and does not override subsequent concerns.
Screening is time-specific and may miss later or more complex swallowing problems.
Intermittent symptoms may still be clinically important and require reassessment.
takeaway: Reassess swallowing when later symptoms conflict with screening results.
learningObjective: Reassess swallowing when later symptoms conflict with screening results.

title: Nutrition deficit concealment
stem: A client has oedema and unchanged weight but visibly reduced muscle bulk and poor intake. What should the nurse do?
options: Request comprehensive nutritional assessment
Conclude nutrition is adequate because weight is stable
Assess only ankle circumference
Wait until the scale shows weight loss
why: Fluid retention can conceal tissue loss on the scale.
Stable total weight can mask loss of lean tissue.
Local swelling does not characterize nutritional status.
Delay may miss established nutritional risk.
takeaway: Do not let fluid weight hide evidence of nutritional decline.
learningObjective: Do not let fluid weight hide evidence of nutritional decline.

title: Deconditioning markers
stem: Which changes suggest a client needs reassessment of an existing mobility plan after illness? Select all that apply.
options: Previously tolerated walking now causes marked fatigue
The client prefers a different walking time
The prescribed aid is unchanged
More assistance is needed for usual transfers
why: Reduced endurance should guide a revised progression.
Preference alone does not demonstrate reduced function.
An unchanged device does not establish adequate current ability.
A functional decline changes safe handling needs.
takeaway: Reassess mobility when functional performance changes.
learningObjective: Reassess mobility when functional performance changes.

title: Pressure despite low score
stem: A mobile client's formal pressure-risk score is low, but they develop focal pain under an oxygen device. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the score without inspecting the site
Add padding over the tender point before checking the skin or device fit
Assess the device contact area directly
Dismiss pressure risk because the score is low
why: Rescoring alone can miss the local problem.
Padding may not remove the pressure and may alter fit; inspect the contact area first.
A global score may not capture localized device pressure.
A score does not override a new clinical symptom.
takeaway: Clinical findings override reassurance from a screening score.
learningObjective: Clinical findings override reassurance from a screening score.

title: Monitoring response to fluids
stem: After prescribed fluids for dehydration, which findings best support improving perfusion? Select all that apply.
options: The chart has a positive intake balance
Urine output and postural symptoms improve
Pulse approaches baseline and alertness improves
The entire ordered bag has infused
why: Recorded balance alone does not prove clinical improvement.
These changes support a favourable physiological response.
Combined trends are more informative than volume infused alone.
Completion does not establish that treatment worked.
takeaway: Evaluate fluid therapy by physiological response rather than task completion.
learningObjective: Evaluate fluid therapy by physiological response rather than task completion.

title: Escalation after temporary recovery
stem: A client briefly returns to baseline after an unexplained faint, then reports new palpitations. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassess and escalate the evolving symptoms
Repeat routine observations after a rest period because consciousness has returned
Attribute the palpitations to anxiety from the faint and provide reassurance
Focus only on the minor elbow bruise
why: Transient recovery does not explain or resolve the event's cause.
New palpitations after unexplained syncope require timely assessment, not routine deferred monitoring.
Anxiety is possible, but the evolving circulatory symptoms need assessment before attribution.
The evolving circulatory symptoms take priority over a minor injury.
takeaway: Continue evaluating unexplained events despite temporary recovery.
learningObjective: Continue evaluating unexplained events despite temporary recovery.

title: ECG artifact check
stem: A stable client has a noisy ECG tracing while shivering, with electrodes lifting from damp skin. What should the nurse do first?
options: Request treatment for the tracing pattern before correcting the loose electrodes
Repeat the tracing without drying or replacing electrodes
File the tracing because pulse rate is normal
Assess the client and correct electrode contact
why: Clinical assessment and a technically usable tracing are needed before treating a likely artefact as confirmed rhythm.
The identified source of interference remains.
A technically poor tracing may still need a usable repeat.
Visible technical problems may distort the tracing.
takeaway: Correct identifiable ECG recording problems while assessing the client.
learningObjective: Correct identifiable ECG recording problems while assessing the client.

title: Chest symptom testing
stem: A client with new chest discomfort has one troponin result within the laboratory range. What should the nurse understand?
options: Further symptom assessment can stop
The next sample can be taken at any convenient time
One early result does not replace the ordered serial assessment
The result independently excludes a cardiac cause
why: Clinical changes remain relevant regardless of one value.
Serial testing depends on the ordered timing protocol.
Timing and trends matter in evaluating possible myocardial injury.
An early normal result may not rule out evolving injury.
takeaway: Interpret cardiac biomarkers with symptom timing and serial testing.
learningObjective: Interpret cardiac biomarkers with symptom timing and serial testing.

title: Timed drug sample
stem: A trough drug level is ordered immediately before the next dose, but the sample was drawn after administration. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the value without mentioning timing
Report the actual dose and collection times
Label it as a trough because that was ordered
Redraw immediately and label the repeat as the trough
why: Dose decisions could be based on an invalid comparison.
The timing error affects interpretation and may require recollection.
Incorrect labelling misrepresents the sample.
A second postdose sample still does not satisfy the ordered predose timing; obtain instructions and report actual times.
takeaway: Preserve accurate timing when therapeutic monitoring samples are mistimed.
learningObjective: Preserve accurate timing when therapeutic monitoring samples are mistimed.

title: Point-of-care quality control
stem: A glucose meter fails its required quality-control check before use. A client's glucose needs testing. What is appropriate?
options: Use a verified alternative testing method
Use it once because the client needs an answer
Average several readings from the failed meter
Compare the reading with the client’s usual value and accept it if similar
why: The failed device cannot be assumed to give reliable results.
Urgency increases the need for a trustworthy measurement.
Repeated faulty readings do not establish accuracy.
Agreement with an expected value does not repair failed quality control.
takeaway: Use verified equipment when a point-of-care device fails quality control.
learningObjective: Use verified equipment when a point-of-care device fails quality control.

title: Glucose and poor perfusion
stem: A hypotensive client has cold poorly perfused fingers and an unexpected capillary glucose result. What should the nurse do?
options: Squeeze the finger repeatedly for a larger drop
Use the capillary value to explain the hypotension before further assessment
Repeat on another cold finger and accept two matching results
Address clinical instability and obtain an approved confirmatory measurement
why: Excess squeezing can further compromise sample quality.
Hypotension requires assessment and the poorly perfused sample may be unreliable.
Agreement between similarly compromised sites does not establish accuracy.
Assess and respond to instability promptly; confirm questionable capillary results without delaying indicated emergency treatment.
takeaway: Use an appropriate confirmation method when capillary sampling is unreliable.
learningObjective: Use an appropriate confirmation method when capillary sampling is unreliable.

title: A1C purpose
stem: A client asks why an A1C is ordered when today's glucose is normal. Which explanation is best?
options: It replaces checking glucose during acute symptoms
It measures the effect of the last meal only
It helps assess glucose exposure over preceding months
It confirms the glucose level at this exact minute
why: Acute decisions may still require current glucose measurement.
The marker reflects a substantially longer interval.
The test provides information beyond a single current reading.
A1C is not a moment-to-moment glucose measure.
takeaway: Distinguish longer-term glucose assessment from a current glucose reading.
learningObjective: Distinguish longer-term glucose assessment from a current glucose reading.

title: Laboratory fasting instructions
stem: A client with diabetes is told to fast for ordered blood tests but has no instructions for morning diabetes medicines. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange an early appointment and leave the morning medication instructions unchanged
Clarify a coordinated fasting and medication plan
Tell the client to omit all medicines that day
Advise the usual doses regardless of fasting
why: Early timing may reduce fasting duration but does not resolve potentially unsafe medication/intake coordination.
Medicine timing and food restriction must be considered together.
Universal omission may be unsafe and is not individualized.
Usual dosing may not fit reduced intake.
takeaway: Coordinate test preparation with medicines affected by food intake.
learningObjective: Coordinate test preparation with medicines affected by food intake.

title: ABG compression
stem: After an arterial blood sample, the puncture site continues oozing in a client taking anticoagulation. What should the nurse do?
options: Maintain appropriate pressure and reassess bleeding and circulation
Release pressure because the usual time has elapsed
Apply a dressing and send the client away immediately
Apply a tighter dressing and defer distal circulation checks until the next round
why: Anticoagulation may require longer haemostasis monitoring.
Elapsed time does not establish that bleeding has stopped.
Ongoing bleeding needs assessment before leaving care.
Ongoing bleeding requires effective haemostasis and circulation assessment; excessive dressing pressure can compromise perfusion.
takeaway: Confirm haemostasis rather than relying only on a timed interval.
learningObjective: Confirm haemostasis rather than relying only on a timed interval.

title: Blood-gas context
stem: A blood-gas sample is collected while the client receives prescribed supplemental oxygen. Which information must accompany interpretation?
options: The usual home oxygen flow and most recent outpatient saturation
The oxygen prescription at admission and the device initially selected
The oxygen flow documented after the sample was collected
The actual oxygen device and setting when the sample was drawn
why: Those do not describe support at this collection.
The original prescription may differ from actual support during sampling.
Later support is not necessarily the support when the blood was drawn.
Blood-gas oxygenation must be interpreted in the context of concurrent support.
takeaway: Record respiratory support accurately when obtaining blood gases.
learningObjective: Record respiratory support accurately when obtaining blood gases.

title: Culture after cleansing
stem: A wound culture is ordered using the facility's wound-swab protocol. The dressing is heavily soiled with old drainage. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the same swab on surrounding intact skin first
Apply an antiseptic then sample without checking instructions
Follow the prescribed cleansing and sampling method
Swab only the removed dressing
why: This can introduce unrelated skin organisms.
Antiseptic exposure may affect culture yield.
Sampling viable wound tissue appropriately reduces misleading surface contamination.
Old dressing drainage may not represent the wound site.
takeaway: Collect wound cultures according to the specified sampling technique.
learningObjective: Collect wound cultures according to the specified sampling technique.

title: Stool specimen separation
stem: A client needs a stool culture and normally urinates during a bowel movement. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Collect a soiled absorbent brief and send it for routine processing
A collection method keeping urine out of the stool sample
Collect directly from toilet water afterward
Pour off visible urine from the mixed collection before sending the stool
why: Absorption and contamination may compromise the intended sample; arrange appropriate collection.
Mixed urine may compromise specimen quality.
Toilet water can contaminate the specimen.
Removing visible liquid does not undo contamination; obtain an appropriate sample per laboratory guidance.
takeaway: Plan stool collection to prevent urine and toilet-water contamination.
learningObjective: Plan stool collection to prevent urine and toilet-water contamination.

title: Specimen preservative
stem: A biopsy sample arrives at the bedside with an unclear preservative instruction. What should the nurse do before transfer?
options: Clarify requirements with the procedural team or laboratory
Place every tissue sample in formalin
Use the preservative supplied for the previous biopsy on the unit
Transfer the specimen into saline because fresh tissue was requested for another client
why: Different analyses require specific handling to preserve diagnostic value.
Some testing requires a different medium or fresh tissue.
Different tests may need different media; do not infer this sample’s requirements from another case.
An unrelated request does not establish the correct handling for this specimen.
takeaway: Confirm specimen-specific handling before adding a preservative.
learningObjective: Confirm specimen-specific handling before adding a preservative.

title: Urine sampling port
stem: A culture is ordered from a client with an established indwelling catheter. Which site should be used according to aseptic policy?
options: Urine standing in the collection bag
The emptied drainage outlet without site preparation
A disconnected catheter-to-tubing junction
The designated sampling port
why: Standing bag urine is less suitable for culture interpretation.
Outlet contamination can affect the sample.
Unnecessary disconnection disrupts the closed system.
The port provides a fresh sample while preserving the drainage circuit.
takeaway: Use the designated sampling port for catheter urine specimens.
learningObjective: Use the designated sampling port for catheter urine specimens.

title: Orthostatic measurements
stem: When recording measurements for postural symptoms, which details most directly link each blood-pressure value to the client’s positional tolerance? Select all that apply.
options: The usual daily exercise duration
The total number of pressure readings taken that day
Position and timing of each reading
Symptoms during each position
why: Exercise history does not establish the conditions or symptoms during these positional readings.
The count does not reveal positions, timing or symptoms during each reading.
Values must be linked to the posture and interval used.
Symptoms help relate numerical changes to clinical tolerance.
takeaway: Link orthostatic readings to position, timing, and symptoms.
learningObjective: Link orthostatic readings to position, timing, and symptoms.

title: Inhaler test instruction
stem: Before ordered spirometry, a client asks whether to take their usual inhaler. The testing instructions are unclear. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume the last client's instructions apply
Clarify the laboratory's medication instructions
Apply the same inhaler-withholding interval used for a previous spirometry client
Advise extra inhaler doses to maximize performance
why: Different testing goals may require different preparation.
Withholding requirements depend on the test's purpose and prescribed plan.
Requirements depend on the purpose and medicine; clarify this test’s instructions.
Unordered use could alter the planned measurement.
takeaway: Use test-specific instructions for medicines affecting respiratory measurements.
learningObjective: Use test-specific instructions for medicines affecting respiratory measurements.

title: Peak-flow comparison
stem: A client following an asthma action plan obtains a lower peak flow than usual. Which comparison is most useful?
options: Their personal best and action-plan zones
Their predicted reference value based on age and height
Their average reading during the most recent exacerbation
Yesterday's result without checking technique
why: Individual reference points guide the prescribed response.
Predicted values can provide context but do not replace the individualized action-plan reference.
An exacerbation average is not the personal-best reference used for plan zones.
A trend needs reasonably consistent technique to be meaningful.
takeaway: Interpret home monitoring against the individual's plan and proper technique.
learningObjective: Interpret home monitoring against the individual's plan and proper technique.

title: EEG medication preparation
stem: A client with epilepsy arrives for an EEG and says they stopped their antiseizure medicine yesterday to improve the test, although the written instructions said to take usual medicines. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the client to take an extra dose now to replace the omitted doses
Record the missed doses and proceed without alerting the EEG team
Encourage continued withholding until the EEG result is available
Assess the client and notify the EEG team of the omitted doses
why: Do not prescribe catch-up dosing independently; clarify the medication plan.
The change in medication exposure affects safety and interpretation and should be communicated.
Unplanned continued interruption may increase seizure risk and is not an authorized preparation plan.
The team must review safety, actual medication exposure and next instructions before proceeding.
takeaway: Clarify unplanned medication interruption before EEG rather than inventing catch-up doses.
learningObjective: Recognize and communicate unplanned antiseizure medication interruption before EEG.

title: Diagnostic uncertainty communication
stem: A client asks whether an abnormal screening test proves cancer. What should the nurse explain?
options: A repeat normal symptom check cancels the result
The result can be ignored if the client feels well
It indicates a need for the recommended diagnostic follow-up
Every positive screening result confirms cancer
why: Absence of symptoms does not resolve an abnormal screen.
Follow-up remains necessary despite subjective wellness.
A screening result is not necessarily a definitive diagnosis.
Screening includes false-positive findings.
takeaway: Distinguish screening abnormalities from confirmed diagnoses.
learningObjective: Distinguish screening abnormalities from confirmed diagnoses.

title: Reference-range difference
stem: A stable client's report from a new laboratory uses a different reference range. What should the nurse do?
options: Compare the numeric values alone without checking units or reference intervals
Use that laboratory's range and the clinical trend
Apply the previous laboratory's flag automatically
Assume the new laboratory made an error
why: Methods, units and ranges affect whether numbers are directly comparable.
Methods and population reference intervals can differ.
Different methods may require different interpretation.
A range difference alone does not establish error.
takeaway: Interpret results using the reporting laboratory's method and reference range.
learningObjective: Interpret results using the reporting laboratory's method and reference range.

title: Sample from an infusion arm
stem: A blood sample drawn near an active IV infusion shows results inconsistent with prior values and clinical findings. What should the nurse consider?
options: Possible sample contamination and appropriate recollection
Treat the new result as a confirmed sudden disease change
Average the result with yesterday's value
Change the infusion prescription solely from the result
why: Infused fluid can distort measurements from an unsuitable site.
The sampling context provides another explanation to investigate.
Averaging does not correct contamination.
Treatment changes require a reliable sample and clinical review.
takeaway: Review sampling conditions when results abruptly conflict with the client.
learningObjective: Review sampling conditions when results abruptly conflict with the client.

title: Unexpected positive urine finding
stem: A catheterized client has bacteria on urinalysis but no new urinary or systemic symptoms. What should the nurse do?
options: Document symptomatic infection from bacteria alone
Request antibiotics without providing clinical context
Request catheter replacement solely because bacteria are present
Report findings with symptoms and catheter history
why: Colonization can occur without symptomatic disease.
Treatment decisions need the clinical picture.
Bacteriuria alone does not establish symptomatic infection or a need for this intervention; report clinical context.
Bacteriuria alone does not establish a symptomatic infection.
takeaway: Distinguish bacteriuria from a diagnosis of symptomatic infection.
learningObjective: Distinguish bacteriuria from a diagnosis of symptomatic infection.

title: Contrast injection pain
stem: During IV contrast injection, a client reports increasing local pain and swelling. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue because brief warmth is expected
Massage firmly before checking the site
Stop the injection and follow the extravasation protocol
Reduce the injection rate and watch whether the swelling stabilizes
why: Local swelling and progressive pain differ from transient generalized warmth.
The site needs assessment and protocol-based care first.
The findings suggest contrast may be leaving the vein.
Continuing injection may increase tissue exposure; stop and follow the extravasation protocol.
takeaway: Distinguish expected contrast sensations from local extravasation signs.
learningObjective: Distinguish expected contrast sensations from local extravasation signs.

title: Unexpected test cancellation
stem: A procedure is postponed after the client followed fasting instructions. What should the nurse clarify promptly?
options: Resume every withheld medicine without review
Revised intake and medication instructions
Only the replacement appointment date
Continue fasting until any new date is available
why: Some medicines may still require procedure-specific timing.
Prolonged fasting and delayed medicines need an updated plan.
The client also needs care instructions for the intervening period.
Unnecessary prolonged fasting can cause harm.
takeaway: Update care instructions when a procedure schedule changes.
learningObjective: Update care instructions when a procedure schedule changes.

title: Serial test comparison
stem: Which conditions improve interpretation of repeated bedside measurements? Select all that apply.
options: Use consistent technique and appropriate equipment
Record interventions occurring between readings
Average measurements from different sites into one number without retaining the individual readings
Change measurement sites without documenting it
why: Technique differences can mimic clinical change.
Treatment may explain changes and support evaluation.
Combining noncomparable measurements can hide differences and prevents interpretation of the original readings.
Unrecorded site differences weaken comparison.
takeaway: Make repeated measurements comparable and document relevant interventions.
learningObjective: Make repeated measurements comparable and document relevant interventions.

title: Communicating a corrected result
stem: A laboratory calls with a corrected result that changes a previously reported critical value. What should the nurse do?
options: Replace the old note without an audit trail
Assume everyone receives the correction automatically
Wait until the next routine handover
Verify the correction and notify the responsible team promptly
why: The original communication and correction need transparent documentation.
Active communication reduces the risk of outdated decisions.
A clinically important correction may require immediate action.
Treatment decisions may need review using the corrected information.
takeaway: Communicate corrected results through a traceable timely process.
learningObjective: Communicate corrected results through a traceable timely process.

title: After cataract surgery
stem: A client reports severe new eye pain with reduced vision after cataract surgery. What should the nurse advise?
options: Treat it as expected mild scratchiness
Use the prescribed postoperative drops and wait to see whether the next dose relieves the symptoms
Seek urgent ophthalmic assessment
Use the next routine follow-up to discuss it
why: The described severity and visual change exceed minor irritation.
Routine prescribed drops do not replace urgent assessment of severe new pain with reduced vision.
Severe pain and visual loss can indicate a significant complication.
Waiting may delay treatment of a vision-threatening problem.
takeaway: Escalate severe pain or worsening vision after eye surgery.
learningObjective: Escalate severe pain or worsening vision after eye surgery.

title: Hip surgery sudden change
stem: A client after hip replacement develops sudden severe hip pain and an obviously changed leg position during a transfer. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the prescribed analgesic and retry the transfer once pain decreases
Stop movement, support the limb, and obtain urgent help
Complete the transfer to see whether pain settles
Ask the client to actively rotate the leg
why: Symptom relief does not establish that the suddenly painful displaced joint is safe to move.
A dislocation or other injury must be assessed before further movement.
Further movement can worsen a suspected mechanical complication.
Rotation may aggravate an injured prosthetic joint.
takeaway: Stop movement when sudden pain and deformity suggest a postoperative joint complication.
learningObjective: Stop movement when sudden pain and deformity suggest a postoperative joint complication.

title: After thyroid surgery
stem: A client reports new tingling around the mouth and hand cramping after thyroid surgery. Which information is most relevant to urgent review?
options: Neuromuscular findings and ordered calcium results
Swallowing comfort and the amount eaten at the last meal
Incision appearance and the amount of surface drainage
Incisional pain score and response to the last analgesic
why: The pattern can indicate postoperative hypocalcaemia.
These do not directly assess the neuromuscular pattern suggesting low calcium.
A normal incision does not exclude a postoperative electrolyte complication.
Analgesic response does not explain the new perioral tingling and hand cramps.
takeaway: Recognize postoperative neuromuscular symptoms that may reflect low calcium.
learningObjective: Recognize postoperative neuromuscular symptoms that may reflect low calcium.

title: Tonsillectomy surveillance
stem: A child recovering from tonsillectomy repeatedly swallows while resting and has fresh blood in the mouth. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer cold fluids and reassess after the child finishes drinking
Encourage forceful throat clearing
Record the blood as expected irritation because the child is not vomiting
Promptly assess and activate the bleeding response
why: Active bleeding requires prompt assessment and the bleeding response, rather than oral intake as the initial plan.
Mechanical irritation may worsen bleeding.
Fresh blood with repeated swallowing warrants prompt action even without vomiting.
Swallowed blood can hide ongoing operative-site bleeding.
takeaway: Consider concealed bleeding when swallowing increases after tonsil surgery.
learningObjective: Consider concealed bleeding when swallowing increases after tonsil surgery.

title: Vascular surgery comparison
stem: After lower-limb vascular surgery, a foot is cooler and the previously palpable pulse is no longer found. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply heat before assessing further
Repeat the pulse check after a period of rest before contacting the team
Urgently escalate the change in distal perfusion
Document it as normal because surgery causes swelling
why: Heating may injure poorly perfused tissue and delay review.
Verification can occur immediately while escalating; new postoperative perfusion loss should not await a rest period.
A new loss compared with baseline may indicate compromised blood flow.
Swelling does not justify ignoring new perfusion loss.
takeaway: Use the preprocedure vascular baseline to identify threatened limb perfusion.
learningObjective: Use the preprocedure vascular baseline to identify threatened limb perfusion.

title: Dialysis access check
stem: A client with an arteriovenous fistula cannot feel the usual vibration over it. What is the best advice?
options: Apply a tight wrap to create pressure
Contact the dialysis team promptly for assessment
Wait until the next routine dialysis appointment
Massage the fistula vigorously
why: Compression can further impair access flow.
Loss of the usual thrill may indicate impaired access flow.
Delay can jeopardize the access if flow is obstructed.
Massage is not a safe substitute for assessment of possible thrombosis.
takeaway: Report loss of the usual fistula thrill promptly.
learningObjective: Report loss of the usual fistula thrill promptly.

title: Protecting a fistula
stem: Which actions protect a mature dialysis fistula during routine care? Select all that apply.
options: Use another suitable site for routine blood pressure
Assess for changes in thrill and local condition
Use the fistula for routine blood draws without a dialysis plan
Allow tight sleeves to compress the fistula
why: Compression over the access arm can affect the fistula.
Surveillance helps detect loss of function or infection.
Unplanned access may damage the dialysis lifeline.
External constriction can impede flow.
takeaway: Protect dialysis access from avoidable compression and unplanned puncture.
learningObjective: Protect dialysis access from avoidable compression and unplanned puncture.

title: Postdialysis dizziness
stem: A client becomes dizzy when first standing after haemodialysis. What should the nurse do first?
options: Encourage walking to complete the discharge routine
Offer unrestricted fluids immediately
Attribute it solely to anxiety before assessment
Assist to a safe position and assess pressure and symptoms
why: Continuing while dizzy increases fall risk.
Fluid replacement must reflect the prescribed renal plan.
A physiological cause needs evaluation in this setting.
Fluid removal may contribute to postdialysis hypotension.
takeaway: Assess postdialysis dizziness before progressing activity.
learningObjective: Assess postdialysis dizziness before progressing activity.

title: Nephrostomy drainage
stem: A client's nephrostomy output falls suddenly, tubing is kinked, and flank discomfort begins. What should the nurse do first?
options: Request a replacement tube before correcting the external kink
Increase oral fluids before checking tubing
Relieve the visible kink and reassess promptly
Flush forcibly without checking the order or protocol
why: A visible external obstruction can be corrected promptly before deciding a replacement is necessary.
Extra intake does not resolve the visible obstruction.
A mechanical obstruction may explain the change.
High pressure can injure the collecting system.
takeaway: Check nephrostomy drainage for mechanical obstruction when symptoms change.
learningObjective: Check nephrostomy drainage for mechanical obstruction when symptoms change.

title: Nephrostomy displacement
stem: A nephrostomy tube is pulled partly out during dressing care. What is the appropriate response?
options: Apply a new dressing and recheck the external mark at the next observation
Secure it from further movement and contact the team urgently
Advance it back to the old marking independently
Resume drainage use without reporting because some urine flows
why: A new displacement needs prompt review; a dressing alone does not establish safe position.
Position and replacement require appropriate assessment.
Blind advancement may injure tissue or enter an incorrect path.
Partial flow does not establish correct position.
takeaway: Do not assume a displaced drainage tube remains correctly positioned.
learningObjective: Do not assume a displaced drainage tube remains correctly positioned.

title: Stoma perfusion change
stem: A newly created stoma becomes dark and dusky compared with its earlier pink appearance. What should the nurse do?
options: Promptly report the change for surgical assessment
Refit a larger pouch opening and reassess colour at the next scheduled pouch change
Clean repeatedly to restore normal colour
Assume every new stoma darkens during healing
why: A colour change can indicate compromised perfusion.
Assess fit as relevant, but do not defer surgical review of a new dusky stoma.
Perfusion-related colour change is not removed by cleansing.
A new dusky appearance requires evaluation.
takeaway: Compare stoma colour with baseline and escalate suspected perfusion loss.
learningObjective: Compare stoma colour with baseline and escalate suspected perfusion loss.

title: Enteral tube migration
stem: A client’s nasogastric feeding-tube external length differs from the documented marking after coughing. What should the nurse do before using it?
options: Rely on the absence of coughing during a water flush
Advance it to the old mark without reassessment
Continue feeding at half rate
Hold use and verify position through the approved process
why: Tolerance of a flush does not prove correct position.
Returning the mark alone does not verify internal location.
A slower rate does not make uncertain placement safe.
A changed external length suggests possible migration.
takeaway: Verify suspected tube displacement before feeding or medication delivery.
learningObjective: Verify suspected tube displacement before feeding or medication delivery.

title: Tube position methods
stem: A newly inserted nasogastric feeding tube awaits confirmation. Which statement should the nurse question?
options: External length should be documented after confirmation
Concerns during insertion should be communicated
A whoosh on air auscultation proves gastric placement
Position must be confirmed using the approved method
why: The baseline helps detect later migration.
Symptoms and insertion difficulties inform assessment.
Auscultation alone cannot reliably distinguish tube location.
Approved confirmation is needed before initial use.
takeaway: Do not rely on air-auscultation alone to confirm enteral tube placement.
learningObjective: Do not rely on air-auscultation alone to confirm enteral tube placement.

title: Gastrostomy dislodgement
stem: A gastrostomy tube inserted two days ago comes out during care. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait until the next scheduled feeding time
Stop tube use and obtain urgent specialist guidance
Replace it blindly with the same tube
Place a small catheter into the opening to preserve it before contacting the team
why: Prompt review matters for safe tract management.
A new tract may be immature and replacement requires expertise.
Blind reinsertion can create a false tract.
An immature tract requires urgent specialist guidance; blind insertion can create a false tract.
takeaway: Treat dislodgement of a recent gastrostomy as an urgent placement problem.
learningObjective: Treat dislodgement of a recent gastrostomy as an urgent placement problem.

title: Refeeding surveillance
stem: A severely undernourished client begins prescribed nutrition support. Which ordered monitoring most directly detects early metabolic or fluid complications of refeeding? Select all that apply.
options: Phosphate, potassium, and magnesium trends
Fluid balance and signs of oedema
The percentage of the planned calories delivered
The number of meals the client reports enjoying
why: These electrolytes can shift as feeding resumes.
Fluid shifts can contribute to clinically important complications.
Delivery helps nutrition assessment but does not directly reveal electrolyte or fluid complications.
Preference is useful but does not show early metabolic tolerance.
takeaway: Monitor electrolytes and fluid status during high-risk refeeding.
learningObjective: Monitor electrolytes and fluid status during high-risk refeeding.

title: New phosphate decline
stem: After nutrition support begins, a high-risk client's phosphate falls below the supplied laboratory range with new weakness. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase calories immediately because weakness means underfeeding
Attribute the weakness to deconditioning and continue the current feed progression
Request the next routine nutrition review after confirming that the prescribed volume was delivered
Promptly notify the team and review the feeding plan
why: More rapid feeding may worsen metabolic shifts.
The new low phosphate after refeeding needs assessment; deconditioning does not explain away the biochemical change.
Delivered volume does not establish metabolic tolerance; the symptomatic electrolyte fall needs prompt review.
The trend may represent refeeding-related electrolyte depletion.
takeaway: Escalate new electrolyte depletion during nutrition reintroduction.
learningObjective: Escalate new electrolyte depletion during nutrition reintroduction.

title: Central insertion respiratory change
stem: Soon after central venous access insertion, a client develops dyspnoea and unilateral reduced breath sounds. What is the priority?
options: Attribute symptoms to procedural discomfort alone
Wait for the planned confirmation image before responding to the breathlessness
Urgent assessment for an insertion-related complication
Give the prescribed analgesic and judge the need for escalation by pain relief
why: Pain does not explain the full unilateral respiratory pattern.
Imaging may be needed, but active respiratory change requires urgent clinical assessment while it is arranged.
The timing and unilateral findings suggest possible pneumothorax.
Analgesia does not resolve the new unilateral respiratory findings.
takeaway: Assess respiratory changes promptly after central access placement.
learningObjective: Assess respiratory changes promptly after central access placement.

title: Radial access circulation
stem: After a radial-artery procedure, a client's hand becomes pale, cool, and increasingly painful beneath a compression device. What should the nurse do?
options: Cover the hand to warm it without further review
Urgently assess perfusion and follow the access-site protocol
Add compression because pain implies bleeding
Encourage repetitive hand exercise before assessment
why: Warming alone can hide progression and delays assessment.
The pattern suggests impaired distal circulation requiring directed adjustment.
More pressure may worsen compromised circulation.
Activity does not correct a possible arterial flow problem.
takeaway: Assess distal perfusion during access-site compression.
learningObjective: Assess distal perfusion during access-site compression.

title: Femoral access bleeding
stem: A client after a femoral-artery procedure develops enlarging groin swelling and dizziness. What should the nurse do?
options: Activate the access-site bleeding response while assessing circulation
Encourage the client to walk to reduce stiffness
Measure and mark the swelling, then wait for the next routine set of observations
Record the swelling for the next routine round
