why: The combination suggests clinically important bleeding.
Movement may worsen bleeding and dizziness increases fall risk.
Measurement is useful but must not delay haemostasis/escalation when the swelling is expanding with symptoms.
Expanding swelling and symptoms require immediate response.
takeaway: Recognize expanding access-site swelling with systemic symptoms as urgent.
learningObjective: Recognize expanding access-site swelling with systemic symptoms as urgent.

title: Regional block recovery
stem: A client's leg remains numb after a regional anaesthetic and they wish to walk to the toilet. What should determine assistance?
options: Absence of pain alone
The client's usual preoperative walking ability
The scheduled time for first ambulation alone
Motor and sensory recovery plus the prescribed mobility plan
why: Analgesia does not establish strength or proprioception.
Previous function does not account for the current block.
Elapsed time cannot substitute for recovery assessment.
Residual block can impair safe weight bearing despite comfort.
takeaway: Assess block recovery before weight-bearing activity.
learningObjective: Assess block recovery before weight-bearing activity.

title: Post-spinal surgery change
stem: A client after spinal surgery develops new bilateral leg weakness and difficulty emptying the bladder. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange routine bladder assessment first and reassess leg strength afterward
Wait until the next therapy assessment
Urgently escalate the combined neurological change
Attribute the weakness to postoperative pain and the voiding difficulty to bed rest
why: Bladder assessment should not postpone urgent escalation of the combined new neurological change.
Delay may miss a time-sensitive complication.
New motor and bladder findings may indicate serious neural compromise.
Those explanations cannot safely dismiss the new paired neurological findings.
takeaway: Escalate new motor changes accompanied by bladder dysfunction.
learningObjective: Escalate new motor changes accompanied by bladder dysfunction.

title: Postoperative airway observation
stem: After neck surgery, which changes deserve immediate assessment? Select all that apply.
options: A dry intact dressing alone
Increasing neck swelling
New difficulty swallowing saliva
A stable mild sore throat without progression
why: An intact surface dressing does not indicate deterioration.
An expanding collection can threaten the airway.
This may indicate evolving swelling or airway risk.
Minor unchanged irritation is less concerning than new compromise.
takeaway: Monitor neck swelling and secretion handling after neck procedures.
learningObjective: Monitor neck swelling and secretion handling after neck procedures.

title: Negative-pressure wound device
stem: A prescribed wound device alarms for a leak and therapy stops. The client is stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess the seal and tubing according to device guidance
Silence the alarm without checking function
Increase pressure beyond the prescription
Leave the device off until the next planned change
why: A leak can interrupt prescribed negative pressure.
Silencing does not restore therapy or explain the leak.
Higher pressure does not substitute for repairing the seal.
Prolonged interruption may require a revised dressing plan.
takeaway: Investigate alarms that interrupt prescribed wound therapy.
learningObjective: Investigate alarms that interrupt prescribed wound therapy.

title: Wound packing count
stem: During an ordered dressing change, the documented packing removal count does not match what was found. What should the nurse do?
options: Insert new packing and document the expected count
Probe deeply without an assessed plan
Assume another clinician removed the missing piece
Stop and resolve the discrepancy before repacking
why: That risks concealing retained material.
Blind exploration can injure the wound.
Assumption does not resolve a clinically significant discrepancy.
Retained material must be considered and communicated.
takeaway: Reconcile wound-packing discrepancies before adding material.
learningObjective: Reconcile wound-packing discrepancies before adding material.

title: New drain-site erythema
stem: A home client with a surgical drain develops expanding insertion-site redness, fever, and new tenderness. Which information most directly describes the current clinical change for prompt review? Select all that apply.
options: The date of the planned routine follow-up appointment
The type of dressing routinely used before symptoms began
The extent and timing of skin changes
Temperature, drainage changes, and systemic symptoms
why: This does not characterize the current febrile local change or determine whether earlier review is needed.
Dressing history may provide context, but the evolving clinical findings are more direct indicators of the current complication.
Progression helps evaluate a possible local infection.
These establish the wider clinical picture and urgency.
takeaway: Report local device-site changes together with systemic findings.
learningObjective: Report local device-site changes together with systemic findings.

title: Young infant fever
stem: A parent reports a rectal temperature of 38.2 °C in a six-week-old infant who is feeding less than usual. The infant’s sibling has a cold. What should the nurse advise?
options: Give an age-appropriate antipyretic and use the repeat temperature to decide about assessment
Arrange urgent in-person assessment now, explaining the significance of fever at this age
Book the next available office visit if reduced feeding continues after the fever settles
Monitor feeding at home because the sibling’s illness provides a likely viral explanation
why: Temperature reduction does not exclude important infection in a young infant and should not delay assessment.
Measured fever with reduced feeding at six weeks needs urgent evaluation; treatment is determined after assessment.
Waiting for persistent symptoms delays assessment during an age of greater infection risk.
A household viral illness does not establish the cause or severity of this infant’s fever.
takeaway: Treat fever in a young infant as requiring prompt assessment.
learningObjective: Treat fever in a young infant as requiring prompt assessment.

title: Infant hydration assessment
stem: An eight-month-old with diarrhoea is following a clinician-prescribed oral-rehydration plan. Compared with the assessment four hours ago, which new findings suggest deterioration? Select all that apply.
options: Wet nappies have become less frequent and contain much less urine
The infant is unusually drowsy and no longer takes the offered small amounts
The infant now takes frequent small amounts without vomiting
Tears have returned during crying after being absent earlier
why: Declining urine output suggests the replacement plan may not be maintaining hydration.
Worsening arousal and inability to take fluids require prompt reassessment of hydration and illness.
Improved tolerance of the prescribed fluid supports progress rather than deterioration.
Returning tears is a reassuring trend when considered with the other hydration observations.
takeaway: Evaluate the direction of intake, urine and alertness changes during oral rehydration.
learningObjective: Evaluate the direction of intake, urine and alertness changes during oral rehydration.

title: Bronchiolitis feeding endurance
stem: An infant with bronchiolitis repeatedly stops sucking to breathe and now takes much less than usual. Which assessment has priority at the bedside?
options: The bottle, nipple flow and technique used during the infant’s usual feeds
The cumulative feed and urine volumes documented over the preceding 24 hours
The infant’s weight trajectory compared with measurements before the illness
The current work of breathing and ability to coordinate sucking, swallowing and breathing
why: Feeding equipment may contribute, but the observed respiratory interruptions require current physiological assessment first.
Intake and output quantify consequences; they do not establish whether the infant can safely sustain the present feed.
Growth history provides context but does not resolve the immediate breathing-related feeding difficulty.
The respiratory pauses may make feeding unsafe or ineffective; current breathing and endurance guide the immediate plan.
takeaway: Assess how respiratory illness affects an infant's feeding ability.
learningObjective: Assess how respiratory illness affects an infant's feeding ability.

title: Early newborn jaundice
stem: A newborn is visibly jaundiced at 14 hours of age. Feeding has appeared effective and vital signs are stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase feeding support and use the next feed’s response to decide whether testing is needed
Review maternal and infant blood groups before deciding whether to request a bilirubin level
Arrange bilirubin measurement and clinical review under the newborn jaundice protocol
Reassess the distribution of visible yellowing at the next routine observation round
why: Feeding support is useful, but jaundice this early requires assessment without waiting for a feeding response.
Blood-group information may help establish cause but should not delay assessment of early jaundice.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours warrants prompt bilirubin and clinical assessment; treatment depends on age and risk.
Visual appearance cannot reliably quantify bilirubin or justify delaying assessment at this early age.
takeaway: Escalate jaundice appearing in the first day of life.
learningObjective: Escalate jaundice appearing in the first day of life.

title: Bilirubin interpretation
stem: A newborn’s bilirubin result arrives without the collection time or age at sampling. What information is most important to verify before the team applies a treatment threshold?
options: The laboratory high flag and the routine reference interval printed beside the value
The postnatal age at sampling, gestational age and relevant clinical risk factors
The numerical difference from the previous result whose collection time is also missing
The feeding frequency and wet-nappy count during the most recent nursing shift
why: A generic laboratory flag does not replace an age- and risk-specific neonatal treatment threshold.
Neonatal bilirubin thresholds depend on age in hours and risk context; missing timing must be resolved.
Without elapsed time, the apparent change cannot be interpreted reliably as a rate of rise.
Feeding and output are important context but cannot substitute for age and risk when applying a threshold.
takeaway: Interpret newborn bilirubin using age and relevant risk factors.
learningObjective: Interpret newborn bilirubin using age and relevant risk factors.

title: Newborn intake warning
stem: A four-day-old with jaundice has a feeding-support plan and a bilirubin recheck booked. Which changes since yesterday warrant contacting the newborn team before the booked review? Select all that apply.
options: The infant now needs repeated stimulation to wake and cannot sustain feeds
The number and amount of wet nappies have declined despite the feeding plan
The infant asks to feed more frequently and has audible swallowing during feeds
The stools are becoming yellow while the infant wakes readily for feeds
why: Poor arousal with worsening intake can accompany significant illness or jaundice and requires earlier assessment.
Falling urine output suggests inadequate intake or hydration and may undermine the jaundice management plan.
More frequent effective feeding is not itself deterioration and may support intake and bilirubin elimination.
Stool transition with ready arousal supports feeding progress rather than the concerning change described by the keyed findings.
takeaway: Recognize feeding and arousal changes that require earlier reassessment during neonatal jaundice follow-up.
learningObjective: Recognize feeding and arousal changes that require earlier reassessment during neonatal jaundice follow-up.

title: Green emesis in infancy
stem: A two-month-old has green vomit and increasing abdominal distension. The infant previously had uncomplicated spit-ups. Which plan has priority?
options: Offer small frequent oral-rehydration amounts and reassess after the next vomiting episode
Use smaller feeds and an upright feeding position to manage a possible reflux flare
Give the previously prescribed antiemetic and review the response before seeking assessment
Arrange urgent assessment and withhold further feeds while following the emergency plan
why: An oral trial may suit some vomiting illnesses, but bilious emesis with distension raises concern for obstruction.
The new green emesis and distension differ from uncomplicated reflux and need urgent evaluation.
Suppressing vomiting does not address a possible obstructive cause and should not postpone assessment.
The new pattern may indicate obstruction; urgent assessment and protocol-directed feeding precautions are needed.
takeaway: Treat green vomiting with distension in an infant as urgent.
learningObjective: Treat green vomiting with distension in an infant as urgent.

title: Child oral-rehydration failure
stem: A three-year-old on a home oral-rehydration plan is becoming lethargic and vomits even the small amounts offered. What should the nurse advise now?
options: Reduce each oral amount further and evaluate the next hour’s intake at home
Give the prescribed antiemetic and restart the oral schedule before deciding about review
Obtain prompt reassessment of circulation, hydration and the route of fluid replacement
Resume the planned oral replacement schedule when a vomiting-free interval occurs
why: A further home trial does not address worsening alertness and failed tolerance of the existing small-volume plan.
An antiemetic may be part of treatment, but its trial should not delay assessment of this deterioration.
Lethargy and failure to retain fluids mean the current plan may no longer be sufficient or safe.
Waiting for vomiting to pause delays evaluation while intake and clinical condition are worsening.
takeaway: Escalate when oral rehydration is failing and the child deteriorates.
learningObjective: Escalate when oral rehydration is failing and the child deteriorates.

title: Postpartum fundal displacement
stem: Six hours after vaginal birth, a client has voided 60 mL twice. The fundus is 2 cm above the umbilicus and right of midline. It firms with massage but remains displaced. Lochia is moderate; pulse is 84/min and blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg. Which assessment and follow-up best address the likely contributor?
options: Assess cramping during feeds; provide prescribed analgesia and evaluate the change in discomfort
Assess bladder filling and emptying; follow the postpartum voiding plan and reassess the fundus
Compare current and previous pad weights; repeat fundal massage if uterine tone decreases
Review placental completeness at birth; request further evaluation if retained tissue is suspected
why: Feeding-related cramping can need relief, but it does not explain persistent fundal displacement with repeated small voids.
Bladder distension can elevate and displace the uterus and impair contraction. Assess emptying, follow the voiding or catheterization plan as indicated, and reassess fundal position, tone and lochia.
Bleeding and tone still need surveillance, but pad weights and massage do not address a possible full bladder contributing to the displacement.
Retained tissue can cause poor contraction or bleeding, but lateral displacement together with repeated small voids more directly points to bladder distension.
takeaway: Relate postpartum fundal position and tone to bladder emptying, then reassess after the voiding plan.
learningObjective: Recognize bladder distension as a contributor to fundal displacement and select focused assessment and follow-up.

title: Postpartum headache assessment
stem: Five days after birth, a client with previously normal antenatal blood pressure reports severe headache, blurred vision and upper abdominal pain. What should the nurse advise?
options: Arrange urgent maternity or emergency assessment, including blood pressure and clinical evaluation
Record several home blood-pressure readings over the afternoon before deciding about assessment
Take the usual analgesic, rest in a dark room and use symptom relief to decide whether to call
Book a later same-day primary-care visit because blood pressure was normal during pregnancy
why: The symptom combination can indicate postpartum hypertensive disease or another serious problem even after a normotensive pregnancy.
Home measurements may provide information but should not delay assessment of these severe symptoms.
Analgesic response cannot safely exclude a serious postpartum cause of headache and visual symptoms.
Normal antenatal readings do not rule out new postpartum disease; the current symptoms set the urgency.
takeaway: Recognize postpartum hypertensive warning symptoms even after discharge.
learningObjective: Recognize postpartum hypertensive warning symptoms even after discharge.

title: Postpartum infection cues
stem: On day four after caesarean birth, which new findings warrant assessment for infection? Select all that apply.
options: Foul-smelling lochia accompanied by worsening pelvic pain
Cramping during breastfeeding that settles after the feed
Incision discomfort with coughing that is less than yesterday
Fever accompanied by increasing uterine tenderness
why: This combination differs from expected lochia and raises concern for uterine or pelvic infection.
Transient feed-related afterpains can accompany uterine involution and are less suggestive of infection.
Improving movement-related incisional discomfort is consistent with recovery unless other concerning findings develop.
New fever with increasing uterine tenderness requires prompt assessment of a possible postpartum infection.
takeaway: Assess worsening postpartum pain with fever or abnormal discharge.
learningObjective: Assess worsening postpartum pain with fever or abnormal discharge.

title: Pregnancy reduced movement
stem: At 32 weeks of pregnancy, a client reports that the baby’s movements are clearly reduced today compared with the usual pattern. Yesterday’s maternity assessment was reassuring. What should the nurse advise?
options: Eat a meal and complete a further period of movement counting before contacting maternity care
Use yesterday’s reassuring assessment to guide observation at home until the pattern returns
Contact the maternity assessment service promptly about the new reduction
Check for a heartbeat with a home Doppler and call if it cannot be found
why: A meaningful new reduction should be reported promptly rather than delaying contact for another home test.
Yesterday’s findings do not establish fetal wellbeing during a new change today.
The maternity team should assess a new reduction in the individual movement pattern.
Audible fetal cardiac activity at home does not establish current wellbeing or replace assessment.
takeaway: Act on a meaningful reduction in the established fetal movement pattern.
learningObjective: Act on a meaningful reduction in the established fetal movement pattern.

title: Pregnancy vomiting risk
stem: A client at 12 weeks of pregnancy has persistent vomiting. Which findings most directly show that hydration or circulation may be compromised? Select all that apply.
options: Nausea begins when the client smells hot food in the kitchen
Measured urine totals 120 mL over eight hours despite attempted fluid intake
Pulse rises from 88/min supine to 118/min standing, with marked dizziness
Vomiting occurs more often after large meals than after small snacks
why: Odour sensitivity helps identify triggers but does not measure hydration or circulatory effects.
Low measured urine in this context suggests inadequate fluid balance and needs prompt assessment.
A substantial postural pulse change with dizziness supports concern about circulatory tolerance.
Meal-related patterns guide symptom management but do not directly establish volume compromise.
takeaway: Distinguish vomiting triggers from objective evidence of maternal hydration or circulation compromise.
learningObjective: Distinguish vomiting triggers from objective evidence of maternal hydration or circulation compromise.

title: Postoperative child pain change
stem: On day three after abdominal surgery, a child who had been improving develops temperature 38.6 °C, guarding and increasing abdominal pain. Which nursing action has priority?
options: Arrange prompt surgical review while assessing the new abdominal and systemic findings
Give the prescribed analgesic and judge the need for review from the next pain score
Assist walking to relieve presumed gas and reassess the abdomen afterwards
Offer a graded oral-fluid trial to see whether bowel recovery continues
why: A reversal of recovery with fever and guarding requires assessment for a complication before routine recovery measures.
Analgesia may be appropriate, but response should not determine whether this new pattern receives review.
Gas discomfort does not adequately explain the combined fever, guarding and worsening trajectory.
An oral trial does not assess the cause of new guarding and fever and should not precede review.
takeaway: Investigate a reversal in postoperative recovery rather than following the usual timeline.
learningObjective: Investigate a reversal in postoperative recovery rather than following the usual timeline.

title: Adolescent exercise syncope
stem: An adolescent faints while running and reports chest tightness immediately before the collapse. They are now awake and speaking normally. What plan is most appropriate?
options: Provide oral fluids and attempt a gradual return once resting symptoms resolve
Check glucose and change the pre-exercise snack before resuming training
Arrange a routine sports-health visit while allowing activity below the usual intensity
Arrange urgent clinical evaluation and withhold further exertion pending assessment
why: Dehydration is possible but does not safely explain exertional syncope preceded by chest symptoms.
Glucose may be relevant to assessment, but a snack change does not address the concerning exertional pattern.
Lower-intensity sport still exposes the adolescent to exertion before an important cause has been evaluated.
This combination warrants urgent assessment before return to exercise; no specific diagnosis can be assumed.
takeaway: Assess exertional syncope before resuming activity.
learningObjective: Assess exertional syncope before resuming activity.

title: Older adult delirium fluctuation
stem: An older adult was attentive at breakfast but is now intermittently inattentive and disorganized. Family confirm a sudden departure from baseline. Which plan best addresses the immediate concern?
options: Review sedating medication times and ask the next shift to compare the cognitive pattern
Use familiar objects and a quieter room as the main response to the change
Assess for delirium and current physiological contributors while reviewing medications and baseline
Arrange formal cognitive screening after the client has had an uninterrupted night’s sleep
why: Medication review matters, but postponing current assessment may miss hypoxia, infection or another reversible acute cause.
Environmental support may help but does not identify the cause of acute fluctuating inattention.
The rapid fluctuating change suggests possible delirium and calls for prompt assessment of contributing illness and exposures.
Later cognitive testing cannot replace assessment of an acute change from a confirmed baseline.
takeaway: Use onset and fluctuation to distinguish acute change from chronic baseline.
learningObjective: Use onset and fluctuation to distinguish acute change from chronic baseline.

title: Reduced sensation after injury
stem: Swelling has increased beneath a hand dressing, and the client reports new fingertip numbness. The radial pulse remains palpable. Which assessment is still most urgent?
options: The amount of wound drainage, dressing staining and time since the last dressing change
Distal colour, warmth, sensation and movement, including possible dressing constriction
The original wound depth, contamination history and appearance of the wound edges
The pain score, analgesic timing and change in wound discomfort after medication
why: Drainage monitoring is useful but does not evaluate the new distal neurological change.
A proximal palpable pulse does not exclude evolving distal nerve or perfusion compromise from pressure.
Wound history helps ongoing care but is less direct than current neurovascular assessment for new numbness.
Pain response does not establish intact sensation or distal perfusion beneath a swelling dressing.
takeaway: Reassess neurovascular status when swelling changes under a dressing.
learningObjective: Reassess neurovascular status when swelling changes under a dressing.

title: Burn limb surveillance
stem: A client with a circumferential lower-leg burn has serial neurovascular observations. Which new findings require prompt review? Select all that apply.
options: Tingling progresses to reduced sensation in the toes
The foot becomes cooler and capillary refill is slower than at baseline
Pain decreases after the prescribed analgesic and supported positioning
A small amount of clear wound fluid appears within the expected dressing pattern
why: New sensory loss may signal nerve or circulation compromise as swelling develops.
Worsening distal perfusion can indicate constriction from the circumferential injury.
Improved comfort is useful but is not itself evidence of worsening neurovascular status.
Expected local drainage needs monitoring but does not indicate distal perfusion loss like the keyed changes.
takeaway: Monitor distal function as swelling evolves beneath circumferential injury.
learningObjective: Monitor distal function as swelling evolves beneath circumferential injury.

title: Splint discharge understanding
stem: A client is discharged with a temporary forearm splint while swelling settles. Which statement shows appropriate understanding of the warning signs?
options: If I can still move my fingers, a new change in their colour can wait for the follow-up visit
If elevation relieves the aching, I can use that improvement to judge new numbness
Because the splint is removable, I can manage new cold fingers by adjusting it without calling
If numbness or colour changes develop, I will seek advice even when the aching has improved
why: Retained movement does not establish adequate distal perfusion when a new colour change develops.
Pain relief with elevation does not rule out a separate new neurological warning sign.
The ability to remove a device does not remove the need for prompt assessment of cold fingers.
New neurovascular symptoms need review independently of whether pain has partially improved.
takeaway: Teach specific distal warning signs with immobilization devices.
learningObjective: Teach specific distal warning signs with immobilization devices.

title: Foreign-body wound history
stem: A client has a foot puncture through footwear with a small surface opening. Which history set most directly identifies deep contamination, retained-material and tetanus risks?
options: Previous foot problems, usual footwear fit and the most recent analgesic dose
Baseline walking ability, current activity demands and the change in pain with weight bearing
Time of injury, penetrating object, possible depth and tetanus immunization history
Home cleansing already performed, available dressing supplies and access to follow-up
why: These provide useful context but do not characterize the penetrating material or immunization protection.
Function and pain matter, but a small painful or painless opening can conceal a deep puncture.
Mechanism, timing and immunization help direct assessment of contamination, retained material and tetanus prevention.
Aftercare history matters but does not replace the injury mechanism and immunization history.
takeaway: Assess the mechanism and preventive history of a puncture wound.
learningObjective: Assess the mechanism and preventive history of a puncture wound.

title: Confusion and retention
stem: After catheter removal, a frail older adult becomes restless and repeatedly voids small drops. Which information most directly evaluates suspected incomplete bladder emptying? Select all that apply.
options: The time and amount of the most recent sedating medication
Bladder distension and a retained-volume measurement obtained under protocol
The removal time and measured volume and timing of subsequent voids
The sleep pattern and frequency of environmental interruptions overnight
why: Medications may contribute to retention or confusion, but this information does not measure emptying.
Examination and an appropriate bladder-volume assessment directly evaluate retained urine.
The post-removal output pattern establishes whether meaningful emptying has occurred.
Sleep disruption may contribute to restlessness but does not establish the degree of urinary retention.
takeaway: Include painful retention among reversible causes of new restlessness.
learningObjective: Include painful retention among reversible causes of new restlessness.

title: Immunosuppressed fever
stem: Eight days after cytotoxic chemotherapy, a client calls at 21:00 with temperature 38.4 °C and chills. The oncology team supplied an after-hours fever plan. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use the oncology fever plan to obtain urgent assessment tonight
Arrange a routine blood count tomorrow before deciding whether to contact oncology
Take the prescribed antipyretic and use the temperature response to decide about assessment
Contact the usual daytime clinic when it opens if the fever remains
why: Fever during a period of possible treatment-related immunosuppression can signal serious infection and requires the urgent pathway.
A blood count may be needed, but arranging a routine test should not delay assessment of measured fever and chills.
An antipyretic can lower temperature without treating the cause or reducing the need for assessment.
Waiting for the daytime service delays care despite an available after-hours fever plan.
takeaway: Apply the prescribed urgent fever plan for immunosuppressed clients.
learningObjective: Apply the prescribed urgent fever plan for immunosuppressed clients.

title: New bleeding after discharge
stem: Four days after colonoscopic polyp removal, a client has repeated episodes of rectal bleeding and new weakness after an initially uncomplicated recovery. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use the usual haemorrhoid treatment and reassess whether the next stool contains blood
Measure further stool loss at home and call if it continues through the next bowel movement
Seek advice about the anticoagulant schedule before deciding whether examination is needed
Arrange urgent assessment of the bleeding and weakness despite the delayed onset
why: A previous haemorrhoid history would not safely explain new repeated bleeding with weakness after polypectomy.
Measurement can help the clinical team but should not postpone assessment when systemic symptoms accompany bleeding.
Medication information is important during assessment, but clarification should not delay review of active symptomatic bleeding.
Delayed post-procedure bleeding can be clinically important; the current symptoms require evaluation.
takeaway: Teach that significant delayed bleeding still needs urgent assessment.
learningObjective: Teach that significant delayed bleeding still needs urgent assessment.

title: Home-monitoring barriers
stem: A client with heart failure is prescribed home weight monitoring but cannot stand safely on the available scale. Which plan best preserves useful monitoring?
options: Use serial ankle measurements as the replacement for the prescribed weight measurements
Record intake and output and omit weights until standing balance returns
Arrange an accessible calibrated weighing method and agree the monitoring plan with the team
Have a family member steady the client on the standard scale for each measurement
why: Ankle measurements may supplement assessment but are not interchangeable with a comparable body-weight trend.
Fluid records may help but should not silently replace a prescribed measure without an agreed clinical plan.
An accessible method can provide comparable measurements while meeting the client’s mobility needs.
Family steadying may create a fall risk and distort the measurement; a suitable accessible method is needed.
takeaway: Adapt surveillance methods when disability prevents standard measurement.
learningObjective: Adapt surveillance methods when disability prevents standard measurement.

title: Caregiver observation escalation
stem: A familiar caregiver reports that a nonverbal adult is breathing faster than usual and cannot tolerate transfers that were manageable yesterday. Which assessment has priority?
options: Review the transfer technique, joint range and equipment fit with the caregiver
Assess current breathing, oxygenation and circulation against the known baseline
Review recent environmental changes and usual behavioural calming strategies
Establish an adapted pain tool and review the client’s usual ways of showing discomfort
why: Musculoskeletal and equipment checks may follow, but they do not explain away the simultaneous new respiratory change.
New faster breathing with functional decline can signal physiological deterioration and needs prompt assessment.
Environmental support may be useful but should not replace assessment of new respiratory and activity intolerance.
Pain communication is important, but current respiratory and circulatory assessment takes priority with these combined changes.
takeaway: Use informed caregiver observations to recognize change from baseline.
learningObjective: Use informed caregiver observations to recognize change from baseline.

title: Pulmonary prevention outcome
stem: A postoperative client is reassessed after an individualized breathing and mobility plan. Which findings best indicate improved lung expansion and clearance? Select all that apply.
options: Chest excursions are deeper and coughing brings up secretions more effectively
The client tolerates a longer walk without needing increased oxygen support
The client completes the breathing sessions at the scheduled times
Breathing sounds quieter after sedating analgesia but chest excursions remain shallow
why: Deeper ventilation and more effective expectoration demonstrate a physiological response to the plan.
Improved activity tolerance with unchanged support suggests improved respiratory reserve.
Completion documents participation but does not show that expansion or clearance improved.
Quieter behaviour or breathing after sedation does not establish effective ventilation when excursions remain shallow.
takeaway: Evaluate pulmonary prevention through respiratory function and support needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate pulmonary prevention through respiratory function and support needs.

title: Fluid response trend
stem: The exhibit shows observations before and two hours after prescribed treatment for volume depletion. Which interpretation best integrates the response?
options: Blood pressure has recovered, so the fluid deficit is fully corrected
The urine response shows renal improvement, but the circulation has not improved
Urine output remains lower than recent fluid intake, so replacement has failed
Several perfusion indicators have improved, and ordered reassessment should continue
why: A better blood pressure is reassuring but one set of observations does not establish complete replacement or sustained recovery.
Pulse, blood pressure and postural symptoms also improve, supporting a circulatory response rather than an isolated urine change.
During replacement, measured urine need not equal recent intake because fluids may be correcting an existing deficit.
Convergent changes in pulse, pressure, urine and symptoms support early improvement; continued monitoring establishes whether it persists.
takeaway: Use converging clinical trends to evaluate fluid response.
learningObjective: Use converging clinical trends to evaluate fluid response.

title: Ventilation despite saturation
stem: A client receiving prescribed oxygen becomes increasingly drowsy. The exhibit shows current arterial blood-gas and saturation results. Which interpretation requires the most immediate attention?
options: A primary metabolic disturbance is producing acidemia without impaired ventilation
Chronic carbon-dioxide retention is fully compensated and explains no new risk
Ventilation is inadequate despite the apparently acceptable oxygen saturation
An oxygenation deficit is the principal abnormality shown by the current results
why: The markedly raised arterial carbon dioxide directly indicates impaired ventilation; the bicarbonate does not support a primary metabolic explanation.
The pH remains acidemic and alertness is worsening, so the findings cannot be dismissed as fully compensated stable retention.
High carbon dioxide with acidemia and worsening arousal indicates ventilatory insufficiency even while oxygen supports saturation.
Oxygen saturation alone does not assess carbon-dioxide clearance; the shown urgent pattern is ventilatory failure.
takeaway: Separate oxygenation from ventilation when evaluating respiratory monitoring.
learningObjective: Separate oxygenation from ventilation when evaluating respiratory monitoring.

title: Bladder retraining outcome
stem: After an individualized voiding plan, which finding most strongly suggests improved bladder emptying?
options: A completed diary with unchanged discomfort
Lower measured residuals with relief of fullness
More toilet visits with persistent small voids
Less pad use without output measurements
why: Recording is useful but does not demonstrate treatment benefit.
Objective residual reduction and symptoms address the intended outcome.
Frequency alone does not establish effective emptying.
Containment use does not directly measure residual urine.
takeaway: Measure emptying directly when evaluating a retention-focused plan.
learningObjective: Measure emptying directly when evaluating a retention-focused plan.

title: Drain patency restored
stem: After a kink in a surgical drain is corrected, which findings support restored function? Select all that apply.
options: Drainage resumes and local swelling eases
The prescribed suction is maintained
The tubing has been replaced but swelling increases
Output stays absent with increasing pain
why: Flow with reduced accumulation supports effective drainage.
A functioning closed-suction system should sustain its intended state.
Equipment change alone does not establish improvement.
Persisting accumulation symptoms argue against restored function.
takeaway: Evaluate device correction by both function and client response.
learningObjective: Evaluate device correction by both function and client response.

title: Bleeding surveillance after biopsy
stem: Immediately after a percutaneous kidney biopsy, pulse was 84/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and puncture pain 3/10. Four hours later the surface dressing is dry. Which observation requires urgent investigation?
options: Pulse 88/min, BP 122/74 mm Hg and puncture soreness 1/10
Pulse 90/min, BP 120/70 mm Hg and an unchanged small bruise
Pulse 86/min, BP 118/72 mm Hg and initially pink urine becoming clearer
Pulse 112/min, BP 96/60 mm Hg and increasing flank pain 6/10
why: Near-baseline circulation with improving local soreness supports recovery while routine monitoring continues.
These near-baseline observations and an unchanged bruise are less concerning than progressive systemic and pain changes.
Near-baseline observations with clearing urine are reassuring compared with haemodynamic deterioration, though surveillance continues.
New tachycardia, falling pressure and increasing flank pain may reflect concealed bleeding; a dry dressing does not exclude it.
takeaway: A dry external dressing does not exclude internal blood loss.
learningObjective: A dry external dressing does not exclude internal blood loss.

title: Refeeding progression decision
stem: An undernourished client has new weakness as the feeding rate is due to increase. The exhibit shows the phosphate trend. Which decision is most appropriate?
options: Proceed with the scheduled increase because body weight has begun to rise
Proceed with the scheduled increase because nausea and abdominal distension are absent
Seek review of the metabolic change before implementing the scheduled increase
Proceed with the scheduled increase because delivered calories remain below target
why: Weight gain may include fluid shifts and does not establish metabolic tolerance of feeding.
Gastrointestinal tolerance does not exclude refeeding-related electrolyte depletion.
The marked fall below the reference range with weakness requires prompt review before advancing nutrition.
An unmet calorie target does not outweigh evidence that the current progression may be causing a metabolic complication.
takeaway: Use biochemical and clinical tolerance before advancing high-risk nutrition support.
learningObjective: Use biochemical and clinical tolerance before advancing high-risk nutrition support.

title: Wound healing comparison
stem: Which paired observations best support healing of a chronic wound under the current plan?
options: More frequent dressing changes with unchanged dimensions
Smaller dimensions and increased healthy granulation
Lower pain after analgesia with unchanged wound deterioration
Less drainage because the opening seals over a swollen cavity
why: Care frequency is a process rather than evidence of healing.
Both indicate progress in tissue repair.
Symptom relief alone does not establish healing.
Reduced external drainage may conceal retained fluid.
takeaway: Interpret wound progress through tissue and size changes rather than task frequency.
learningObjective: Interpret wound progress through tissue and size changes rather than task frequency.

title: Delirium intervention outcome
stem: A client with delirium is reassessed after sleep support, sensory aids and treatment of contributing illness. Which findings support cognitive improvement? Select all that apply.
options: The client sustains attention throughout a conversation
Thoughts are more organized across repeated observations
The client is quieter after sedation but continues to lose the thread of questions
The client makes fewer spontaneous movements and spends less time out of bed
why: Recovered attention addresses a core feature of delirium rather than behaviour alone.
Consistent improvement across observations is stronger evidence than one brief lucid interaction.
Reduced agitation after sedation does not establish recovery of attention or thinking.
Reduced activity may reflect hypoactivity or sedation and does not by itself show cognitive recovery.
takeaway: Evaluate delirium through attention and cognition rather than quietness alone.
learningObjective: Evaluate delirium through attention and cognition rather than quietness alone.

title: Antibiotic culture mismatch
stem: A client taking an antibiotic for a culture-confirmed infection feels somewhat better. The final susceptibility report identifies resistance to the prescribed agent. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue the planned course without additional review because symptoms have improved
Obtain a repeat culture and wait for its result before contacting the prescribing team
Document symptom improvement as evidence that the organism has been cleared
Send the susceptibility result and current clinical response for prompt treatment review
why: Partial symptom improvement does not resolve a mismatch between the organism and the prescribed treatment.
Another sample may be appropriate if ordered, but it should not delay communicating an actionable final result.
Symptom improvement does not establish microbiological clearance or invalidate susceptibility testing.
The team needs both laboratory and clinical information to reassess therapy; the nurse does not independently substitute an antibiotic.
takeaway: Integrate susceptibility results with response when reviewing treatment effectiveness.
learningObjective: Integrate susceptibility results with response when reviewing treatment effectiveness.

title: Positive clot screen
stem: Two days after surgery, a client develops unexplained pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. The D-dimer is positive, and diagnostic imaging is being arranged. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: The result is unlikely to matter because the resting pulse remains within range
The postoperative setting explains the result sufficiently to exclude a new thrombus
The result must be interpreted with clinical findings and further diagnostic assessment
The positive result establishes pulmonary embolism as the cause of the symptoms
why: A single normal pulse does not exclude a clinically important thromboembolic cause of these symptoms.
Surgery can elevate D-dimer, but that does not safely explain away new chest pain and dyspnoea.
D-dimer is nonspecific; the symptoms and further testing determine whether a thrombus or another process is present.
A positive D-dimer alone does not confirm pulmonary embolism.
takeaway: Distinguish a positive clot-screening test from a confirmed diagnosis.
learningObjective: Distinguish a positive clot-screening test from a confirmed diagnosis.

title: Neutrophil result priority
stem: A client on myelosuppressive therapy has a low absolute neutrophil count flagged by the laboratory. Which associated finding most increases urgency?
options: A small old bruise that is fading
A new fever and chills
Stable pallor without new symptoms
An unchanged mild appetite reduction
why: A resolving bruise does not establish a new infectious complication.
Low neutrophil protection makes infection symptoms particularly concerning.
Pallor may relate to anaemia but does not carry the same infection cue.
A stable appetite change is less urgent than new fever.
takeaway: Interpret neutropenia together with signs of infection.
learningObjective: Interpret neutropenia together with signs of infection.

title: Platelet precautions evaluation
stem: A client with treatment-related thrombocytopenia discusses home care. Which actions demonstrate appropriate bleeding precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Uses a soft toothbrush and contacts the team about new gum bleeding
Checks with the team before starting a nonprescription medicine
Uses a disposable blade razor for a close shave as part of the usual routine
Adds nonprescription ibuprofen to manage a new mild headache
why: Gentle oral care reduces trauma, and new bleeding should be reported rather than dismissed.
Nonprescription medicines can affect platelets or interact with treatment, so review supports safe selection.
A blade can cause cuts; an appropriate electric razor generally reduces skin injury.
Ibuprofen can impair platelet function and should not be added without team review in this context.
takeaway: Evaluate bleeding-risk teaching through concrete self-care and reporting behaviours.
learningObjective: Evaluate bleeding-risk teaching through concrete self-care and reporting behaviours.

title: Renal recovery pattern
stem: The exhibit shows trends after treatment for acute kidney dysfunction. Which interpretation best supports the next monitoring plan?
options: Creatinine has fallen, indicating that renal function has returned to the documented baseline
The urine response provides enough evidence to replace further biochemical checks with output monitoring
The fall from yesterday is too small to interpret because creatinine must first enter the reference range
Creatinine and urine output are improving, but the persistent rise above baseline still needs monitoring
why: The current creatinine of 130 µmol/L remains above the documented baseline of 75 µmol/L.
Improved output does not establish recovered filtration or stable electrolytes; prescribed biochemical monitoring remains relevant.
The direction of change can inform assessment before full normalization, especially when it agrees with output and clinical findings.
The trend supports improvement, while the residual abnormality means recovery is incomplete.
takeaway: Evaluate renal recovery against baseline and multiple trends.
learningObjective: Evaluate renal recovery against baseline and multiple trends.

title: Effective airway clearance
stem: A client performs prescribed huff coughing after coaching. Which outcome best demonstrates effective clearance?
options: The nurse records all planned sessions
The client coughs longer but remains exhausted and congested
Secretions are expelled and breath sounds improve
The client describes the technique correctly
why: Documentation of attempts is a process measure.
More effort without clearance may indicate an ineffective strategy.
The observation directly reflects movement of airway secretions.
Knowledge alone does not demonstrate clearance.
takeaway: Judge airway-clearance techniques by secretion movement and respiratory response.
learningObjective: Judge airway-clearance techniques by secretion movement and respiratory response.

title: Compression tolerance evaluation
stem: A client starts prescribed compression therapy for venous disease. Which findings support ongoing safe tolerance? Select all that apply.
options: Toes become cooler despite less ankle swelling
Reduced swelling without new distal pain or numbness
Skin remains intact at device edges
A tight rolled top leaves persistent skin indentations
why: Reduced swelling does not excuse compromised distal perfusion.
Benefit and absence of neurovascular symptoms support tolerance.
Inspection checks for pressure-related adverse effects.
Focal constriction indicates a fit or application problem.
takeaway: Evaluate compression benefit together with distal circulation and skin response.
learningObjective: Evaluate compression benefit together with distal circulation and skin response.

title: New pulse deficit in context
stem: A client who usually has a regular pulse reports new palpitations. Two nurses simultaneously count an irregular apical pulse of 96/min and radial pulse of 82/min for one full minute. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and the client is alert. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Assess symptoms and perfusion, and arrange rhythm assessment for the new pulse deficit
Repeat the two pulse counts at different times to determine which reading is accurate
Use the radial rate to classify the rhythm as satisfactory because it is within range
Use the apical rate as the sole finding and recheck routinely if palpitations settle
why: The simultaneous counts show a 14/min deficit, suggesting not every apical beat produces a palpable radial pulse; the new irregularity needs rhythm and clinical assessment.
Sequential counts would lose the same-time comparison needed to distinguish a true deficit from rate variation.
A numerically normal radial rate does not exclude an arrhythmia or explain the deficit.
An apical rate describes ventricular contractions but does not remove the significance of a new irregular rhythm with a peripheral deficit.
takeaway: Interpret a new pulse deficit with rhythm and perfusion findings rather than treating a normal rate as reassuring.
learningObjective: Interpret a new pulse deficit with rhythm and perfusion findings rather than treating a normal rate as reassuring.

title: Measured fluid balance
stem: During a shift, a client receives 800 mL orally and 500 mL IV; measured urine is 900 mL and emesis 200 mL. What is the recorded measured balance? Exclude unmeasured losses; use mL.
options: Positive 400 mL
Negative 200 mL
Positive 1300 mL
Positive 200 mL
why: This ignores the 200 mL of measured emesis.
The subtraction direction is reversed.
This is total intake without subtracting measured output.
Intake 1300 mL minus measured output 1100 mL equals positive 200 mL.
takeaway: Include all measured routes while stating limits of the balance calculation.
learningObjective: Include all measured routes while stating limits of the balance calculation.

title: Fever treatment evaluation
stem: A client receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy is being assessed after a fever call. The prescribed antipyretic lowers temperature from 38.5 °C to 37.4 °C, but rigors and marked weakness continue. Which plan best reflects this response?
options: Use the lower temperature as the main recovery indicator and reduce observation frequency
Continue home symptom monitoring and seek further assessment if the fever returns
Continue urgent infection assessment, reporting the original fever and persistent systemic symptoms
Repeat temperature at the next medicine interval before deciding whether blood tests are needed
why: The medicine can reduce temperature without treating infection; persistent rigors and weakness are not evidence of recovery.
Recurrent fever is not required to justify assessment in this immunosuppressed client with ongoing systemic symptoms.
The response is symptomatic, not proof of infection resolution; the team needs the pretreatment fever and the remaining findings.
Waiting for another temperature risks delay despite continuing concerning symptoms.
takeaway: Do not equate a lower temperature after antipyretic use with resolution of infection.
learningObjective: Do not equate a lower temperature after antipyretic use with resolution of infection.

title: Home oxygen review
stem: A client uses prescribed home oxygen. Which reported changes warrant clinical review of the current plan? Select all that apply.
options: More portable cylinders are used because outings are longer, with unchanged settings and exercise tolerance
Breathlessness increases during the same walk that was manageable last week
The client feels a new need to exceed the prescribed settings to manage usual activities
Saturation remains within the individual target on the prescribed setting, with unchanged breathlessness and exercise tolerance
why: Longer time away can explain greater cylinder use without a physiological change, although supply planning may need adjustment.
Worsening tolerance of a comparable task suggests a change in condition or support needs.
The perceived need for increased settings requires clinical assessment and an authorized plan, rather than independent adjustment.
A stable target reading with unchanged tolerance supports the current plan rather than a deterioration trigger.
takeaway: Review changing oxygen needs while following the individualized prescription.
learningObjective: Review changing oxygen needs while following the individualized prescription.

title: Risk after symptom relief
stem: A client on an individualized retention plan voids 180 mL and reports partial relief. An immediate bladder scan, repeated correctly under protocol, shows 420 mL remaining. The prescribed plan requires escalation when postvoid residual exceeds 350 mL. What should the nurse do next?
options: Follow the prescribed persistent-retention plan and report the measured residual
Encourage another oral drink and wait for the next spontaneous void before acting
Repeat the scan at the next routine four-hour interval because some urine was passed
Use the improvement in fullness to continue scheduled toileting without escalation
why: The verified residual exceeds the explicit client-specific threshold despite a measured void and partial symptom relief.
Additional intake and waiting do not address retained urine that already meets the agreed escalation criterion.
Passing urine does not negate a verified high residual, so routine delayed reassessment would not follow the plan.
Subjective relief is useful, but it does not establish adequate emptying when the objective threshold is exceeded.
takeaway: Apply an individualized residual-volume threshold despite partial symptom relief after voiding.
learningObjective: Apply an individualized residual-volume threshold despite partial symptom relief after voiding.

title: Nutrition surveillance quality
stem: A client’s nutritional risk appears to be worsening while peripheral oedema varies. Which longitudinal record would best support evaluation by the care team?
options: Daily weights from different scales, supplement volumes supplied and the meals most often requested
Weekly bed weights, tray percentages served and a list of foods the client usually avoids at home
Current weight, daily oedema grades and the number of scheduled dietitian visits completed
Comparable weights with oedema noted, measured intake and current barriers to eating over time
why: Noncomparable weights and supplied rather than consumed supplements can misrepresent change.
Served food is not actual intake, and historical avoidance may not identify the present eating barrier.
Oedema matters, but one weight and completed appointments do not show the intake and weight trajectory.
Comparable measurements, fluid context and actual intake help distinguish tissue loss, fluid effects and modifiable barriers.
takeaway: Track comparable measurements and actual intake when reviewing nutritional risk.
learningObjective: Track comparable measurements and actual intake when reviewing nutritional risk.

title: Device-pressure response
stem: An oxygen interface is refitted after pressure-related tenderness. Which reassessment best shows tissue improvement while maintaining the prescribed treatment?
options: Tenderness is unchanged, the skin remains intact and saturation stays within the individual target
Tenderness is reduced, the skin remains intact and saturation falls below the individual target
Tenderness is reduced, the skin remains intact and saturation stays within the individual target
Redness is reduced, pressure pain increases and saturation stays within the individual target
why: Oxygenation is maintained, but persistent tenderness does not establish improvement of the pressure problem.
Tissue comfort improves, but the lower saturation suggests the refit may compromise treatment delivery.
This combines improving tissue tolerance with continuing effective prescribed oxygen support.
Less visible redness does not outweigh increasing pressure pain, which requires further assessment.
takeaway: Evaluate device adjustments for both tissue benefit and maintained function.
learningObjective: Evaluate device adjustments for both tissue benefit and maintained function.

title: Risk teaching transfer
stem: A client correctly recalls postprocedure warning signs but cannot identify whom to contact after hours. Which teaching action best addresses the remaining gap?
options: Review each warning sign again and ask the client to name the signs from memory
Rehearse an after-hours symptom scenario and have the client demonstrate how to obtain help
Arrange an earlier routine follow-up appointment and repeat the appointment details
Provide another written information sheet and ask the client to read it before going home
why: The signs are already recalled; repeating them does not establish the route for obtaining help.
A practical scenario checks whether the client can find and use an accessible contact route when a warning occurs.
Earlier planned follow-up does not solve access to urgent advice outside office hours.
Another leaflet may help, but demonstrated use is needed to verify the identified application gap.
takeaway: Evaluate whether teaching can be used to obtain help, not merely recalled.
learningObjective: Evaluate whether teaching can be used to obtain help, not merely recalled.

title: Functional recovery after sedation
stem: Before colonoscopy with sedation, a client walks independently with a cane. In recovery they are alert, vital signs are stable and pain is controlled, but they still need two people to steady them while walking. What follow-up plan best addresses the remaining risk?
options: Continue supervised recovery and reassess walking against baseline before confirming discharge readiness
Use a wheelchair for departure and have the accompanying adult provide the usual help at home
Provide a walker in place of the cane and rely on the adult escort to supervise its first use
Base readiness on alertness and stable vital signs while advising extra rest after arrival home
why: The new assistance requirement shows incomplete functional recovery despite reassuring resting observations and requires reassessment.
A wheelchair may facilitate transport but does not establish safe transfers or walking once home.
Changing equipment without demonstrating safe use does not resolve the observed post-sedation instability.
Alertness and vital signs are necessary observations but do not address the demonstrated fall risk below baseline.
takeaway: Include functional recovery and safe mobility when evaluating discharge readiness after sedation.
learningObjective: Include functional recovery and safe mobility when evaluating discharge readiness after sedation.
